file: 2001/2001-12-30_hand writing_answer questions_return calls_i'll be away_bad odor_windy_phantom_monkeys_duct tape.gif
title: Unreadable Handwriting From Unreachable Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, take care of this. It's urgent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't read your hand-writing. What does it say?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have time to answer your questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't try to call me. I don't return calls.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you come to my office I'll be away.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And then, like a bad odor on a windy day, the Phantom Manager vanished.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think it says, "Floog smort qlak munta hawthnort."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does it mean?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think it involves monkeys and duct tape.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert an urgent note, then refuses every way Dilbert could get clarification: no questions, no phone calls, no visits to his office. After the boss disappears, Dilbert asks Alice to decipher the illegible handwriting, and she guesses at nonsense words.
punchline: The boss makes an urgent task impossible by being both illegible and unreachable, so the staff are left guessing, and the best interpretation is absurd gibberish involving monkeys and duct tape.
summary: A manager leaves a scrawled urgent note and makes himself impossible to contact, leaving his employees to decode nonsense on their own.

file: 2001/2001-10-17_stock market expert_buy stock_sell house_track record_one week chart_buy buy.gif
title: Dogbert's Absurd Stock Tip Works

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Stock market expert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...Everyone should buy stock in that company. Sell your house if necessary.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Should we worry that the P/E is 900, your track record is terrible and you only recommend stocks you own?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, Ron, as you can see from the one-week chart, this stock only goes up.

transcript.speaker: Man on phone
transcript.text: Buy! Buy!

setting: A television financial news studio, with a viewer watching at a desk
situation: Dogbert, appearing as a stock market expert on a TV program, urges everyone to buy a stock, even if they must sell their house. The host points out the sky-high P/E ratio, his terrible track record, and that he only recommends stocks he owns. Dogbert dismisses all of it by pointing to a one-week chart, while a viewer on the phone frantically orders his broker to buy.
punchline: Dogbert brushes off every legitimate red flag by citing a meaninglessly short chart, and gullible investors immediately rush to buy anyway, pumping up the stock he owns.
summary: A canine market guru shrugs off pointed questions about his dubious record by waving at a short-term chart, and a credulous viewer starts buying at once.

file: 2001/2001-02-11_nephew_job interview_bowling_heavy balls_work_experince_taught_snack bar_whacked_new boss.gif
title: Interviewing the Boss's Bowling Nephew

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Boss
transcript.text: My nephew wants a job. Interview him and tell me what you think.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see... your work experience is... bowling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you a professional bowler?

transcript.speaker: Nephew
transcript.text: I only bowled once.

transcript.speaker: Nephew
transcript.text: But the balls were heavy. It seemed like work to me.

transcript.speaker: Nephew
transcript.text: That experience taught me everything I know.

transcript.speaker: Nephew
transcript.text: Unfortunately, I don't remember most of it.

transcript.speaker: Nephew
transcript.text: But I remember you're not supposed to bowl in the snack bar.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recommend having him whacked.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: He's your new boss.

situation: The boss asks Dilbert to interview his nephew, who wants a job. The nephew's only work experience is having bowled once, and his answers show he is clueless and forgetful. Dilbert recommends having him whacked, only to learn the nephew is about to become his new boss.
punchline: Dilbert's blunt recommendation to eliminate the incompetent candidate backfires when he learns nepotism has already made the nephew his boss.
summary: A manager's unqualified relative bumbles through an interview, and the evaluator's harsh verdict comes too late because the hire is already his superior.

file: 2001/2001-08-30_all night_comp day_security video_pile of debris_cucbicle_conversation_jumping all over.gif
title: Security Video Contradicts Comp Day Request

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I was here all night. Is it okay if I take tomorrow as a comp day?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to our security video you slept all night on a pile of debris in your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it just me or is this conversation jumping all over the place?

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks the Boss for a comp day because he claims to have worked all night. The Boss points out that security video shows Wally actually slept the whole night on a pile of debris in his cubicle. Wally ignores the accusation and complains that the conversation is jumping around.
punchline: Caught lying about working overnight, Wally deflects by pretending the Boss is the one making the conversation incoherent.
summary: A slacker employee seeking time off for supposed overtime is busted by surveillance footage and simply changes the subject.

file: 2001/2001-06-20_5 dollars per night_mini bar_motion detector_three hundred_charged near it_long night.gif
title: Motion-Detecting Mini-Bar Hotel Trap

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: The room costs five dollars per night.

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: The mini-bar has a motion detector; you'll be charged three hundred dollars every time you get within eight feet of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's going to be a long night.

setting: Hotel front desk, then a hotel room
situation: Dilbert checks into a hotel and is told the room costs only five dollars a night. The clerk then reveals the mini-bar has a motion detector that bills him three hundred dollars each time he comes within eight feet of it. In the hotel room, Dilbert sits rigidly on the far side of the bed, as far from the mini-bar as possible.
punchline: The suspiciously cheap room is a trap, since the hidden mini-bar fees make it far more expensive than it first appears, and Dilbert must stay motionless all night to avoid them.
summary: A bargain hotel rate turns out to hide a booby-trapped refreshment cabinet that bills a fortune for simply walking nearby.

file: 2001/2001-09-11_better job_cubicle 45750r_magic portal_round of layoffs_six months_911 inside job.gif
title: The Magic Portal Is Layoffs

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm being moved to the Magic Portal, cubicle 4S750R!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Everyone who sits in the Magic Portal gets a better job within six months!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There isn't a cubicle 4S750R, is there?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The first round of layoffs are always the cruelest.

situation: A cheerful coworker carrying a box of his belongings announces he is being moved to a special cubicle called the Magic Portal, and that everyone who sits there gets a better job within six months. Wally and Dilbert, holding coffee mugs, suspect something is off. Wally asks if the cubicle even exists, and Dilbert implies it is really a layoff.
punchline: The 'Magic Portal' is a euphemism for being laid off, and the cubicle number is fake, so the promised better job is simply unemployment.
summary: A hopeful employee carries his box to a mythical cubicle that supposedly leads to promotion, while his colleagues realize he has actually been fired.

file: 2001/2001-10-12_anne l. retentive_task_deliverable_task not verb_falling apart_timeline project.gif
title: Boss Misuses Jargon to Torment Grammarian

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anne, I'm going to task you with a deliverable.

transcript.speaker: Anne L. Retentive
transcript.text: Gaaa!! Task is not a verb!! My world is falling apart!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask her to timeline her project.

situation: The Boss tells an employee named Anne that he is going to 'task' her with a 'deliverable.' Anne, a stickler for grammar, is horrified that 'task' is being used as a verb and nearly has a breakdown. The Boss, pleased with her reaction, plans to torment her further the next day with another noun-turned-verb.
punchline: The Boss realizes he can deliberately torture the grammar-obsessed Anne by misusing business jargon, and gleefully plans to ask her to 'timeline' her project tomorrow.
summary: A manager discovers that turning nouns into verbs sends a pedantic coworker into a meltdown, so he plans to keep doing it on purpose.

file: 2001/2001-04-23_weekly wally report_stock options_maple_someone lost more.gif
title: Wally's Stock Options Consolation Report

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now for the weekly Wally report.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wally struggled to maintain his morale despite the ninety percent drop in his stock options.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then he remembered that someone lost much, much, much more than he did.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: Wally gives his weekly report to the team in the third person, describing how he is coping with a ninety percent crash in the value of his stock options. He cheers himself up by remembering that someone else lost far more than he did. The Boss, seated at the table, reacts with a smug expression.
punchline: Wally takes comfort in the fact that the Boss, who presumably held far more company stock, lost much more than he did, a bit of schadenfreude at management's expense.
summary: Narrating his own report in third person, Wally finds solace in his collapsed stock options by gloating that his boss is losing far more.

file: 2001/2001-06-27_meeting to discuss_employee retention_employees quit_useless meetings_reasons_first meetings.gif
title: Retention Meeting Won't Discuss Reasons

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're having a meeting to discuss employee retention.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell them that employees quit because there are too many useless meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We won't be getting into reasons at the first meeting.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a meeting will be held to discuss employee retention. Dilbert suggests the message to give the attendees: people quit because there are too many useless meetings. The Boss dismisses this, saying the first meeting won't cover reasons.
punchline: The company plans to address employees quitting over useless meetings by holding yet another meeting, one that deliberately avoids discussing the actual cause.
summary: A manager schedules a gathering to tackle staff turnover but refuses to examine why people are leaving, even when the cause is pointed out.

file: 2001/2001-07-29_power supply_product overheats_burst into flames_level city_military application_costs_ten million_free hammer_consulting job_uninhabited_atoll.gif
title: Overheating Power Supply Sold to Military

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The power supply in our product overheats.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I think they might burst into flames.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: I'm no engineer but obviously it could level a whole city.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: The military application is obvious.

transcript.speaker: General
transcript.text: How much do they cost?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: Does ten million dollars sound like too much?

transcript.speaker: General
transcript.text: For that kind of money I expect a free hammer!

transcript.speaker: General
transcript.text: And a consulting job when I retire.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If an uninhabited atoll doesn't blow up tomorrow you're in big trouble.

setting: Conference room and office at Dilbert's company
situation: Dilbert reports that his product's power supply overheats and could burst into flames. Instead of fixing it, the marketing staff pitch the dangerous defect to a military general as a weapon for ten million dollars. The general agrees, and the Boss then orders Dilbert to make sure a demonstration blows up an uninhabited atoll.
punchline: A serious product defect is reframed as a feature, sold as a weapon to a general who only wants a free hammer and a post-retirement consulting job, and the Boss threatens Dilbert to make the explosion happen on demand.
summary: A flaw that could incinerate a city gets repackaged by sales as a military selling point, and the engineer is left to guarantee the explosion.

file: 2001/2001-03-19_reduce staff_almost worked to death_ted.gif
title: Layoff List of Overworked Employees

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We need to reduce staff by twenty.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Here's a list of the people you've A-L-M-O-S-T worked to death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have another project for you ...uh...Ted.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Aack!

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells the Boss that twenty staff must be cut. He hands over a list of employees the Boss has nearly worked to death, spelling out the word 'almost' to make the point. The Boss then consults the list and assigns yet another project to Ted, who panics.
punchline: The list of nearly-dead overworked employees is treated by the Boss as a list of people to give more work to, so the layoffs become literal death-by-workload and Ted is next.
summary: The HR cat produces a roster of near-casualties of the Boss's overwork, and the Boss promptly uses it to pick his next victim.

file: 2001/2001-01-24_discount brokerage_open an account_money eveaporates_photo synthesis_yes haw.gif
title: Brokerage Quiz Requires Wrong Answer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Discount Brokerage

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can only open an account if you meet my stringent requirements.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: True or false: Money evaporates because of photosynthesis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: True?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't yell yee-haw!

setting: Dogbert's desk at a discount brokerage office
situation: Dogbert, running a discount brokerage, tells Dilbert he must meet stringent requirements to open an account. He asks a nonsensical true-or-false question claiming money evaporates because of photosynthesis, and Dilbert guesses 'True?'. Dogbert immediately accepts him, and Dilbert privately thinks about not shouting 'yee-haw' in celebration.
punchline: The only requirement for opening an account is giving a wrong, gullible answer, implying the brokerage wants clueless customers whose money it can easily take.
summary: A canine broker screens a would-be investor with a nonsense quiz and welcomes him only after he answers incorrectly.

file: 2001/2001-05-16_accepting bribes_vendor_golf lessons_trip to veags_price sheets.gif
title: Boss Condemns Bribes, Then Compares Perks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, you can't keep accepting bribes from sales people who want access to me.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Bad!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Didn't a vendor recently take you on a golf trip to Vegas?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That is so-o-o different!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Let's compare price sheets.

situation: The Boss scolds his assistant Carol for accepting bribes from salespeople who want access to him, while Catbert scolds her too. Carol points out that a vendor recently took the Boss on a golf trip to Vegas. The Boss insists it is completely different, so Carol suggests they compare the value of their respective perks.
punchline: The Boss condemns Carol's bribes while ignoring that he accepts far bigger ones himself, and Carol sarcastically proposes comparing price sheets to see who got the better deal.
summary: A manager lectures his assistant about taking gifts from salespeople, only to be reminded that he enjoyed a lavish vendor-funded getaway himself.

file: 2001/2001-12-10_innovative design firm_observe methods_steal from them_secret_hiring smart people_involves easles.gif
title: Stealing Innovation From Design Firm

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've hired the world's most innovative design firm.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll observe their successful methods and steal them for our own. Heh heh heh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe their secret is hiring smart people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm hoping it involves easels.

situation: The Boss announces to the team that he has hired a famously innovative design firm so the company can observe and copy its methods. Dilbert suggests the firm's secret may simply be hiring smart people. The Boss ignores the point and says he hopes the secret involves easels.
punchline: The Boss cannot grasp that innovation comes from talented people, and hopes instead that a cheap, superficial prop like easels is the key to their success.
summary: A manager plans to copy an elite design consultancy's techniques, dismissing the idea that its edge is talent and hoping the trick is a piece of equipment.

file: 2001/2001-04-15_most valuable asset_rampant ignorance_really cost_better jobs_across the street_don't know bugs_wearing trash cans_accidental exposure_consultant_business.gif
title: Consultant Sells Ignorance and Trash Cans

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What is your most valuable asset?

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: Employees?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hee!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your most valuable asset is rampant ignorance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, you would never start a project if you knew how much it would really cost.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Employees stay here because they don't know there are better jobs across the street.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Customers buy your products because they don't know about all the bugs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good point.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend wearing trash cans on your heads to avoid any accidental exposure to knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Man with trash can on head
transcript.text: Did he tell you he was a consultant?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He said he was selling trash cans.

setting: Conference room during a consulting presentation
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells a table of managers that their most valuable asset is rampant ignorance, listing how their projects, employees and customers all depend on people not knowing the truth. He then recommends they wear trash cans on their heads to avoid accidental exposure to knowledge. In the last panel the managers walk around with trash cans on their heads, having bought into the pitch.
punchline: The consultant's real scheme was to sell trash cans, and the managers were ignorant enough to fall for a pitch that proved his point.
summary: A canine advisor convinces executives that not knowing things is their greatest strength, then profits by selling them headgear to keep it that way.

file: 2001/2001-06-12_leave work_boss harrassment_work is done_make more_exercise in fulity_exercise is good.gif
title: Exercise in Futility Is Good

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leaving at seven?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of my work is done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then get some more work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would make my life an exercise in futility.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exercise is good for you.

setting: Office hallway near Dilbert's cubicle at the end of the workday
situation: The Boss checks his watch and questions Dilbert about leaving at seven. Dilbert says all his work is finished, and the Boss tells him to go get more work. When Dilbert complains that finishing work only to be handed more would be futile, the Boss twists his words into a fitness reference.
punchline: The Boss willfully misreads 'exercise in futility' as a literal endorsement of exercise, dismissing Dilbert's complaint that finishing work only earns him more work.
summary: A manager refuses to let a finished employee go home and brushes off his protest about endless work with a cheerful non-sequitur.

file: 2001/2001-03-15_billion shares_dot com subsidary_fire everyone_presdient_raise_stock_promoting.gif
title: Promoted to Fire Everyone for Stock

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm promoting you to president of our dot-com subsidiary.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your job is to fire everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would I get a raise?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How does a billion shares of stock sound?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being promoted to president of the company's dot-com subsidiary, then reveals the job is to fire everyone there. Dilbert asks about a raise and the Boss offers him a billion shares of stock instead of money.
punchline: The offered billion shares are worthless in the collapsing dot-com bubble, so the 'compensation' is a way to avoid paying real money for an unpleasant job.
summary: A manager hands Dilbert a grand title that really means laying off an entire failing internet division, and sweetens it with stock that is obviously worthless.

file: 2001/2001-06-04_work ratio_one in eight_talking about work_count as wrok.gif
title: Work-to-Gabbing Ratio at the Coffee Break

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's the lowest ratio of work-to-gabbing that is still considered "work"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd have to say one-in-eight, maybe one-in-nine.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sounds right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does talking about work count as work?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well... I'm not enjoying it.

setting: Office break area, with coffee mugs in hand
situation: Dilbert and a balding coworker stand around holding coffee mugs while the coworker asks how little actual work can be mixed into idle chatter and still be called work. Dilbert estimates one part work to eight or nine parts gabbing. Dilbert then asks whether talking about work counts as work, and the coworker judges it by whether he is enjoying it.
punchline: The coworker's test for whether talking about work counts as work is whether it's unpleasant, implying that work is defined by misery rather than productivity.
summary: Two colleagues over coffee casually calculate how much chatter can pass as labor and end up defining work by how much they dislike it.

file: 2001/2001-05-05_rebooting computer_kicks computer_roof top_feel better.gif
title: Tech Support Reboots Computer Violently

transcript.speaker: Tech support woman (on phone)
transcript.text: Try rebooting your computer.

transcript.speaker: Tech support woman (on phone)
transcript.text: Thanks. I feel much better.

setting: Tech support desk, then a rooftop
situation: A tech support worker with big hair tells a caller over the phone to try rebooting their computer. In the next panel she is on a rooftop kicking a computer off the edge of the building. Back on the phone, she thanks the caller and says she feels much better.
punchline: The tech support worker takes out her frustration with endless clueless callers by literally booting a computer off a roof, twisting the word 'reboot' into a violent stress release.
summary: A weary help desk employee gives stock advice to a caller, then vents her frustration by punting a computer off a skyscraper.

file: 2001/2001-10-25_tour of accounting_random number geneartor_randomness.gif
title: Accounting's Random Number Generator Monster

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tour of Accounting

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Over here we have our random number generator.

transcript.speaker: Random Number Generator
transcript.text: Nine nine nine nine nine nine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sure that's random?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: That's the problem with randomness: you can never be sure.

situation: A guide shows Dilbert around accounting and introduces the department's random number generator, which is a horned creature sitting on a rock. The creature repeatedly outputs the number nine, and Dilbert questions whether that's truly random. The guide responds that randomness can never be verified.
punchline: The generator spitting out only nines is clearly not random, but the guide dismisses the doubt with a pseudo-philosophical excuse that you can never be sure about randomness.
summary: A tour of accounting reveals a random number generator that only says nine, and the guide shrugs off any suspicion.

file: 2001/2001-01-20_exactly man_said in meeting_wong_proof_humanoid response.gif
title: The Exactly Man Agrees Automatically

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The "Exactly" Man

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Everything you said in the meeting was wrong. Here's the proof.

transcript.speaker: Exactly Man
transcript.text: Exactly!!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Okay, I'm not even sure that was a humanoid response.

situation: Tina, the big-haired engineer, holds up a paper and tells a seated coworker that everything he said in the meeting was wrong. The coworker, the "Exactly" Man, springs up and cheerfully shouts "Exactly!!" as if agreeing with her. Tina is baffled by the reflexive response and questions whether it was even human.
punchline: The Exactly Man's habit of enthusiastically agreeing with everything is so automatic that he agrees with being told he was wrong, making him seem robotic.
summary: A coworker who reflexively agrees with everyone cheerfully endorses a colleague's accusation that he was entirely mistaken.

file: 2001/2001-03-26_job interview_advice_juggling_items_confident_desk items.gif
title: Dogbert's Disastrous Interview Juggling Advice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any advice for my job interview?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try juggling the items on his desk. It will make you seem confident.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry.

setting: Dilbert's home, then the interviewer's office
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for tips before a job interview. Dogbert advises him to juggle the items on the interviewer's desk to look confident. Dilbert follows the advice, and the interviewer ends up slumped unconscious in his chair while Dilbert holds a stapler and a box.
punchline: Dogbert's bad advice backfires: juggling the desk items has apparently knocked out the interviewer, so Dilbert can only apologize.
summary: Following his dog's absurd coaching, a job candidate turns an interview into an accident that leaves the interviewer out cold.

file: 2001/2001-06-08_travel request_apporved_otherwise_being useless_olympic sport.gif
title: Useless Boss Should Be Olympic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you look at my travel request?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not yet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Assume it's approved unless I tell you otherwise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's too bad that being useless isn't an Olympic sport.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dilbert standing in front of his desk
situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether he has reviewed his travel request. The boss hasn't looked at it and tells Dilbert to simply assume it's approved unless told otherwise. Dilbert replies that it's a shame uselessness isn't an Olympic event, implying the boss would win gold.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically suggests his boss would be an Olympic champion at being useless, since he can't even be bothered to review a simple request.
summary: A manager who ignores an employee's paperwork gets mocked as a would-be medalist in uselessness.

file: 2001/2001-08-21_dating attractive men_dumb self centered_intelligent homely guy_gym_free weights_girl talk_dilbert_women.gif
title: Amber Warns Against Homely Guy

transcript.speaker: Amber's friend
transcript.text: I'm tired of dating attractive men who are dumb and self-centered.

transcript.speaker: Amber's friend
transcript.text: Maybe I can find an intelligent homely guy and clean him up.

transcript.speaker: Amber
transcript.text: No!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I work in a set with those five-pounders?

transcript.speaker: Amber
transcript.text: Don't do it, Amber!

setting: A gym with free weights and exercise equipment
situation: Two women at a gym talk about being tired of dating dumb, self-centered attractive men. One suggests finding an intelligent homely guy and cleaning him up, which alarms her friend Amber. Dilbert then walks up, towel around his neck, and asks to share their light weights, making him the obvious candidate.
punchline: Right after the woman considers dating an intelligent but homely man, Dilbert appears, and Amber's panicked plea implies he is exactly the unattractive guy she'd be settling for.
summary: A woman contemplating a makeover project in the form of a smart but unattractive boyfriend is interrupted by Dilbert asking to use the small dumbbells.

file: 2001/2001-06-14_new things to say_fill airtime_let other people talk.gif
title: Running Out of Things to Say

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'm running out of new things to say.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'll have to start repeating myself just to fill the airtime.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could let other people talk.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: So, anyway, I'm running out of new things to say.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee mug tells Dilbert that he is running out of new things to say. He then announces that he will have to repeat himself to fill the airtime. Dilbert suggests he simply let other people talk, but the coworker ignores this and repeats his original complaint.
punchline: The talkative coworker is so incapable of listening that he responds to the suggestion of letting others speak by literally repeating himself, proving his own point.
summary: A chatterbox who fears running out of material dismisses the obvious fix and just recycles his own opening line.
keywords: running out of things to say

file: 2001/2001-10-30_circuit design_mention_didnt_psychic_conversation.gif
title: Dilbert Thinks Silence Is Psychic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I noticed that the circuit design looked like a bug. I was going to mention it but then I didn't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm psychic!

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Unless you're saying out loud every thought that crosses your mind.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: It's called conversation.

situation: Dilbert tells his date a story about noticing that a circuit design looked like a bug but deciding not to mention it. He then excitedly concludes that he must be psychic. His date points out that everyone's unspoken thoughts are private unless they actually say them aloud, which is simply conversation.
punchline: Dilbert mistakes the normal state of not voicing a thought for a psychic power, while his date sarcastically explains that sharing thoughts out loud is just ordinary conversation.
summary: A socially clueless engineer proudly claims mind-reading powers after failing to speak a thought, and his date deadpans that talking is how people share what they think.

file: 2001/2001-05-19_date_complain_all night_called a loser_personality_one thing_complaint_psychology.gif
title: Complaining About One Thing Only

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My date complained about her life all night long!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I complain about just one thing and she calls me a loser.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you complain about her personality?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's one thing!

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert sitting on the couch
situation: Dilbert vents to Dogbert about a bad date, griping that she complained about her entire life all night yet called him a loser for complaining about just one thing. Dogbert asks what that one complaint was, and Dilbert admits it was her personality.
punchline: Dilbert insists he only complained about one thing, not realizing that criticizing someone's entire personality is hardly a minor gripe, which explains why she called him a loser.
summary: After a disastrous date, Dilbert protests his own fairness until Dogbert reveals that his single complaint was aimed at her whole personality.

file: 2001/2001-01-17_ad agency_stick man_fire_gets eaten_exact science.gif
title: Stick Man Versus Giant Wolverine

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Ad Agency

transcript.speaker: Ad Agency Man
transcript.text: The stick man runs through a tire fire and gets eaten by a giant wolverine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will that make people like us?

transcript.speaker: Ad Agency Man
transcript.text: It's not an exact science.

setting: A conference room at an advertising agency
situation: An ad agency man presents a storyboard sketch of a stick man who runs through a tire fire and is eaten by a giant wolverine. The Boss, seated with Dilbert and another coworker, asks whether the ad will make people like the company. The presenter dodges the question by saying advertising is not an exact science.
punchline: The ad pitch is absurdly violent and unrelated to making anyone like the company, and the presenter hides the lack of any real marketing logic behind the vague claim that advertising is not an exact science.
summary: An advertising pitch featuring a doomed stick figure is excused as guesswork when the client asks if it will make customers fond of the company.

file: 2001/2001-08-20_drool_hydrogenerator_save energy_sleeping.gif
title: Harnessing Boss's Drool for Energy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Each of us must do his part to save energy.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: ZZZZZ

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could build a tiny hydro-generator for his drool.

situation: The Boss lectures his staff at a meeting about everyone doing their part to save energy. Meanwhile a coworker at the table has fallen asleep with his mouth hanging open. Dilbert points at the sleeping man and sarcastically proposes capturing his drool to generate power.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the boss's energy-saving speech by suggesting the sleeping coworker's drool could power a tiny hydroelectric generator, highlighting how boring the meeting is.
summary: A manager preaches conservation while an attendee snoozes through it, prompting a wisecracking engineer to propose turning the slumberer's saliva into electricity.

file: 2001/2001-04-06_high school reunion_whos incredible_point to name_gullible people.gif
title: Dilbert's Reunion Book Backfires on Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm bringing my copy of "Who's Incredible" to my high school reunion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If anyone asks how I'm doing, I'll casually open the book and point to my name.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I got rich selling a book called "Who's Incredible" to gullible people.

setting: Dilbert's home, then a high school reunion party
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he plans to bring his copy of the book "Who's Incredible" to his high school reunion and casually show off his listing in it. At the reunion, Dilbert stands holding the book among well-dressed classmates while a man in a blue suit boasts about how he got rich selling that very book to gullible people.
punchline: The book Dilbert hopes will prove he is impressive is a vanity directory sold to gullible people, so being listed in it proves nothing, as a wealthy classmate who profited from selling it points out.
summary: A man planning to flaunt his entry in a prestige directory learns at his reunion that its real achievement was making its publisher rich off the gullible.

file: 2001/2001-07-20_the sociopth_typing is optional_eaten before_some bread.gif
title: Never Tip Your Waiter Consequences

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Sociopath

transcript.speaker: Sociopath
transcript.text: Tipping is optional so I never do it.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Um... Have you eaten here before?

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: Here's some bread.

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: A man at a restaurant proudly tells his date that he never tips because tipping is optional. She nervously asks if he has eaten at this restaurant before. The waiter then throws a loaf of bread that hits the man in the head.
punchline: The waiter retaliates against the non-tipper by hurling bread at him, implying that the man's stinginess has been punished before and that his date foresaw the consequences.
summary: A cheapskate diner boasts about never leaving a gratuity and gets pelted with a flying bread roll by the waiter.

file: 2001/2001-11-25_acquired by foreign company_merger of equals_make money_combined company_giant_latent psychic abilities_pain from distance.gif
title: Merger of Equals With Psychic Giants

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm happy to announce that we're being acquired by a foreign company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry that they'll dominate us. This will be a merger of equals.

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Merger of equals

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Except that they make money and we don't.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And their CEO will lead the combined company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And every one of them is a giant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And they've developed their latent psychic abilities so they can cause pain from a distance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gaaa!! I'm sorry I said too much! You are my master!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you worried?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nah. If they read my mind, they'll all go blind.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his employees that the company is being acquired by a foreign firm and insists it is a merger of equals, then keeps listing facts that contradict that claim. After he mentions the acquirers' psychic powers, he clutches his head in pain and grovels to them. Dilbert asks Wally if he is worried, and Wally answers with a crude joke about his own thoughts.
punchline: The supposed 'merger of equals' is plainly a one-sided takeover, and the boss's pained surrender shows how powerless his own side is; Wally's reply jokes that his mind is so unpleasant that it would harm any psychic who read it.
summary: A manager's reassurance that a takeover is an even partnership collapses as he admits the buyers are richer, bigger, in charge, and able to hurt him telepathically.

file: 2001/2001-03-09_die from shame_loss_throw it_window repair business_honest vendor.gif
title: The Honest Vendor's Terrible Product

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Honest Vendor

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Five minutes after you buy it you'll want to throw it through a window.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: We sell these at a loss but we make it up with our window repair business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It fell off.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Sometimes the components actually die from shame.

situation: A candid vendor pitches a hardware gadget to Dilbert while Dilbert examines it. The vendor admits the product is so frustrating that buyers will want to throw it through a window, and that the company profits from window repairs. When a part falls off in Dilbert's hands, the vendor says components sometimes die from shame.
punchline: The vendor's brutal honesty about his shoddy product, including a business model that profits from customers' rage, makes the sales pitch a self-inflicted disaster.
summary: A salesman cheerfully confesses that his flimsy gadget will drive buyers to smash windows, and that this is where his firm's real profit lies.

file: 2001/2001-09-27_illegal to clone humans_frame clone_for crime_same thing to me_immoral.gif
title: Framing the Boss's Clone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, the technology to clone you exists, but it's illegal to clone humans.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If the cops find out, we can frame my clone for the crime.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is so wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why? He'd do the same thing to me!

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that human cloning technology exists but is illegal. The Boss cheerfully proposes blaming his own clone if the police find out. When Dilbert objects that it's wrong, the Boss justifies it by saying the clone would do the same to him.
punchline: The Boss assumes his clone would be just as unscrupulous as he is, so framing him is treated as fair play.
summary: A manager plans to pin his own illegal duplicate for the crime, reasoning that the copy would betray him just the same.

file: 2001/2001-02-13_boss_sneaking up on_computer_walk past_muscles cramping_technology.gif
title: Small Font Hides Slacking From Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that work? I can't see what's on the screen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If he sees me I'll pretend I'm in mid-stride, just passing by.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The small font is working.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Muscles cramping.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good.

situation: The Boss leans precariously over a cubicle wall trying to see whether Dilbert is working or goofing off, but cannot read the screen. Dilbert holds a frozen mid-stride pose with one leg stretched out over the cubicle partition, ready to pretend he was just walking by. Wally phones in to report that the small font trick is working, while Dilbert's muscles cramp from holding the pose.
punchline: Dilbert goes to absurd physical lengths to maintain a fake alibi of 'just passing by' because his tiny screen font prevents the boss from telling whether he is working, so avoiding work becomes more exhausting than working.
summary: A boss strains to spy on an employee's screen while the employee holds a ridiculous frozen pose to fake innocence.

file: 2001/2001-12-26_need approval_equipment_installed.gif
title: Approving Expenses Without Understanding Them

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your approval for this expense. The equipment is already here and installed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I left out the description because you wouldn't understand it anyway.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's a fine line between managing and being totally useless.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Luckily it looks the same.

situation: Dilbert brings the Boss an expense form for equipment that has already been purchased and installed, and asks for approval after the fact. He admits he left off the description because the Boss wouldn't understand it anyway, and the Boss signs without objection. The Boss muses about the fine line between managing and being useless, and Catbert remarks that the two look the same.
punchline: Catbert points out that a manager rubber-stamping things he doesn't understand looks exactly like a useless one, so nobody can tell the difference.
summary: A boss blindly signs off on an after-the-fact purchase he can't comprehend and wonders about the line between managing and uselessness, only to be told the two are indistinguishable.

file: 2001/2001-04-12_pristine beauty_elbonia_see first_protestors_stop drilling signs_protesting drilling_beauty_health.gif
title: Protesters Shown Picture of Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Protester
transcript.text: You're ruining the pristine beauty of Elbonia!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is a picture of pristine Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Protester
transcript.text: ...And then you said, "It doesn't matter if we see it first." Then I said...

setting: Outdoors in Elbonia, on a street near a building and a parked car
situation: Protesters carrying 'Stop Drilling' signs accuse the Boss of ruining the pristine beauty of Elbonia as he walks past with a briefcase. The Boss simply holds up a photo of a lone bare tree and says it shows pristine Elbonia. In the last panel, the protesters have moved on to chatting about an unrelated argument while one of them works under the hood of a car, their protest forgotten.
punchline: The Boss placates the activists with a picture of the land's supposed beauty, and they lose interest in the cause almost instantly, showing how shallow and easily distracted their protest is.
summary: Demonstrators outraged about environmental damage are brushed off with a single photograph and soon drift into gossiping about their own squabbles.

file: 2001/2001-01-15_ad agency_creative team_peter peters_robert roberts_holly hollister.gif
title: Creative Team Has No Wit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you to meet our ad agency's creative team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pete Peters, Robert Roberts, and Holly Hollister.

transcript.speaker: Creative Team Member
transcript.text: Witty remark, anyone?

transcript.speaker: Creative Team Member
transcript.text: I've got nothing.

situation: The Boss introduces the ad agency's creative team to the staff gathered around a conference table. The three agency people have repetitive names, and when one of them asks the group for a witty remark, another admits he has nothing.
punchline: The supposedly creative ad agency team can't come up with a single witty remark, even though their names are lazy repeats and creativity is what the company is paying them for.
summary: A boss presents an ad agency's three-person creative team, who immediately show they have no clever ideas to offer.

file: 2001/2001-01-19_exactly man_sell ten million_idea won't work_idea makes better.gif
title: The Exactly Man Agrees Contradictorily

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The "Exactly" Man

transcript.speaker: Exactly Man
transcript.text: Your idea won't work. No one would buy this kind of product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We already sell ten million of these per year. My idea just makes them better.

transcript.speaker: Exactly Man
transcript.text: Exactly!!

situation: A co-worker known as the Exactly Man tells Dilbert that his idea will fail because nobody would buy this kind of product. Dilbert points out that the company already sells ten million of them a year and his idea only improves them. The Exactly Man cheerfully responds 'Exactly!' as if he had been agreeing all along, leaving Dilbert baffled.
punchline: The Exactly Man reflexively says 'Exactly!' to whatever is said last, even when it flatly contradicts his own argument, showing he never actually listens or holds a consistent position.
summary: A colleague who agrees with everything dismisses an idea and then enthusiastically agrees with the rebuttal that proves him wrong.

file: 2001/2001-01-12_motivation fairy_rewarding_blurry vision_long hors_no raises_no cubicle_hair coming out_wally fairy.gif
title: Motivation Fairy Demotivates Employee Completely

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Motivation Fairy

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It seems like your job isn't very rewarding.

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: Vision getting blurry.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Long hours. No raises. No cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: Hair coming out in clumps.

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: He's good. He's very good.

situation: Wally sits at a desk and tells the Motivation Fairy, who is perched on his monitor, that his job isn't very rewarding. As Wally lists his grievances (long hours, no raises, no cubicle), the fairy grows visibly distressed, with blurry vision and hair falling out. The fairy flies away, impressed by how thoroughly Wally has demotivated him.
punchline: The fairy who is supposed to motivate employees is instead demoralized by Wally's litany of workplace misery, and ends up admiring Wally's skill at being demotivating.
summary: A fairy sent to inspire a worker instead gets crushed by the worker's bleak description of his job and flees, grudgingly impressed.

file: 2001/2001-11-30_think aloud_cost_monkeys_swallow tongue_distarctions_stream of consciousness.gif
title: Thinking Aloud Backfires Badly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, let me think aloud for a minute.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The cost will be $3,000... losing focus... monkeys are funny... my tongue is digesting in my mouth.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That didn't help as much as I had hoped.

situation: The Boss, holding a sheet of paper, announces he will think aloud while Dilbert sits silently across the desk. His stream of consciousness starts with a budget figure but quickly degenerates into random, absurd thoughts about monkeys and his tongue. He then admits the exercise did not help much.
punchline: Speaking your thoughts aloud only exposes how scattered and nonsensical the boss's thinking really is, so it produces no useful decision.
summary: A manager tries verbalizing his reasoning for a coworker, only to ramble through one costly figure and several random nonsense thoughts before conceding the technique failed.

file: 2001/2001-11-09_town hall meeting_improve communication_actual town hall.gif
title: Town Hall Meeting With Rigged Questions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to have a "town hall" meeting to improve communication.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But it's not in an actual town hall. And I'll have questions in advance, so it's not a meeting per se.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Who do we give our questions to?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think you'll find that it doesn't matter.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces a "town hall" meeting meant to improve communication, then admits it won't be held in a real town hall and that he will collect the questions beforehand. When a coworker asks who should receive their questions, the Boss says it won't matter, implying the questions will not influence anything.
punchline: The supposed communication-improving meeting is a sham, since employees' questions will be ignored no matter who they submit them to.
summary: A manager touts a communication-boosting gathering that turns out to be a staged event where nobody's input counts.

file: 2001/2001-10-29_talking clock_after midnight_talking alarm.gif
title: Boss's Phone Insults Him at 3:14

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My home phone turns into a talking clock after midnight.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, I didn't believe it either until Wally taught me how to use it.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: It's 3:14 in the morning you #%@^&!* idiot!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yup.

setting: Office cubicle, then the Boss's bedroom at night
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his home phone mysteriously becomes a talking clock after midnight, and says Wally showed him how to use it. In the last panel, the Boss sits in his bathrobe at 3:14 a.m. as the phone announces the time while cursing and calling him an idiot. He happily thinks 'Yup.'
punchline: Wally has secretly rigged the Boss's phone to abuse him at night, and the Boss is too clueless to realize he is being insulted, accepting it as a feature.
summary: A gullible manager proudly shows off a late-night phone feature that is really a prank that berates him every time he calls.

file: 2001/2001-10-20_layoffs_odor_dna_rodents_snakes_weasels_never mind.gif
title: Layoff Q&A Insults Pre-Empted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll take one more question about the layoffs... Yes, you in the back.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I'd appreciate it if this question didn't involve my odor, my DNA, or any comparisons to rodents, snakes or weasels.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Never mind.

setting: Company auditorium during a layoff announcement
situation: The Boss stands at a podium with a microphone, taking questions from employees about upcoming layoffs. He calls on someone in the back but first rules out insulting questions about his smell, genes, or resemblance to vermin. The employee who was about to ask drops the question, having apparently planned exactly those insults.
punchline: The Boss's long list of banned insults reveals that he knows employees see him as a rodent-like weasel, and it leaves the questioner with nothing else to ask.
summary: A manager fielding layoff questions forbids a list of personal insults, and the staffer in the back gives up because that was the whole question.

file: 2001/2001-04-07_own cubicle_highschool reunion_adults_more specific.gif
title: Dilbert's Vague Reunion Proposition

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: High school reunion

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I started with nothing. Now I have my own cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Say, now that we're both adults, would you like to... you know?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got to be more specific.

situation: Dilbert brags to a woman at his high school reunion that he now has his own cubicle, then awkwardly asks if she would like to 'you know' now that they are adults. She says yes to his vague proposition, and he realizes in a thought bubble that his wording is too unclear.
punchline: Dilbert is so socially inept that even when someone agrees to his proposition, he realizes he never actually said what he was proposing and must clarify.
summary: An awkward engineer at a class reunion gets a yes to a proposal so vague he has to rethink his pitch.

file: 2001/2001-02-05_cockeyed_creepy guy_fail_good work_hired creep_products features_cape_cane.gif
title: Boss Hires Creep for Product Features

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a creep to help determine our product's features.

transcript.speaker: Creep
transcript.text: You need more features.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When can you have that done?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!

situation: The Boss introduces a strange, hunched man in a cape and cane whom he has hired as a creep to help decide a product's features. The creep's only advice is that the product needs more features, and the Boss praises him for it. The Boss then asks Dilbert, the engineer, when he can deliver all of it, and Dilbert screams in despair.
punchline: The hired expert provides vague, useless advice that merely adds more work, and the Boss takes it as brilliant insight while the engineer is left to implement it.
summary: A manager lauds a bizarre consultant's obvious suggestion to add more features, then dumps the resulting workload on a horrified engineer.
keywords: when can you have that done

file: 2001/2001-03-04_incompetent vp_fired_fvaor_laugh_resignation_announcement_terse_incompetence_ambiguaous_meaning.gif
title: Catbert Fires Fred, Terse Announcement

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Fred, you're an incompetent VP.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're fired.

transcript.speaker: Fred
transcript.text: May I ask for one favor?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Sure. I could use a laugh.

transcript.speaker: Fred
transcript.text: Please don't make my resignation announcement terse.

transcript.speaker: Fred
transcript.text: If it's terse, everyone will know I was fired for incompetence.

transcript.speaker: Fred
transcript.text: Does that smile mean you'll do what I ask?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry if that was ambiguous. Let me try again.

transcript.speaker: Fred
transcript.text: I'm still not getting your meaning.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Re: Fred

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Career dead.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, fires an incompetent vice president named Fred. Fred asks that his resignation announcement not be terse so no one will realize he was fired for incompetence, and Catbert grins in response. When Fred can't interpret the smile, Catbert's announcement email turns out to be a curt, terse message, which Dilbert reads at his desk.
punchline: Catbert grants Fred's favor in the cruelest way, sending the shortest possible announcement, 'Career dead', which makes Fred's firing for incompetence painfully obvious.
summary: A fired executive pleads for a gentle send-off, but the sadistic HR cat delivers the bluntest announcement imaginable.

file: 2001/2001-09-16_act ineterested_air gap_boring_doing at work_hurt when i hurt_mother_no empathy for son_no pain_dilberts mother_family.gif
title: Mom Doesn't Care: Air Gap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want to hear what I'm doing at work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: Not so much.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're supposed to act interested because you're my mother.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: Well...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: I'm not saying you're boring; it's just that everything you talk about is boring.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the same as saying I'm boring.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: Only when you talk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But you care about me, right? When I hurt, you hurt?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: Actually, the electrical impulses in your brain don't fly across the air gap to my brain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: You could be writhing in agony and I wouldn't feel a thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: Air gap.

setting: Dilbert's mother's home, sitting with coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert offers to tell his mother about his job, but she bluntly says she isn't interested and that everything he says is boring. When he appeals to her motherly empathy, she explains that his pain doesn't transfer to her across the physical gap between their brains. He says "Ouch" and she responds only with "Air gap."
punchline: Dilbert's mother uses the IT security term 'air gap' to coldly justify why she feels no empathy, and keeps deflecting his hurt with the same phrase.
summary: A son seeking maternal interest and sympathy gets a deadpan lecture on brain-to-brain isolation instead.

file: 2001/2001-06-11_expectations_16 hours a aday_make tired_workers_demands boss_workers not listening.gif
title: Sixteen-Hour Days Sound Tiring

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I expect everyone to work sixteen hours a day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It seems like that would make us tired.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wouldn't that make you tired?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I wasn't listening.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces that he expects everyone to work sixteen hours a day. Dilbert points out that this would be exhausting, and a colleague next to him echoes the same concern in a follow-up question. The colleague then admits he wasn't paying attention to the meeting at all.
punchline: The coworker's question seems like a thoughtful objection to the unreasonable demand, but he reveals he was not listening, so his remark was only an echo of Dilbert's.
summary: A manager demands marathon workdays, and the employees' pushback turns out to be partly accidental since one of them was tuned out the whole time.

file: 2001/2001-06-13_leave work early_doctor appt_female issues_get out of work_worked_80 hour week_boss_zombie.gif
title: Boss Flees Female Medical Details

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It looks like someone is leaving early.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I started at 5 a.m. and I've already worked eighty hours this week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have a doctor appointment for... female...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No details! Go go go!!!

situation: The Boss catches Alice carrying her bag and heading out early. She points out she has already worked eighty hours that week, and he is unmoved. As soon as she starts to mention a female medical appointment, he panics, covers his ears and urges her to leave.
punchline: Alice's long hours earn no sympathy from the Boss, but the mere hint of female medical issues makes him instantly let her go, showing she can get out of work by exploiting his squeamishness.
summary: A worker stuck with punishing hours finds that only a vague mention of women's health problems can make her manager hurry her out the door.

file: 2001/2001-04-01_hardening_given more work_central nervous system_suddenly stiff_ripening asok_apathy cream_air hole.gif
title: Hardening Asok With Overwork

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you like to join me for a hardening?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: What's that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A hardening is when an employee is given more work than his central nervous system can handle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: His whole body suddenly goes stiff.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been ripening Asok all month.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purrrr Purrrr

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So much work... no time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I have another assignment for you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I heard a hardening. Get the apathy cream.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He'll be okay when the apathy sinks in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We forgot the air hole.

situation: The Boss invites Catbert to watch a 'hardening', in which an employee is overloaded with so much work that his body goes rigid. After ripening Asok with work all month, the Boss hands him one more assignment and Asok seizes up stiff. Wally and Dilbert arrive to treat him with apathy cream, but have forgotten to leave an air hole.
punchline: Overworked Asok is treated like a ripened, rigid specimen, and his coworkers' fix is to bury him in apathy cream and forget to let him breathe.
summary: A cruel manager piles on work until an engineer locks up stiff, and his coworkers treat the collapse with a numbing cream while carelessly forgetting a breathing hole.

file: 2001/2001-07-27_bonus_did well_hiring freeze_shrink empire_hand shaking situation_hand_questioning clean.gif
title: Bonus Without Work, Boss Won't Shake

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company did well so you get a bonus despite the fact you did no work all year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd fire you but I can't replace you because there's a hiring freeze and I don't want to shrink my empire.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This might be a hand-shaking situation but I don't know where your hand has been.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Off you go.

situation: The Boss tells a seated, balding employee that he is getting a bonus even though he did no work all year. He admits he would fire him but cannot because of a hiring freeze and his reluctance to shrink his empire. He then declines to shake hands, citing hygiene concerns, and dismisses him.
punchline: The Boss rewards an idle employee only to protect his own headcount, then insults him by refusing a handshake, showing that the bonus is about the boss's self-interest rather than merit.
summary: A manager reluctantly hands a bonus to a do-nothing worker because he cannot afford to lose a head from his department, then snubs the traditional handshake.

file: 2001/2001-04-11_oil wells_albanian wild life preserve_extinction_seven species_useless_species_eat and grunt.gif
title: Useless Species Eat and Grunt

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our oil wells in the Elbonian wildlife preserve have caused the extinction of seven species.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Luckily, they were useless species who did nothing but eat and grunt.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Mm... Mm... Mm...

situation: The Boss presents a slide showing that company oil wells in an Elbonian wildlife preserve have wiped out seven species. He reassures the room that the lost species were useless because they only ate and grunted. Two meeting attendees, one of them eating, sit and make munching grunts.
punchline: The attendees, who sit in meetings doing nothing but eating and grunting, are unwittingly the very kind of 'useless' creature the Boss just dismissed, so his logic could apply to them too.
summary: A manager shrugs off an ecological disaster by calling the victims worthless, while his audience quietly eats and grunts exactly like them.

file: 2001/2001-11-23_elbonia_manuafacture mud_water_bags_fertile soil_huge demand_bottled water_bags of soil_bottled air to morons_elbonians.gif
title: Elbonians Buy Bottled Water, Make Mud

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: We manufacture our mud using bottled water and bags of fertile soil.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a huge demand in my country for bottled water and bags of soil.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Is anyone selling bottled air to you morons yet?

situation: Dilbert visits Elbonia, where two locals stand in the mud holding a bottle of water and a bag of soil. They explain they make their mud by combining bottled water and bagged fertile soil. Dilbert says his country has huge demand for those same products, and an Elbonian replies by asking whether anyone sells bottled air to them yet.
punchline: The Elbonians mock consumers in Dilbert's country for paying for water and dirt, which are free and plentiful, and suggest bottled air is the next absurd product they'll buy.
summary: Dilbert learns that Elbonians make mud from the same packaged water and soil that his countrymen eagerly buy, and they sarcastically wonder what he'll pay for next.

file: 2001/2001-01-05_created software_copyrighted work_available_for free_plunge_depression_creativity_psychology.gif
title: Free Software Destroys Creativity, But Neat

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I created software that makes all copyrighted work on the net available for free!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that destroy all forms of creativity and plunge us into a depression?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes... but it is very neat.

setting: Office, standing in a hallway or cubicle area
situation: A coworker proudly tells Dilbert he has written software that releases every copyrighted work on the internet for free. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, points out that this would wipe out creativity and trigger an economic depression. The coworker cheerfully admits it, but says it is still impressive.
punchline: The programmer acknowledges the catastrophic consequences of his creation but is only interested in how technically cool it is.
summary: A proud programmer admits his world-wrecking invention would ruin the economy, yet defends it purely because it is clever.

file: 2001/2001-07-07_unibrow_growing one_ban_work related converstaion_lunch time_break room.gif
title: Unibrow Talk Ends Lunch Ban

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm thinking about growing a unibrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should rethink our ban on work-related conversation during lunch.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Please.

situation: Three coworkers eat lunch together under a rule that bans talking about work. One of them announces he is thinking of growing a unibrow, and the others sit through an awkward silence. Dilbert then suggests dropping the ban on work talk, and Asok eagerly agrees.
punchline: The lunch table's non-work conversation is so dull and absurd that discussing work becomes the more appealing option.
summary: A pointless remark about facial hair convinces lunching coworkers that talking shop beats small talk.

file: 2001/2001-03-07_take this one_hige mistake_security reliability_xq-7.gif
title: Salesman Undermines His Own Product

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take this one.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: No, no, no. Huge mistake.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You need the security and reliability of the XQ-7

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I'll take the XQ-7

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Shoot! I wish my company made that one.

setting: A sales meeting at a desk
situation: Dilbert tells a salesman he will buy one product, and the salesman talks him out of it, steering him toward the more secure and reliable XQ-7. Dilbert agrees to buy the XQ-7 instead. The salesman then admits his own company does not make that product.
punchline: The salesman is so honest, or so inept, that he talks the customer out of his own company's product and into a competitor's.
summary: A sales rep so thoroughly convinces a buyer to choose a rival's better product that he loses the sale entirely.

file: 2001/2001-05-02_thirty million dollars_nigerina_banker_bank information_email_ten percent commission_tube sock_fell behind dryer_ratbert_typing_computer_answering scam_technology.gif
title: Ratbert Answers Nigerian Banker Scam

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: A Nigerian banker needs my help getting thirty million dollars out of his country!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: All I need to do is give him my bank information by e-mail and I'll get a ten percent commission!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Dear Gustava, my bank is a tube sock that fell behind the dryer.

setting: Dogbert's home or office, with a blue armchair and a computer desk
situation: Ratbert excitedly tells Dogbert about an e-mail from a Nigerian banker who wants help moving thirty million dollars, promising Ratbert a ten percent commission in return for his bank details. Dogbert sits in an armchair, facing away. In the last panel Ratbert types a reply to the scammer, revealing that his 'bank' is a lost tube sock.
punchline: Ratbert is gullible enough to answer the advance-fee scam, but his bank information is so worthless (a sock behind the dryer) that the scammer will gain nothing from him.
summary: A trusting little rat eagerly replies to a get-rich-quick e-mail, only to hand over account details that are laughably worthless.

file: 2001/2001-08-16_handwriting analysis_disturbed loner_steals_liberal_absolutely necessary.gif
title: Handwriting Analysis Gets Dilbert Burned

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Handwriting analysis

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your handwriting proves that you're a disturbed loner who steals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Take this thief away!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this part absolutely necessary?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Liberal

setting: A conference room, then a pyre outdoors
situation: Dogbert, acting as a handwriting analyst, examines a sample and declares that Dilbert is a disturbed loner who steals. He immediately orders police to take Dilbert away. Dilbert ends up tied to a stake on a pile of kindling while Dogbert thinks the word 'liberal'.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd instant verdict from handwriting leads to Dilbert being prepared for execution, and Dogbert's thought of 'liberal' suggests he is mentally brushing off Dilbert's protest as soft-hearted squeamishness about the burning.
summary: A pseudo-scientific handwriting reading condemns an innocent man to a bonfire with no trial in sight.

file: 2001/2001-01-22_mordac_monitor_pc arrived_weak memories_cheese with whine_memorizing calendar.gif
title: New PC Without Monitor Denied

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Mordac, my new PC arrived without a monitor.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Bah! Only interns with weak memories need monitors!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please. I am having enough difficulty memorizing my calendar.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Did you want any cheese with that whine?

setting: Office cubicle area with Mordac's desk
situation: Dilbert tells Mordac, the head of IT security, that his new PC was delivered without a monitor. Mordac dismisses the complaint, claiming only interns with poor memories need monitors. Dilbert pleads that he is already struggling to memorize his calendar, and Mordac sarcastically asks if he wants cheese with his whining.
punchline: Mordac's obstructive IT department withholds basic equipment and mocks employees for complaining, with the absurd claim that people should memorize everything instead of using a monitor.
summary: An IT gatekeeper scoffs at an employee's request for the missing screen that should have come with his computer.

file: 2001/2001-03-21_bowling alley_dumb_dumbest idea_going someplace_not happy_take charge men_going somewhere.gif
title: Take-Charge Man Goes Bowling

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I like take-charge men who just say, "C'mon, we're going someplace."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: C'mon, we're going to the bowling alley!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That's the dumbest idea I've ever heard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I see how this works.

setting: Outdoors or undefined space against a plain blue background, a date-style conversation
situation: A woman tells Dilbert she likes take-charge men who simply announce they're going somewhere. Dilbert decisively declares they're going to the bowling alley, and she immediately calls it the dumbest idea she's ever heard. Dilbert concludes he now understands how this works.
punchline: The woman claims to want decisive men but rejects the very first decision Dilbert makes, revealing that her stated preference is contradictory and that he can't win.
summary: A man tries to act on a woman's stated preference for decisiveness and is instantly shot down, leaving him to realize the rules are rigged.

file: 2001/2001-10-02_clone of boss_procedure failure_knick knack_small creature_part horse_part human_tiney_antennas.gif
title: Boss Clone Is a Knickknack

transcript.speaker: Clone
transcript.text: I'm a clone of your boss?

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: The procedure didn't exactly work. So you're not so much a human being as you are a...

transcript.speaker: Clone
transcript.text: God?

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: Knickknack.

setting: A laboratory, with the scientist in surgical mask and cap standing at a table
situation: A masked scientist in a lab tells a small, deformed creature that it is a clone of someone's boss. The cloning procedure failed, leaving a tiny horse-bodied creature with antennae-like tufts and a human-ish face. The creature hopefully guesses it might be something grand, but the scientist deflates it by calling it a knickknack.
punchline: The failed clone hopes it has become something godlike, but the scientist bluntly calls it a mere decorative trinket, and the creature's grand self-image is crushed.
summary: A botched cloning experiment leaves a tiny, misshapen replica who hopes for greatness but is dismissed as a shelf ornament.

file: 2001/2001-11-15_dangerous looking biker_heart of gold_theme_used to be preppy_psycho hill billy.gif
title: Psycho Hillbilly Is Not a Theme

transcript.speaker: Wild-haired man
transcript.text: I used to be preppy. Then I was a dangerous-looking biker with a heart of gold.

transcript.speaker: Wild-haired man
transcript.text: I call my current look the "psycho hillbilly."

transcript.speaker: Wild-haired man
transcript.text: What's your theme?

transcript.speaker: Balding coworker
transcript.text: This isn't a theme.

transcript.speaker: Wild-haired man
transcript.text: Oh... sorry, man, I had no way of knowing.

setting: Conference table in an office meeting room
situation: A shirtless, wild-haired, bearded man at a conference table describes his series of looks, from preppy to biker to "psycho hillbilly," and asks his balding coworker what his theme is. The coworker, calmly drinking from a mug, replies that his appearance isn't a theme at all.
punchline: The man treats ordinary workplace attire as a themed costume, and the coworker's flat reply reveals that nobody else has a look at all, while the man's apology shows he never realized there was no costume theme to follow.
summary: A man who keeps reinventing his wild personal image assumes everyone else has a theme too, and is embarrassed to learn the plain-dressed coworker simply doesn't.

file: 2001/2001-12-28_email_fax_letter_copy of message_voice mail.gif
title: Boss Communicates Through Every Channel

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I just sent you an e-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's a copy of my message but I'll just tell you what it says.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
