transcript.text: It says I sent you a voice mail telling you to look for a fax that says I want to talk to you.

situation: The Boss walks up to Alice and announces he has just emailed her. He hands her a printed copy of the email and then recites its contents aloud. The message turns out to say that he left a voice mail telling her to look for a fax saying he wants to talk to her, while Alice grows visibly angry.
punchline: The Boss uses email, paper, voice mail and fax to deliver a message he could have conveyed by simply speaking to her, which he ends up doing anyway.
summary: A manager buries a simple request under a stack of redundant communication methods while standing right in front of the person he wants to reach.

file: 2001/2001-04-25_coworkers naked_no more donuts_boredom.gif
title: Imagining Coworkers Naked Backfires Horribly

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe I can stave off the boredom by imagining my co-workers naked.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: AAAGH! NO-O-O-O!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No more donuts for you.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Hey, don't even kid about that.

situation: Alice sits bored at a meeting table and decides to pass the time by picturing her co-workers naked. She immediately recoils in horror, clutching her head and screaming. She then blames the bald, bespectacled coworker beside her, telling him he can't have any more donuts.
punchline: The mental image of her coworker naked was so disturbing that Alice concludes his donut habit is to blame, and he is offended even by the joke of it.
summary: A bored woman's attempt to liven up a meeting with a mental trick leaves her traumatized and scolding a colleague about his snack habits.

file: 2001/2001-12-05_manage time_high priorities_low priorities_freakin loser.gif
title: Time Management: Do Everything Or Lose

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can teach you to manage your time more efficiently.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Put all of your high priorities on one list and your low priorities on another.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then do everything on both lists even if it kills you, otherwise you're a freakin' loser.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert standing on the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, offers to teach the Boss time management while standing on his desk. His method is to sort tasks into high and low priority lists, then he reveals that everything on both lists must still get done. The Boss sits back in his chair and listens calmly.
punchline: The supposed time-management advice is just prioritizing for show followed by doing all the work anyway, with an insult as the only incentive, so nothing is actually saved.
summary: A consultant dog sells a productivity system that sorts tasks into two lists and then demands that every item on both be completed regardless.

file: 2001/2001-07-02_writing code_doing job_excellent benefits_package_eating sandwhich_crime pays_working_other compnay_stolen sandwhich.gif
title: Moonlighting Coder Steals Colleague's Sandwich

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I spend all day writing code for another company while it looks like I'm doing my job here.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Crime pays and it also has an excellent benefits package.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you eating my sandwich?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm saving mine for dinner.

situation: At a meeting table, a coworker casually admits he spends his workday writing code for another company while appearing to do his job. He boasts that crime pays and comes with great benefits. Dilbert then notices the coworker is eating his sandwich, and the coworker shrugs it off by saying he's saving his own for dinner.
punchline: The dishonest coworker who cheats his employer also steals Dilbert's lunch, proving that 'crime pays' extends to petty theft with no shame.
summary: A man who secretly works a second job on company time celebrates his dishonesty, then casually helps himself to a colleague's lunch.

file: 2001/2001-01-29_stock analyst_good things_company_weasels_business.gif
title: Weasel Stock Analysts Take Bribes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your stock will rise if a stock analyst says good things about your company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How is that even possible?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One word: Weasels.

transcript.speaker: Weasel
transcript.text: I just found my new pick-and-shovel core holding.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that a stock analyst praising his company will push its stock price up. When the Boss asks how that could be possible, Dogbert answers that analysts are weasels. A literal weasel analyst then accepts a basket full of cash from the Boss's company and declares it his new core holding.
punchline: Stock analysts are literally weasels who can be bought, so their glowing recommendations are paid for with bribes rather than based on the company's merits.
summary: A consultant dog explains that a bribed weasel analyst can inflate a company's stock, and the basket of cash handed over proves it.

file: 2001/2001-05-13_carol_connections in war zones_flights_good rating_humilation_parkside strangler_phone messages_press conference_secretary_vague objectives_complaining.gif
title: Carol Resents Her "Good" Review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, your overall performance rating is "good."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Aaag! Good is bad! What did I do to deserve this humiliation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, you gave me six hundred phone messages that said, "It might have been Bob."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You can't tell me that none of them were from a Bob!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You arranged for all of my flights to have connections in war zones.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Excuse me for trying to save the company some money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You held a press conference to announce that I was the Parkside Strangler.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: And he refuses to take any responsibility for giving me vague objectives.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway or break area
situation: The Boss gives his secretary Carol a performance rating of "good," and she is outraged. He lists her disastrous actions: useless phone messages, flights routed through war zones, and a press conference accusing him of being a serial killer. In the last panel Carol complains to a coworker that the boss won't accept blame for giving her vague objectives.
punchline: Carol has committed outrageous acts of sabotage yet considers a "good" rating an insult and blames her boss's vague objectives, while the boss's "good" rating is absurdly generous.
summary: A secretary who wrecked her boss's travel, messages, and reputation is furious at an average review and blames unclear goals.

file: 2001/2001-11-22_elbonia_business plan_expanded offering_pet grooming_lingerie_as agency_bug in bikini.gif
title: Elbonian Mud, Lingerie, and Pigs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Our business plan was to sell mud to people who live in mud.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Later we shrewdly expanded our offerings to include pet grooming and lingerie.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Frankly, I blame our ad agency for what happened next.

situation: Two tall-hatted Elbonian businessmen explain their failed company to Dilbert using presentation cards. Their original plan was to sell mud to people who already live in mud, then they added pet grooming and lingerie. The final card shows a pig wearing a bra and panties, and they blame their ad agency.
punchline: A business plan built on selling mud to people surrounded by mud was doomed, and the Elbonians shift the blame to their ad agency for the absurd pig-in-lingerie marketing they ended up with.
summary: Elbonian entrepreneurs walk Dilbert through their ridiculous product line and pin the mess on their advertisers.

file: 2001/2001-02-18_call cemter_reduce call_questions_products_interface_average call_bonus_priesthood_mistake.gif
title: Dilbert Games the Call Center Metrics

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The call center

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carl, reduce your average call time or you're history.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Beep beep beep beep

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: What?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a question about your product.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Faster! Faster! Faster!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... it's about the interface.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Great. Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your average call time is way down. You get a bonus.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Maybe it's a mistake to do this job while I study for the priesthood.

setting: A call center, with Carl at his cubicle and Dilbert phoning in from his own desk
situation: The boss threatens call center worker Carl with termination unless he cuts his average call time. Dilbert phones in with a product question and hangs up the instant Carl rushes him off the line, making Carl's average plunge. The boss rewards Carl with a bonus.
punchline: Carl is rewarded for rushing callers and hanging up quickly rather than helping anyone, and he wryly notes that his dishonest, metrics-gaming job is at odds with his plan to become a priest.
summary: A pressured phone-support worker is handsomely rewarded for hanging up on customers faster, which clashes with his religious aspirations.

file: 2001/2001-10-24_accounting trolls_spit on data_tour of department.gif
title: Accounting Trolls Spit on Data

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: Go ahead, Larry, spit on his data.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: PTOO!!

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: Can I give you a little tour of our department?

setting: Accounting department, a cave-like office with trolls at desks and computers
situation: Dilbert brings his data to the accounting department, where the troll staff order a colleague named Larry to spit on it. Larry spits a huge green glob that engulfs Dilbert. A troll then cheerfully offers the slimed Dilbert a tour of the department.
punchline: After brutally slimed the visitor's data and the visitor himself, the accounting troll carries on with polite, cheerful hospitality as though nothing unusual happened.
summary: Creature-like accountants gleefully drench a visiting engineer in spit, then offer to show him around as if it were a normal welcome.

file: 2001/2001-01-23_brokerage firm_discount_lowest commissions_customers_keeping records.gif
title: Discount Brokerage With Abuse, No Records

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to start up a discount brokerage firm.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll offer my lowest commissions to customers who don't mind bad advice and verbal abuse.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did I mention that I won't be keeping any records?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't need to.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits next to Dilbert on the couch and announces he is launching a discount brokerage firm. He explains that the lowest commissions go to customers who tolerate bad advice and verbal abuse, then adds that he won't keep any records. Dilbert, snacking on chips, replies that he didn't need to say so.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan reply implies the lack of record-keeping was already obvious from the scam-like nature of Dogbert's business plan, which is plainly incompetent and untrustworthy.
summary: Dogbert pitches a bargain stock-trading business built on terrible service and no paperwork, and Dilbert drily says that last part was already obvious.

file: 2001/2001-12-06_gifts under $25_rules are rules_worth_$26.gif
title: Gift Limit Passed Along Loophole

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you, but I can only accept gifts under $25. How much is this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, thanks anyway.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson
transcript.text: Rules are rules.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You're very nice for a salesperson. But how much is this worth?

situation: A salesperson offers Dilbert a wrapped gift, but Dilbert says he can only accept gifts under $25. The salesperson says it's worth $26, so Dilbert hands it back and the salesperson says rules are rules. The salesperson then gives the same gift to a woman in another office who asks the same question.
punchline: The salesperson is also bound by rules, so he ends up passing along the same gift, revealing that everyone applies the gift limit mechanically, and the gift just circulates until someone is allowed to take it.
summary: A rejected too-expensive present gets handed over to someone else who also wants to check its price.

file: 2001/2001-07-22_inform carol_whereabouts_wandering around_canceled policy_stupid policy_work for carol_keeping track everyone.gif
title: Reporting Your Whereabouts to Carol

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yesterday I needed to ask Dilbert a question but I couldn't find him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, each of you must inform Carol of your whereabouts at all times.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Handle it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll be wandering around with my coffee cup.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I find a newspaper I'll take a break in Marketing's luxurious rest facilities.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I'll stop by the cute intern's cubicle to do some flirting.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I stand in her doorway so she can't escape.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think I'm making progress.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm becoming immune to pepper spray.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I canceled your stupid policy.

situation: After being unable to find Dilbert, the Boss orders everyone to report their whereabouts to Carol at all times. Wally cheerfully obeys by describing in detail his daily routine of wandering with a coffee cup, loafing in the restroom, and harassing the intern. Carol, the recipient of these reports, finally cancels the policy.
punchline: Wally complies with the tracking policy so literally, and so unflatteringly, that Carol is driven to cancel it, since she has to listen to his reports of loafing and creepy flirting.
summary: A new rule forcing employees to report their locations backfires when Wally dutifully narrates his idle and inappropriate wanderings to the assistant stuck listening.

file: 2001/2001-05-23_bar_burp_chug chardonnay_drinks_drunk_drunkards_gross_guzzled_hit on_pig_scene_sloshed_slurred words_strictly business_business man_date_animals.gif
title: Business Meeting Becomes Wine-Chugging Contest

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is strictly business, right? We're going to talk about your company's product.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I'll bet I can chug more Chardonnay than you can.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're a hanshum man and so ish your twin bruver.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BURP

setting: A bar with a wooden counter and beer taps
situation: Alice meets a vendor's salesman at a bar and insists the meeting is strictly business. He challenges her to a chardonnay-chugging contest. By the end she is drunk and slurring a flirtatious compliment while he lies burping on the bar with an empty bottle beside him.
punchline: Alice's insistence on keeping things professional collapses as she gets drunk and ends up slurring a come-on at the salesman, even imagining his twin brother is equally handsome.
summary: A woman who insists on keeping a bar meeting purely professional gets goaded into a wine-chugging contest and ends up tipsy and flirting.

file: 2001/2001-08-10_ergonomic evaluation_key board_supposed to hurt_feel hands_whole body numb.gif
title: Work Should Hurt, Boss Says

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: May I have an ergonomic evaluation of my chair and keyboard?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, work is supposed to hurt. That's how you know you're doing it right.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I can't feel my hands!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My whole body is numb!

situation: Asok asks his boss for an ergonomic evaluation of his chair and keyboard. The boss refuses, claiming that work is supposed to hurt and that pain proves you're doing it right. Asok then complains that he can't feel his hands, and the boss proudly responds that his whole body is numb.
punchline: The boss believes suffering equals productivity, so he treats total numbness as evidence he is the hardest worker, making a request for basic workplace safety sound like weakness.
summary: A junior employee asking for ergonomic help is brushed off by a boss who treats physical pain as proof of good work and brags about being completely numb.

file: 2001/2001-04-05_whos incredible list_can buy book_leather bound_gullible.gif
title: Dilbert Falls For Vanity Book Mailer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! I've been selected for the "Who's Incredible" list!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For seventy-five dollars I can buy a leather-bound book with my name in it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha! And people said I was too gullible to be a success!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Dear occupant"

situation: Dilbert excitedly reads a letter claiming he has been selected for a "Who's Incredible" list and gets excited about paying $75 for a leather-bound book with his name in it. He gloats that he is not too gullible to be a success. Dogbert, reading the same mailing, quietly points out that it is addressed to "Dear occupant", meaning it is a mass mailing.
punchline: Dilbert is flattered by a generic junk mail solicitation addressed to "Dear occupant", proving he is exactly as gullible as people say.
summary: A man thrilled by a supposed honor learns from his dog that the flattering letter was just bulk mail sent to everyone.

file: 2001/2001-12-03_scheduling a meeting_week include_using conference room_milled around_used another room.gif
title: Meeting Scheduled, Room Was Occupied

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My accomplishments for the week include scheduling a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But some people were using the conference room so we milled around for a while and gave up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could have used another room.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What part of "gave up" is confusing you?

situation: At a status meeting, Wally proudly lists scheduling a meeting as his main accomplishment for the week. He explains that the meeting never happened because the conference room was occupied and everyone just milled around and gave up. The Boss suggests using another room, and Wally sarcastically responds as if the boss is being dense.
punchline: Wally treats giving up at the first minor obstacle as a legitimate, final outcome, and mocks the boss for suggesting any further effort.
summary: A lazy employee reports a meeting he scheduled but never held, and scoffs when his manager suggests a simple workaround.

file: 2001/2001-07-05_work indoors_rain_can't control weather_roof guy.gif
title: Roofer Leaves Roof Off Before Rain

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: I got the roof off. I'll be back next week to finish.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if it rains?

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: Then I'll work indoors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My house will be ruined.

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: I can't control the weather.

setting: Dilbert's home, living room and front door
situation: A roofing contractor tells Dilbert, who is reading the newspaper, that he has removed the roof and will return next week to finish. When Dilbert asks what happens if it rains, the contractor shrugs it off and says he'll work indoors. Dilbert protests that his house will be ruined, and the contractor disclaims responsibility.
punchline: The contractor carelessly leaves the house exposed to the elements and then dodges all accountability for the foreseeable damage by claiming he can't control the weather.
summary: A home repairman strips off a homeowner's roof, leaves for a week, and brushes aside the obvious risk of a storm.

file: 2001/2001-09-25_assistant manager_clone me_boss_came to you_brilliant employee.gif
title: Brilliant Employee Needed to Clone Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a brilliant employee to be my assistant manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why I came to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the first nice thing...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your job is to clone me.

situation: The Boss approaches Dilbert at his computer and says he needs a brilliant employee to serve as his assistant manager, then tells Dilbert that is why he came to him. Dilbert starts to remark that this is the first nice thing the boss has ever said to him, but the boss cuts in to explain that the actual job is to clone him.
punchline: The apparent compliment turns out to be a setup: the boss only wants a brilliant employee so he can have a copy of himself, and he interrupts Dilbert's moment of gratitude to say so.
summary: A boss flatters his smartest worker with a promotion offer, only to reveal the role is simply to duplicate the boss himself.

file: 2001/2001-09-23_schematic_office politics_ruin teds career_say bad things_rumor mill_ted is history_backfired_tested_phil quit.gif
title: Office Politics Map Used to Sabotage Ted

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've created a schematic of office politics in my company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nicely done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's say I want to ruin Ted's career...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could say bad things to Tina about Ted. Tina carpools with Ming and Ming takes yoga classes with Carol.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And Carol is a secretary for Ted's boss, so Ted would be history.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Of course it wouldn't be ethical to test the system.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Unless...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...You use the Phil-Alice-Larry circuit to get Ted rehired.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yup yup.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And that's why Ted is worthless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, where's Phil today?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He quit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do I listen to you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because of a little thing I call charisma.

situation: Dilbert has drawn a detailed diagram of the office rumor network and explains how a nasty word about Ted could travel through carpools and yoga classes to reach Ted's boss. Dogbert nudges him to test the system, and Dilbert spreads the rumors, only to learn that the person he used as a go-between, Phil, has quit. Dilbert asks Dogbert why he listens to him.
punchline: Dogbert's bad advice led Dilbert to try an unethical experiment that backfired, and Dogbert shrugs it off by crediting his own charisma for Dilbert's willingness to follow him.
summary: After mapping out how gossip could wreck a coworker, Dilbert is talked into trying it, and the plan falls apart when a key link in the chain quits.

file: 2001/2001-10-21_bad attitude_bad news_bad perfromance_boss meeting_downsized_dump_free from tyranny_rational_profits.gif
title: Employees Choose Bad Attitude, Bad Performance

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Bad news.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The employees figured out that they won't get raises next year because profits are in the dumps.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And they're being rational about it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We are free from the tyranny of having to work hard for raises.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ooh- yah!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But there's a delicate balance because we don't want to be down-sized.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I figure we can either have bad attitudes or bad performance but not both.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I'll try having a bad attitude.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm a bad performance man my-self.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I just realized that my entire job can be done by guessing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, dip-weed.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells the boss that employees have worked out they won't get raises because profits are down, and that they are reacting rationally. In a meeting, Wally and Dilbert celebrate being free from working hard for raises, and each picks a way to slack off: Dilbert chooses a bad attitude, Wally chooses bad performance, so neither gets downsized. A coworker then realizes his whole job can be done by guessing, and the boss insults him.
punchline: With raises off the table, employees rationally decide to slack off in exactly one way each, and the boss's reaction shows his management is so poor that guessing is as good as working.
summary: When pay raises vanish, workers coolly divide up the ways to underperform while avoiding layoffs, and one even concludes his job is pure guesswork.

file: 2001/2001-05-31_mobile tech platform_own wheelbarrow_lost lung.gif
title: Boss's Absurdly Heavy Mobile Battery

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, order an extra battery for my mobile technology platform.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Do you want the one that straps to your back or the one with its own wheelbarrow?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I just lost a lung.

situation: The Boss, wearing a clunky portable computer strapped to his body, tells his assistant Carol to order an extra battery for his mobile technology platform. Carol sarcastically offers two bulky options, and the Boss then trudges along hunched over, crushed by an enormous battery pack on his back.
punchline: Early mobile computing was so heavy and impractical that the Boss's extra battery physically cripples him, proving Carol's sarcastic warning right.
summary: A manager who demands more power for his cumbersome portable computer ends up buckling under the weight of a giant battery.

file: 2001/2001-12-01_fired_can't pay rent_live in cubicle_fires_become cannibal_regrets later.gif
title: Fired Employee Moves Into Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm fired?!! Now I can't pay my rent!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Would it be okay if I lived here in my cubicle?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see why not.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Can I have fires and become a cannibal?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I might regret this later...

situation: An employee holding a paper learns he has been fired and realizes he can no longer pay his rent. He asks the Boss if he can live in his cubicle, and the Boss casually agrees. The employee then escalates by asking to build fires and become a cannibal, and the Boss only mildly hesitates.
punchline: The Boss is so indifferent to the fired employee's fate that he agrees to let him live in the cubicle and only reluctantly hesitates at the prospect of cannibalism, showing management cares more about convenience than the employee's wellbeing.
summary: After being laid off, a worker negotiates with his boss to turn his cubicle into a home, and the boss barely objects even to the idea of cannibalism.

file: 2001/2001-01-03_save millions_project_twenty million_year to complete_topper_one better_do better.gif
title: Topper Always Tops Every Claim

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My project will save the company a million dollars.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: Mine saves twenty million.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My project will take a year to complete.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: Mine takes a week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Topper, I have half a mind...

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I have one percent of a mind.

situation: Dilbert and his coworker Topper sit at a meeting table with the Boss between them. Every time Dilbert describes his project, Topper claims his own project is far better, with bigger savings and a faster schedule. When Dilbert threatens to give Topper a piece of his mind, Topper one-ups him again by bragging about having even less of one.
punchline: Topper's compulsive one-upmanship extends even to an insult, so he boasts about having less of a mind than Dilbert, which is actually an admission of stupidity.
summary: A competitive coworker outdoes every boast at the table, right down to the size of his own intellect.

file: 2001/2001-07-06_roof gets shingled_chaos driven_climate ocntrol_rest randomizer_rain shingles_roof.gif
title: Garbage Man's Personal Weather Controller

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope it doesn't rain until my roof gets shingled.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Why don't you use your personal chaos-driven climate control apparatus to control the rain?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I... uh... don't have one.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: You can use mine. Just reset the randomizer when you're done.

setting: Suburban street outside Dilbert's house, beside the curb and garbage can
situation: Dilbert stands outside in a yellow raincoat, worrying aloud that rain will come before his roof is shingled. The garbage man, who is emptying a trash can, asks why he doesn't just use his personal chaos-driven climate control device. When Dilbert admits he has none, the garbage man pulls out a remote-like device and offers to lend his own.
punchline: The garbage man casually owns and lends out a personal weather-control device, treating it as an ordinary household item that everyone is expected to have.
summary: A sanitation worker offers a bewildered homeowner the loan of his private weather-controlling gadget as though it were a borrowed lawn tool.

file: 2001/2001-06-28_more with less_work smarter_broadening focus_doesn't mean anything_excuse leaderhsip.gif
title: Wally Mocks Boss's Buzzword Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to do more with less.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I propose that we work smarter while broadening our focus.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, that doesn't mean anything.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, excuse my leadership.

situation: The Boss opens a meeting by announcing that the team must do more with less. Wally responds by proposing they work smarter while broadening their focus, and when the Boss objects that this means nothing, Wally retorts that he is merely imitating leadership.
punchline: Wally shows that the Boss's own management jargon is just as meaningless as his, implying that empty buzzwords are what leadership actually consists of.
summary: A manager is told his empty slogan sounds no different from the vague jargon he uses himself when a slacker copies his style.

file: 2001/2001-05-15_sales people_phone calls_taking brides_supplement_income_natural extention_empowerment_micromangement brewing.gif
title: Bribes as Natural Empowerment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, why do you keep putting sales people through to me?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm taking bribes to supplement my income. It's a natural extension of empowerment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I sense some micromanagement brewing.

situation: The Boss, holding a phone, asks his assistant Carol why she keeps transferring sales calls to him. Carol calmly says she is taking bribes from the salespeople and frames it as a natural extension of the empowerment he gave her. The Boss reacts by threatening to start micromanaging her.
punchline: Carol justifies her corruption as the logical result of management's empowerment buzzword, and the Boss's only concern is to retaliate by reasserting control rather than addressing the bribery.
summary: A secretary who accepts payoffs to route salespeople to her boss defends it as workplace empowerment, and he responds by threatening to hover over her work.

file: 2001/2001-08-28_lower costs_retirement package_smart employees_rewrite mission statement_fit better_retired by now.gif
title: Retirement Package Drives Out Smart Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: First, we'll lower costs by offering a retirement package that induces all the smart employees to leave.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we'll rewrite our mission statement to make it fit better.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new mission statement is, "If you can read this you should have retired by now."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ouch.

setting: The Boss's office, sitting in an armchair
situation: The Boss lounges in an armchair with a coffee mug, explaining his cost-cutting plan to Catbert: offer a retirement package so attractive that the smart employees leave. He then proposes rewriting the mission statement to fit the diminished workforce. Dilbert reads the new statement aloud while Dogbert winces.
punchline: The new mission statement openly insults the remaining staff, implying that anyone who can still read it is too incompetent to have taken the retirement package and left.
summary: A manager plans to gut his workforce of talent with early retirement and then tailor the company's motto to the leftover staff.

file: 2001/2001-10-03_six sigma program_doomed_same consulatant_worthless progarms_totally different name.gif
title: Same Consultant, Renamed Management Fad

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You've got to implement a Six Sigma program or else you're doomed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Aren't you the same consultant who sold us the worthless TQM program a few years ago?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I assure you that this program has a totally, totally different name.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When can we start?

situation: Dogbert, posing as a consultant, tells the Boss he must implement a Six Sigma program or be doomed. The Boss recognizes him as the consultant who sold a useless TQM program years ago. Dogbert says only that this program has a completely different name, and the Boss eagerly agrees to start.
punchline: The Boss is satisfied by a new name alone, showing that management will buy the same ineffective fad again if it is rebranded.
summary: A consultant repackages a failed management program under a new label, and the gullible boss signs up immediately.

file: 2001/2001-03-12_afraid of change_operation_someone listened to you_gender change_move to china.gif
title: Boss's Change Advice Taken Literally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't be afraid of change.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You're right! I'm going to get a gender change operation and move to China!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've always wondered what would happen if someone listened to you.

situation: At a meeting, the Pointy-Haired Boss tells the group not to be afraid of change. An employee enthusiastically announces he will take the advice to an extreme, getting a gender change operation and moving to China. A coworker remarks that he has always wondered what would happen if anyone actually followed the boss's advice.
punchline: The boss's empty management platitude is taken to an absurd extreme, and a coworker sarcastically notes that nobody normally listens to the boss's advice.
summary: A manager's vague encouragement about embracing change prompts a worker to announce a drastic personal transformation, drawing a dry remark about the rarity of anyone heeding the boss.

file: 2001/2001-01-30_equity analyst_rate stock_banking investment_wall_between businesses_weasels.gif
title: Chinese Wall? Use the Window

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Equity Analyst

transcript.speaker: Equity Analyst
transcript.text: I'll rate your stock a "must buy now" if you give us your investment banking business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Aren't you supposed to have a Chinese wall between those two businesses?

transcript.speaker: Equity Analyst
transcript.text: Am I too early?

transcript.speaker: Banker
transcript.text: Use the door, idiot.

situation: An equity analyst, drawn as a rat-like figure, offers the Boss a glowing stock rating in exchange for his company's investment banking business. The Boss points out that the two divisions are supposed to be separated by a Chinese wall. In the last panel the analyst's head pokes through a wall into a banker's office, and the banker tells him to use the door.
punchline: The supposedly impassable Chinese wall between analysis and investment banking is literal here, so the analyst pokes through it, and the banker's irritation at the shortcut shows the barrier is flimsy and routinely ignored.
summary: A stock analyst trades a rosy rating for banking business, and the supposed barrier between the two departments turns out to be a thin wall he can pop his head through.

file: 2001/2001-02-20_positive reinforcement_addicted_wearing off_crazy woman_drool_lunch room_boss words.gif
title: Addicted to Positive Reinforcement

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I experienced something called positive reinforcement today.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm addicted to it now... But it's wearing off... Must get more...

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Say something nice about me!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For a crazy woman you don't drool much.

situation: Tina tells her coworkers she received positive reinforcement for the first time and has become hooked on it. As the effect fades she demands more, asking someone to say something nice about her. Wally responds with a backhanded compliment.
punchline: Wally's idea of a nice compliment is that Tina is crazy but at least doesn't drool much, showing how little positive reinforcement she is likely to get from her coworkers.
summary: A coworker craving praise after a taste of encouragement gets only an insulting compliment from a colleague.

file: 2001/2001-02-15_never thought_organic pain_racing toward oblivion_self delusion_key to happiness.gif
title: Dogbert's Unhelpful Happiness Advice

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The key to happiness is self-delusion.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't think of yourself as an organic pain collector racing toward oblivion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never had that thought... until now.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't blame me; I said don't.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch beside Dilbert and offers him advice on how to be happy, recommending self-delusion. He then tells Dilbert not to think of himself as a doomed collector of pain, which plants that very idea in Dilbert's head. Dilbert objects that he never had that thought before, and Dogbert shrugs off any blame.
punchline: Telling someone not to think about something bleak makes them think about it, and Dogbert dodges responsibility by pointing out that he technically said not to.
summary: A dog doling out happiness tips accidentally hands his friend a gloomy new worry and then denies any fault.

file: 2001/2001-01-16_ad agency_cat_sarcasm_like sarcasm_laughter_over done_animals.gif
title: Ad Agency Pitches Sarcastic Cats

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Ad Agency

transcript.speaker: Ad Agency Man
transcript.text: This cat will say something.

transcript.speaker: Ad Agency Man
transcript.text: Then this other cat will say, "Yeah, right."

transcript.speaker: Ad Agency Man
transcript.text: It's like sarcasm.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This explains so much.

setting: Ad agency presentation in a conference room
situation: An ad agency representative presents a campaign concept using drawings of two cats. He explains that one cat says something and the other replies "Yeah, right," and he has to point out that this is sarcasm. The Boss roars with laughter while Dilbert sits beside him and dryly observes that this explains a lot.
punchline: The ad agency thinks sarcasm is a novel concept worth explaining, the Boss finds it hilarious, and Dilbert's sarcastic remark implies this is why so many ads are mindlessly bad and why management loves them.
summary: A marketing pitch built on a talking-cat gag that must be labeled as sarcasm delights the clueless boss and gives Dilbert a sarcastic insight into bad advertising.

file: 2001/2001-06-25_marketing acronyms_wrong ones_different meaning_o.r.d_b.g.g._q.r.b._doesn't require nudity.gif
title: Marketing Acronyms Mean Something Else

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Per Marketing's request, I did an O.R.D. for the B.G.G. that resulted in a Q.R.B.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Then I discovered that Marketing uses those acronyms for different things.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Their version doesn't require nudity, just to pick one example.

situation: Asok explains to colleagues at a meeting that he completed a task for Marketing using a string of acronyms. He then admits he learned Marketing uses those same acronyms to mean different things. He notes that his interpretation involved nudity, which Marketing's did not.
punchline: Asok's jargon-laden work was based on a mistaken guess at the acronyms, and the unexplained task he performed apparently involved nudity that Marketing never intended.
summary: A young engineer admits to his team that he guessed at Marketing's cryptic acronyms and ended up doing something far more embarrassing than needed.

file: 2001/2001-03-18_approval_marketing_pathetic plan_knowing plans_interest_smite enemies_cloud of doom_sales projections_business.gif
title: Marketing Head Is a Demon

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get approval from Marketing.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Marketing Demon
transcript.text: I reject your pathetic plan.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any interest in knowing what the plan is?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Marketing Demon
transcript.text: Not unless you're proposing to smite my enemies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I prefer to call them customers. And yes, they'll take it in the shorts.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Marketing Demon
transcript.text: As an added inducement I will give you this cool little cloud of doom.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Marketing Demon
transcript.text: I'm going to staple you to my sales projections.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doom

setting: Office, the Marketing department's demonic lair
situation: Dilbert is told by the Boss to get approval for his plan from Marketing. The Marketing head turns out to be a red devil who rejects the plan without hearing it, is interested only in smiting enemies, and surrounds himself with ominous clouds of doom. Dilbert pitches the plan as hurting customers, and the demon is delighted.
punchline: Marketing is literally portrayed as a demon who cares only about smiting enemies and who is pleased by a plan that harms customers.
summary: Seeking sign-off from a devilish marketing chief, an engineer discovers that the plan's appeal lies in how badly it will treat the customers.

file: 2001/2001-10-15_stock market expert_buy stocks_fundamentals_go on tv.gif
title: Stock Expert Hypes Own Picks

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd be a good stock market expert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd buy stocks and then go on TV and recommend them so they go up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about the fundamentals?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It doesn't get more fundamental than that!

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert, who is working at his computer, that he would make a good stock market expert. His plan is to buy stocks and then go on TV to recommend them so that their prices rise. When Dilbert asks about fundamentals, Dogbert claims his scheme is the most fundamental approach of all.
punchline: Dogbert twists the investing term 'fundamentals' to describe his market-manipulating scheme, mocking TV stock pundits who talk up stocks they already own.
summary: Dogbert outlines a self-serving plan to get rich by hyping his own stock picks on television and brushes off concerns about company fundamentals.

file: 2001/2001-08-12_give decion_more information_study_get information_business case_justify funding_relief_other deadlines_laser like focus_customer.gif
title: Endless Demands Before Any Decision

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You need to give me a decision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to give me more information.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You need to give me funding to do a study to get the information.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to give me a business case to justify the funding.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You need to give me relief from my other deadlines so I can work on the funding request.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to give me everything to infinity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I win! Yes!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We might be losing our laser-like focus on the customer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: On the who?

setting: The Boss's office and a hallway
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for a decision, and the Boss answers with a growing chain of demands: more information, then funding for a study, then a business case, and so on. Dilbert counters with his own demands until the Boss escalates to an impossible 'everything to infinity' and celebrates winning the exchange. Dilbert then comments that the company is losing its focus on the customer, and Wally asks 'On the who?'
punchline: The company is so wrapped up in internal bureaucratic one-upmanship that employees have literally forgotten the customer exists.
summary: A pointless game of escalating demands between a manager and his employee ends with a coworker revealing nobody remembers who the customer is.

file: 2001/2001-08-09_moral money_doing hood_buy prodcuts_logo_coffee mug_ten million dollars_morale dollars.gif
title: Morale Money Buys Overpriced Mugs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Introducing "Morale Money." Now you can earn play money for doing good work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can use it at the company store to buy products that have our logo.

transcript.speaker: Store Clerk
transcript.text: The coffee mug costs ten million Morale Dollars.

setting: Conference room, then the company store
situation: At a meeting, The Boss announces a new reward program called Morale Money, play money employees earn for good work and can spend on logo products at the company store. Dilbert then goes to the store to redeem his currency and is told that a simple coffee mug costs ten million Morale Dollars.
punchline: The reward currency is practically worthless because prices are set so absurdly high that employees could never afford anything, exposing the program as an empty gesture instead of real recognition.
summary: A manager rolls out a fake currency as a perk, but the only item on offer carries a price nobody could ever pay.

file: 2001/2001-06-01_no raise_not enough questions_meetings_care about job_thirst for knowledge_likes wood.gif
title: Asking Questions to Earn a Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a raise because you don't ask enough questions in meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Questions show that you care about your job and have a thirst for knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who else likes wood?

setting: Conference room / meeting table in the office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he can't get a raise because he doesn't ask enough questions in meetings, explaining that questions demonstrate caring and a thirst for knowledge. In the final panel, Dilbert attends a meeting with coworkers and raises his hand to ask a deliberately pointless question.
punchline: Dilbert complies with the Boss's absurd criterion by asking a meaningless, off-topic question ('Who else likes wood?'), showing that the metric rewards the appearance of curiosity rather than real engagement.
summary: Told that his lack of questions is blocking his raise, an employee obliges by posing an irrelevant question to a roomful of colleagues.

file: 2001/2001-03-06_water_avoid work_glug_wally_drinks water.gif
title: Wally's Water Bottle Work Avoidance

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I use my huge bottle of water to avoid work.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Glug glug glug glug glug glug glug

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, would you...um... Wally? Uh... Wally...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Glug glug glug glug

situation: Wally, holding a huge water bottle, tells Dilbert that he uses it to avoid work. He then starts chugging from it, and when the Boss walks up to ask him something, Wally keeps drinking and the Boss can't get his attention.
punchline: Wally demonstrates his technique in real time: by constantly gulping from a giant water bottle, he makes himself too busy drinking to be given any work, and the Boss is too timid to interrupt.
summary: A slacker coworker shows how an oversized water bottle lets him dodge his manager's requests simply by drinking nonstop.

file: 2001/2001-12-21_end war_sell it_sign for a dollar_petition to end war.gif
title: Selling a Petition to End War

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting a petition to end war. Do you want in on this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who are you going to give it to?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Say what?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was hoping to sell it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll sign it for a dollar.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert, holding a clipboard, asks Dilbert to sign a petition to end war. Dilbert asks who the petition will be delivered to, and Dogbert admits he has no recipient in mind and plans to sell it instead. Dilbert, reading the newspaper, calmly offers to sign it for a dollar.
punchline: Dogbert's idealistic-sounding petition turns out to be a money-making scheme with no real goal, and Dilbert shrugs and treats his own signature as a commodity for sale too.
summary: A scheming dog circulates an anti-war petition with no destination in mind, and his friend cynically puts a price on his signature.

file: 2001/2001-10-07_service anniversary_20 years_one year pins_asked for money_six years_pay for pins_card with wrong name_unappreciative_creepy business practices.gif
title: Twenty One-Year Pins, Billed to Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Happy service anniversary, Alice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're out of twenty-year pins so I got twenty of the one-year pins.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can pin these babies all over your blouse... or fishing hat if you prefer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The card says, "To Kathy" but it was never opened. For some reason she quit the day she got her twenty pins.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Incidentally, I have to charge you $262 for the pins. The company doesn't pay for them.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: First of all, I've only worked here for about six years...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow. You look older. Anyway, just give me the $262 and throw away eight pins and we'll call it good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are you rolling up your sleeve? Are you going to pin them to your arm?

situation: The Boss visits Alice's cubicle to mark her service anniversary and hands her a bag of twenty one-year pins because the twenty-year pins ran out. He reveals the card was meant for a different employee, then announces she must pay $262 for the pins. Alice points out she has only worked there six years, and she ends up rolling up her sleeve in rage.
punchline: The company 'honors' Alice's service with cheap, mismatched pins that she has to pay for herself, and the boss is oblivious to the insult, even misreading her violent anger as eagerness to pin them on.
summary: A clueless manager gives an employee a bag of cheap pins for an anniversary she hasn't reached, then bills her for them and shrugs off her fury.

file: 2001/2001-10-10_evil director_contrators_company air_employees only_own air supply_using light.gif
title: Contractors Can't Breathe Company Air

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil HR Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Contractors are not allowed to breathe company air, Carl.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This air is for employees only. You need to supply your own air.

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: MMB BMF RMN HMR!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does anyone understand Carl?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey! He's using our light!

setting: Office cubicle and a conference room
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, pops over a cubicle wall to tell a contractor named Carl that he may not breathe company air and must bring his own. In the meeting room, Carl is now wearing a breathing apparatus and can only make muffled noises, while a coworker complains that he is using the company's light.
punchline: Treating contractors as non-employees is taken to an absurd extreme, with HR denying them even the air and light that everyone in the office relies on.
summary: An evil HR cat bans a contractor from using the office air, leaving him muffled in a breathing mask while colleagues begrudge him the lighting too.

file: 2001/2001-08-24_dating beautiful woman_advice_garbageman_exciting_mysterious_delightful_like fresh garbage_compost.gif
title: Garbage Man's Dating Advice Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm dating a beautiful woman. Do you have any advice?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: A beautiful woman is like a heap of fresh garbage: exciting, mysterious and delightful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any advice that doesn't compare my girlfriend to garbage?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: How about compost?

setting: Outdoors by a garbage can, where a garbage man is working
situation: Dilbert asks a garbage man for advice about dating a beautiful woman. The garbage man compares her to a heap of fresh garbage, calling it exciting, mysterious and delightful. When Dilbert asks for advice that doesn't compare his girlfriend to garbage, the garbage man suggests compost instead.
punchline: The garbage man can only think in terms of his trade, so his attempt at a less insulting comparison is just another kind of trash, compost.
summary: A man seeking romantic tips from a sanitation worker gets nothing but waste-based metaphors, each as unflattering as the last.

file: 2001/2001-07-08_layoffs_fly on wall_poof_wally as fly_rational budget decions_who do we hate_fly eating donut_mean_board of directors.gif
title: Wally Becomes Fly on Layoff Wall

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They must be talking about the layoffs.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd like to be a fly on that wall.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Poof!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Great... the one time I get my wish...

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Let's focus on our priorities and make rational budget decisions.

transcript.speaker: Managers
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Back to reality, I'll fire Ted; he creeps me out. Who else do we hate?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Hey, my donut is getting eaten by the world's ugliest fly!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Bonanza!

setting: Office hallway and a management conference room
situation: Dilbert and Wally notice managers meeting about layoffs, and Wally wishes he could be a fly on the wall. He is instantly turned into a fly and sneaks into the meeting. The managers pretend to be rational, laugh it off, then admit they choose who to fire based on who they dislike.
punchline: The managers' layoff decisions are based on personal dislike rather than rational budgeting, and Wally, as a fly, gets to witness it while also happily eating a donut.
summary: Wally's wish to eavesdrop on a layoff meeting comes true, revealing that the executives pick victims out of petty dislike.

file: 2001/2001-12-14_labor market_own paper_unleash hound_broken copier.gif
title: Don't Make Me Unleash the Hound

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our copier is broken. May I use yours?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Only if you use your own paper.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just need one copy and my office is about a mile away.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Don't make me unleash the hound.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a hound?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Technically he's a web designer in a tight labor market.

setting: A coworker's cubicle in the office
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker if he can use her copier because his is broken, but she refuses to give him paper. When he pleads that he only needs one copy, she threatens to unleash her hound, who turns out to be a web designer in a ratty fur-trimmed outfit crouched behind her desk.
punchline: The coworker's 'hound' is actually a laid-off web designer who has taken a degrading job as her guard dog because of the weak job market.
summary: A stingy office worker guards her copier with an attack 'dog' who is really an unemployed web designer reduced to menial work.

file: 2001/2001-11-24_elbonia_dollar of severence_rich_motivated by slogans_elbonians_mud pool_standing in mud pool.gif
title: One Dollar Severance Makes Elbonians Rich

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm authorized to give each of you one dollar of severance pay.

transcript.speaker: Elbonians
transcript.text: We're rich!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much were we paying you?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Nothing. We were entirely motivated by slogans.

situation: Dilbert visits Elbonia to lay off the local workers and hands each of them a single dollar as severance pay. The Elbonians, standing in the mud, cheer that they are rich. Dilbert then learns that the company had never paid them anything at all.
punchline: The company had been getting work out of its Elbonian staff for free, running on nothing but motivational slogans, so even a one-dollar severance is more than they ever earned.
summary: A tiny layoff payout turns out to be the first money a group of overseas workers ever received from the company.

file: 2001/2001-05-03_snails_offcie_slime trail_hand lotion_second sign_addicted_office.gif
title: Slime Trail Is Hand Lotion

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think we have snails in the office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a slime trail on everything.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That might be the second sign that I'm addicted to hand lotion.

situation: Dilbert tells a female co-worker he suspects snails have invaded the office because there is a slime trail on everything. In the last panel she is shown pumping hand lotion from a large dispenser, with lotion dripping everywhere, and thinks to herself that this is a sign of her addiction.
punchline: The mysterious slime trail is actually caused by the co-worker's compulsive overuse of hand lotion, which she realizes is evidence of her addiction.
summary: A man blames snails for slimy surfaces around the office, while his colleague privately realizes her lotion habit is the real culprit.

file: 2001/2001-04-16_mandatory lunchtime meetings_life work balance_high five_catbert.gif
title: Catbert's High-Five Injures The Boss

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: How about mandatory lunchtime meetings?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On the subject of work-life balance!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: High five!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Uh-oh. He's been high-fiving Catbert again.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, proposes mandatory lunchtime meetings as a work-life balance initiative, and The Boss enthusiastically agrees and goes in for a high five. In the last panel The Boss walks past the cubicles with his hand in a bandage, and Wally and Dilbert recognise what has happened.
punchline: Catbert's cruel policy ideas are so appealing to The Boss that he keeps high-fiving the clawed cat and getting hurt, while the idea of forced lunch meetings as 'work-life balance' shows how little the company cares about balance.
summary: The Boss cheerfully endorses an HR scheme that eats into employees' lunch hours and ends up with a bandaged hand from celebrating with a clawed cat.

file: 2001/2001-09-30_slow walking women_squeeze_oblivious_time stands still.gif
title: Dilbert Stuck Behind Slow Walkers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... slow-walking women.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't squeeze around.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll make footstep noise so they'll notice and move.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Stomp. Stomp. Stomp.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It didn't work. They're oblivious slow-walking women!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Time stands still as I wait to take my next step.

transcript.speaker: Woman in magenta suit
transcript.text: Oh no... it's a pair of oblivious slow-walking women.

transcript.speaker: Woman in magenta suit
transcript.text: I'll throw you over the top. Then you open the side door so I can go around.

transcript.speaker: Woman in purple
transcript.text: Third one today.

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink
transcript.text: Weird.

situation: Dilbert gets stuck behind two women walking slowly side by side in a corridor. He tries stomping his feet to get them to move aside, but they don't notice. Later, a woman in a magenta suit gets stuck behind Dilbert and the pair, and complains about the same thing.
punchline: Dilbert is the oblivious slow walker in the next scenario, and the women, who throw him over their heads without a second thought, find it unremarkable that this happens to them three times a day.
summary: A hallway pedestrian jam leaves Dilbert fuming at dawdling walkers until the tables turn and he is the obstacle, and the women casually fling him out of the way.

file: 2001/2001-05-26_the boyfriend project_progress_seen in public_slimmed down_toned up_changed clothes_no combover_nobel prize_wrestiling_party_cocktail party_feeding words_socializing_mistakes_speech_control.gif
title: Scripted Boyfriend Embarrasses Her Publicly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Boyfriend Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: You're making good progress.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: I'm ready to be seen with you in public. But don't do any talking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And that's why I think there should be a Nobel Prize for wrestling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: I said...

setting: A woman's home, then a cocktail party
situation: A woman has been remaking a bald man into her ideal boyfriend, complete with a 'Before' picture showing his old look. Satisfied with his progress, she agrees to take him out in public but orders him not to speak. At a party he blurts out a foolish opinion about a Nobel Prize for wrestling, and she realizes she had given him lines to say.
punchline: Her makeover project fails the moment he opens his mouth, because she improved his appearance but cannot control the nonsense he talks, even when she hands him a script.
summary: A woman who has remodeled her boyfriend lets him attend a party on the condition that he stays silent, but he promptly says something ridiculous.

file: 2001/2001-08-25_awkward_couch_green_lights on_meet new girlfreind_save energy_smooch_turn lights_dinosaur.gif
title: Girlfriend Turns Out To Be Dinosaur

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I turn off the lights to...um...save energy?

transcript.speaker: Girlfriend
transcript.text: I'm green with that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmm... Smooch smooch

transcript.speaker: Girlfriend
transcript.text: Smooch smooch

transcript.speaker: Neighbor
transcript.text: I came down to meet your new girlfriend but now I think it'll be awkward.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch with his date and asks to turn off the lights, claiming it is to save energy. In the dark the two smooch, and when the lights are back on we see his date is a green dinosaur. A neighbor holding a mug has come down to meet the new girlfriend and decides the moment is awkward.
punchline: Dilbert's date's joke about being 'green with that' is literal, because his new girlfriend is a green dinosaur, and the neighbor is left to awkwardly walk in on them.
summary: A man dims the lights for some romance, and a visitor discovers his cuddly new partner is a large green reptile.

file: 2001/2001-01-09_motivation fairy_magic wand_enjoy working_utter futility_wally myth_spell_cast.gif
title: Motivation Fairy Meets Wally

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: Hello, employee. I'm the Motivation Fairy.

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: My magic wand will make you enjoy working despite the utter futility.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Knock yourself out.

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: Wally?! Gaa! I thought you were a myth!

situation: A flying Motivation Fairy in pink pajamas hovers over a seated employee, announcing that her magic wand will make him enjoy his work despite its futility. The employee calmly tells her to go ahead, and she recognizes him as Wally, shocked because she thought he was a myth.
punchline: Wally is so famously unmotivated and lazy that even the Motivation Fairy believed he was only a legend, implying he is immune to motivation efforts and barely seen working.
summary: A magical fairy offering to make a worker enjoy pointless labor is stunned to discover the unflappable slacker she'd only heard legends about.

file: 2001/2001-06-16_designed product_gaping hole_market_miracle team work_actual afeatures_eaten by squirrels.gif
title: Teamwork Ruins Product, Squirrels Fantasized

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I designed a product that could fill a gaping hole in the market.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But thanks to the miracle of teamwork it turned into a product with no actual features.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In phase three I fantasized about my co-workers being eaten by squirrels.

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: Hee!! Hee!!

setting: Office presentation room with a whiteboard
situation: Dilbert gives a presentation using a pointer, walking through the history of a product project. His elaborate plan diagram in the first panel shrinks to an almost blank board with a couple of marks in the second. In the third panel he describes fantasizing about squirrels eating his co-workers while a small inset shows a figure laughing in bed.
punchline: Group collaboration strips a promising product of all its features, leaving the designer so frustrated that he daydreams about his colleagues being devoured by squirrels.
summary: A designer recounts how a brilliant product idea was whittled down to nothing by committee work, and how he coped by imagining violent rodent revenge.

file: 2001/2001-08-04_rash of thefts_acts suspicious_cut meeting_posters_break room_police_arrest_man screams_legal.gif
title: Suspicious Man Wants Meeting Cut Short

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've had a rash of thefts. Be on the lookout for anyone who acts suspicious.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can we cut this meeting short? The posters in the break room got me all motivated!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then why are they there?!!

setting: Conference room and hallway at the office
situation: The Boss warns his staff at a meeting to watch for anyone acting suspicious because of a series of thefts. A coworker immediately asks to cut the meeting short, claiming the break room posters have motivated him. In the last panel a police officer is arresting him, and he protests that the posters are there to motivate people.
punchline: The coworker is arrested for suspicious behavior because his sudden eagerness to leave looks like guilt, and his complaint that the motivational posters are supposed to inspire exactly that falls flat.
summary: A manager asks for vigilance about thieves and gets handcuffed attention on an employee whose conveniently timed burst of enthusiasm looks anything but innocent.

file: 2001/2001-08-15_who might steal_analyze handwriting_double blind study_scientific studies_scientists dotted i's_smiley faces.gif
title: Handwriting Analysis Debunked By Smiley Faces

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can analyze your employees' handwriting to find out who might steal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Has handwriting analysis been tested in double-blind scientific studies?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, but the scientists dotted their i's with smiley faces so I know they're liars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, offers to analyze employees' handwriting to identify potential thieves. The Boss asks a sensible question about whether the method has been scientifically validated. Dogbert admits it has been tested, then dismisses the results by claiming the scientists' smiley-face i-dots prove they are liars.
punchline: Dogbert applies his pseudoscience to discredit the very scientists who tested it, and the gullible Boss is impressed rather than skeptical.
summary: A scam-minded consultant brushes off scientific testing of his handwriting trick by using the trick itself to declare the researchers dishonest.

file: 2001/2001-02-27_huge_management training_stupid mistake_class_school_learn from it_education.gif
title: Dogbert Grills Trainee About Mistakes

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Management training

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What would you do if you made a huge, incredibly stupid mistake?

transcript.speaker: Trainee
transcript.text: I would try to learn from it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you learn anything from your answer?

situation: Dogbert, acting as the instructor at a management training session, asks a trainee what he would do after making a huge, incredibly stupid mistake. The trainee earnestly answers that he would try to learn from it. Dogbert replies by asking whether he learned anything from that answer, implying the answer itself was the stupid mistake.
punchline: Dogbert implies that the trainee's earnest, cliched answer was itself a huge, incredibly stupid mistake, and mockingly asks if he learned from it.
summary: A trainee's pat answer about learning from mistakes is turned against him when the instructor treats the answer itself as the blunder.

file: 2001/2001-07-01_approval_computer purchse_capital budget_ceo_apparoval_asks for things_assemble computer_cubicles_cheap boss_need approval.gif
title: Buying a Computer in Ten-Dollar Pieces

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your approval to buy a computer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Eh! Eh!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's a freeze on the capital budget. Only our CEO can approve it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could you ask him to...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Eh! Eh!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want to be known as the guy who always asks for things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could assemble a computer from components that are each within my approval limit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your approval limit?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ten dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be in my cubicle, banging my head against the wall.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is why I keep them in soft-walled containers.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Thud thud thud

setting: The Boss's office and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Dilbert asks his boss to approve buying a computer. The boss says the capital budget is frozen and only the CEO can approve it, but he refuses to ask because he doesn't want to look like someone who always asks for things. He suggests Dilbert build a computer from parts that each fall under his ten-dollar approval limit.
punchline: The boss is so afraid of being seen as needy that he proposes an absurd workaround, then smugly notes that cubicles have soft walls so his frustrated employees can bang their heads without damage.
summary: A timid manager would rather have his engineer assemble a computer from ten-dollar parts than ask the CEO for a purchase approval.

file: 2001/2001-05-30_ultimate tool_mobile professional_pda_phone_pager_digital camera_fax_email_laptop_shredder_clips belt_too large_everything.gif
title: The Do-Everything Gadget Belt Clip

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found the ultimate tool for the mobile professional.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a combination PDA, phone, pager, digital camera, fax, e-mail, laptop and shredder.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It clips right to my belt!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has found the perfect gadget for mobile professionals and lists its many functions, from PDA to shredder. In the last panel he holds up the device, which is a huge, bulky machine the size of a small appliance, and claims it clips right to his belt. Dilbert sits silently across the table.
punchline: A device that combines every gadget imaginable is absurdly large and impractical, so the claim that it clips to a belt is obviously ridiculous and shows the Boss's lack of judgment.
summary: A manager raves about an all-in-one portable gadget, then reveals it is a gigantic contraption he supposedly wears on his belt.

file: 2001/2001-11-10_prestigious award_attendance_typo_obsecenity_name spelled wrong.gif
title: Award Certificate Misspells Asok Obscenely

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Asok, you are the winner of a prestigious award for attendance.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My name is misspelled... as an obscenity.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Typo.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Typo? You added four letters!!

situation: Alice hands Asok a certificate for a prestigious attendance award. Asok notices that his name has been misspelled in a way that spells out an obscenity. Alice dismisses it as a simple typo, and Asok angrily points out that four extra letters were added.
punchline: Alice's casual dismissal of the error as a 'typo' is absurd because the misspelling required deliberately adding four letters, implying the insult was intentional.
summary: A co-worker presents a so-called honor to a colleague, but the paperwork turns his name into a vulgar word, and she brushes it off as an accident.

file: 2001/2001-02-23_sould_alice_manager_claim ticket_demoted_play sax.gif
title: Alice Surrenders Her Soul

transcript.speaker: Soul
transcript.text: Hello, Alice. I'm your soul.

transcript.speaker: Soul
transcript.text: You're a manager now; you won't be needing me.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: Here's a claim ticket in case you get demoted or learn to play sax.

situation: A small cloud-shaped soul appears before Alice and announces it is her soul. It explains that she no longer needs it now that she has been promoted to manager. A devil then takes the soul away and hands Alice a claim ticket in case she is ever demoted or takes up the saxophone.
punchline: Becoming a manager requires giving up your soul, and the only ways to get it back are to lose the job or become a saxophone player, implying management is soulless and sax players are the opposite.
summary: Promoted to management, Alice has her soul removed by a devil who gives her a receipt for retrieving it later.

file: 2001/2001-09-05_no problems_week_issues_opportunites_challenges_valuable learning experinces.gif
title: No Problems, Just Learning Experiences

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm pleased to report that I had no problems this week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I only had issues, opportunities, challenges and valuable learning experiences.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you do any work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It didn't seem necessary.

setting: Conference room during a weekly status meeting
situation: Wally gives his weekly status report to The Boss, with Dilbert sitting beside him. He proudly claims to have had no problems, then rattles off a list of euphemisms for problems. The Boss asks whether he did any work, and Wally says it didn't seem necessary.
