punchline: Wally's euphemism-laden status report is just cover for the fact that he did no work at all, since he saw no need to.
summary: A slacking employee dresses up his idle week in positive corporate buzzwords until his manager asks the obvious question.

file: 2001/2001-07-31_exit interview_helpful data_personal problems_unethical weasel_main reason for living.gif
title: Exit Interview Honesty Gets Rewritten

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The exit interview

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What would you say is your main reason for leaving?

transcript.speaker: Departing Employee
transcript.text: I can't stand working for an unethical weasel.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yep, personal problems.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm glad that we collect this helpful data.

setting: The Boss's office during an exit interview
situation: The Boss conducts an exit interview with an employee who is quitting. The employee honestly says he can't stand working for an unethical weasel, and the Boss simply records it as 'personal problems'. Catbert, the HR director, sits nearby and approves of the data being collected.
punchline: The company claims to gather useful feedback from exit interviews, but the Boss rewrites honest criticism of himself as a personal issue, so the data is meaningless.
summary: A quitting worker bluntly blames his dishonest boss, who calmly logs the complaint as something unrelated to management, while HR praises the usefulness of the records.

file: 2001/2001-12-11_creativity exercise_device_converts air to electricty_create a missle_defense laser_scissors holder.gif
title: Team Three's Scissors Holder

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Creativity exercise

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Team one made a device that converts air to electricity.

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Team two used their hour to create a missile defense laser.

transcript.speaker: Audience
transcript.text: Clap clap

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Team three, do you need more time?

transcript.speaker: Team three member
transcript.text: It's a scissors holder!

setting: Corporate training room during a creativity exercise
situation: A facilitator reviews what each team built during a one-hour creativity exercise. Team one built a device that converts air to electricity and team two built a missile defense laser, both drawing applause. Team three, which includes Wally, has only produced a crude scissors holder and sheepishly presents it.
punchline: After two teams announce world-changing inventions, the third team's humble scissors holder reveals the gap between the impressive and the mediocre, with Wally's team clearly not trying very hard.
summary: Two teams unveil astonishing inventions in a workshop, and then a third group reveals their pitifully ordinary creation.

file: 2001/2001-11-12_ceos goal_improve revenue_fired_contratcor_cancelled my contract.gif
title: Fired and Rehired as Contractor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO's goal is to improve our revenue per employee. So I'm going to fire you and bring you back as a contractor.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Last week his goal was to reduce the number of contractors. So you cancelled my contract and hired me as an employee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, it looks like someone doesn't like having his cheese moved.

situation: The Boss tells a seated employee he will be fired and rehired as a contractor to improve the CEO's revenue-per-employee metric. The employee points out that last week the boss cancelled his contract to hire him as an employee to meet the opposite goal. The Boss responds by blaming the employee for resisting change.
punchline: The Boss flips the same worker's status back and forth to chase whatever metric the CEO currently favors, then accuses the confused employee of being resistant to change.
summary: A manager shuffles a worker between contractor and employee status to satisfy conflicting executive targets, then blames the worker for not adapting.

file: 2001/2001-09-10_bad data_data_grossly inaccurate_managing is hard.gif
title: Boss Strains to Ignore Bad Data

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All of our data is grossly inaccurate... but I need data in order to manage.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I concentrate hard enough I can forget that the data is bad, then I can use it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have to give him credit; managing is harder than it looks.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss admits that the company's data is grossly inaccurate but says he needs data to manage. He decides to concentrate hard enough to forget the data is bad so he can use it, and he visibly strains and sweats while trying. A coworker comments that managing is harder than it looks.
punchline: The Boss's difficult 'management' work is merely the mental effort of deliberately deceiving himself into trusting data he knows is worthless, and a coworker sarcastically praises it as real effort.
summary: A manager strains to convince himself that data he knows is junk is trustworthy enough to base decisions on.

file: 2001/2001-07-26_evolution class_two day course_surfing student_cocky squirrel_janiotr_three thousand pound squirrel.gif
title: Dogbert's Evolution Class Produces Giant Squirrel

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: By the end of my two-day evolution class I had one surviving student.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He's probably the cockiest squirrel I've ever seen. Toward the end he weighed three thousand pounds.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you asked me who's the unluckiest person in the world, I'd have to say it was the janitor.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a table over breakfast
situation: Dogbert sits at the table with Dilbert, who is in a bathrobe, and recounts his two-day evolution class. His only surviving student was a squirrel that evolved into an enormous, arrogant creature. Dogbert then concludes that the unluckiest person in the world is the janitor, implying the giant squirrel killed him.
punchline: Dogbert casually reveals through understatement that his class evolved a three-thousand-pound squirrel that presumably killed the janitor.
summary: Over breakfast, Dogbert describes how his rapid evolution course turned a squirrel into a giant, smug beast and darkly hints at the janitor's grim fate.

file: 2001/2001-08-02_team work_natures way_identify weak_perpetuating genes_negative spin_boss puts spin.gif
title: Teamwork Identifies the Weak

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Teamwork is nature's way of identifying the weak.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The strong, such as myself, put all of our energy into perpetuating our genes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now this is when you usually try to put a negative spin on everything.

situation: Wally stands in front of the Boss's desk and delivers a speech about teamwork, claiming it exists only to expose weaker people while the strong focus on passing on their genes. The Boss, seated in his chair, then remarks that this is the point where Wally typically puts a negative spin on things.
punchline: The Boss thinks Wally is about to turn negative only now, after Wally has already delivered an openly cynical and self-flattering rant about teamwork.
summary: Wally offers a Darwinian, self-congratulating take on teamwork to his boss, who oddly believes the pessimism hasn't started yet.

file: 2001/2001-10-18_stock market expert_core holding_dead cat bounce_secret economic model_book sales_financial markets.gif
title: Dogbert's Pointless Stock Market Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Stock market expert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If your core holding is a falling knife, you can dollar cost average through the dead cat bounce.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My secret economic model says you should change your cash allocation from 12.4% to 12.3%.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My new book is, "If you aren't churning, you aren't learning."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't come back.

setting: Dilbert's living room, watching a TV show
situation: Dilbert watches a TV program in which Dogbert poses as a stock market expert, spouting jargon and giving absurdly precise advice. He then plugs his new book, whose title promotes excessive trading. Dilbert, sitting on the couch with a laptop, tells him not to come back.
punchline: The expert's advice is jargon-heavy and meaninglessly precise, and his book title encourages churning, which earns him commissions while costing investors money, so the audience wants no more of him.
summary: A cartoon dog posing as a financial pundit on television dispenses empty, overly precise investment tips and promotes a book pushing constant trading, until his viewer dismisses him.

file: 2001/2001-07-12_donut head_face_hole_hole in head_man is brief_no face_real no brainer_resume_blank paper.gif
title: Blank Resume, Blank Face Interview

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Frankly, the job is a real no-brainer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your résumé is a blank piece of paper; I like a man who can be brief.

transcript.speaker: Man eating donut
transcript.text: You're ruining my donut experience.

setting: Conference room during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate who has a hole where his face should be. He says the job is a no-brainer and praises the candidate's blank résumé as admirably brief. Meanwhile, a man at the conference table is bothered because the candidate's hollow head spoils his enjoyment of his donut.
punchline: The candidate's head is literally a hollow donut shape, so the boss's 'no-brainer' job and love of brevity fit him perfectly, while the donut-eating colleague complains that the donut-headed man is spoiling his snack.
summary: A boss happily interviews a candidate with a hole through his head and a blank résumé, while a colleague eating a donut objects to the unsettling resemblance.

file: 2001/2001-10-11_air_company resources_contractor_demands_gravity_hover_using earth_cheap_resources.gif
title: Contractor Can't Use Company Gravity

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carl, you're only a contractor. You have to stop using company resources.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Mmn nph hbm mrm!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, I know you bring your own air, but you still use our gravity.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Fbm gmp rkr!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If it's not too much to ask, could you hover?

situation: The Boss tells Carl, a contractor who wears a breathing apparatus and brings his own air, to stop using company resources. Carl's muffled replies are indecipherable, so the Boss points out that Carl still uses the company's gravity. The Boss then asks him to hover instead, and Carl ends up awkwardly suspended.
punchline: The Boss is so obsessed with cutting contractor costs that he begrudges even gravity, absurdly demanding that Carl hover to avoid using a resource the company supposedly owns.
summary: A penny-pinching manager objects that a contractor who carries his own oxygen is still freeloading off the office's gravity.

file: 2001/2001-10-08_ceo_smashed pay_share the pain_six million to four_sandwich bag underwear_intern is poor.gif
title: CEO Shares Pain, Employee Wears Sandwich Bags

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO has voluntarily slashed his pay from six million per year to four.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In a written statement he said he wants to, "share the pain."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you feel better now?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I make my own underpants from sandwich bags.

situation: The Boss reads from a paper announcing that the CEO has voluntarily cut his salary from six million to four million dollars, claiming he wants to share the pain with employees. He asks the lowest-paid employee if he feels better now. The employee replies that he makes his own underpants from sandwich bags.
punchline: The CEO's pay cut from six to four million is a trivial gesture compared to the genuine poverty of an ordinary employee, making the claim of sharing the pain absurd and insulting.
summary: A manager touts an executive's still-enormous pay cut as solidarity, and a destitute worker responds with a grim confession about his homemade clothing.

file: 2001/2001-11-02_asok in hr_harassment compliants_alice_caboose_psychic powers.gif
title: Asok Handles Caboose Harassment Complaint

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Asok works in H.R.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Asok, I want you to handle all the harassment complaints.

transcript.speaker: Complainant
transcript.text: And as I left the room I could feel Alice's eyes checking out my caboose.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So... you have psychic powers?

transcript.speaker: Complainant
transcript.text: My eyes are up here, pal.

situation: Catbert, the H.R. director, assigns Asok to handle all harassment complaints. A bald, bespectacled employee then files a complaint, claiming he felt Alice's eyes on his rear as he left the room. Asok, taking the claim literally, asks if he has psychic powers, and the man snaps that his eyes are up here.
punchline: Asok's naive literal-mindedness makes him ask how the man could feel someone staring at his back, prompting the man to sarcastically scold him for looking at the wrong place, so Asok's question turns into the very kind of staring he was being told about.
summary: A new H.R. hire hears a harassment complaint and responds with a clueless question that gets him rebuked.

file: 2001/2001-06-17_bug in software_email address book_send message_hard data_fix bug_money_finds mothers name_compares face to animals.gif
title: Software Bug Insults Your Mother

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We found a bug in our software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It searches your e-mail address book for your mother's name.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every Sunday it uses your e-mail to send her a message...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...comparing her face to various parts of animals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any hard data that proves we should fix the bug?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can't throw money at every problem.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It's your mom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You miserable [expletive symbols]!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See what I mean?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. I get this call every day.

setting: Conference room during a software status meeting
situation: Dilbert presents a software bug to the Boss and other managers: it finds the user's mother's name in the address book and emails her insults every Sunday. The Boss demands hard data before spending money to fix it, until his own mother calls him on the phone and berates him. When Dilbert asks if he sees the problem, the Boss says he gets this call every day.
punchline: The Boss is only convinced by hard data when it arrives in the form of his own mother's angry call, and his claim that it happens daily suggests the bug has been insulting her for a long time or that his mother simply yells at him regularly.
summary: A flawed program mails nasty messages to users' mothers, and the boss's refusal to fund a fix collapses when his own mom phones in to complain.

file: 2001/2001-09-09_bet_billion to one_dance_immature_join pool_lottery pool_office pool_rational person_longshot.gif
title: Lottery Pool Bet and Victory Dance

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you want to join the lottery pool?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No rational person would put money on a billion-to-one longshot.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You will.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I won't.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll bet a hundred dollars that you will.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're on.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If you don't join the pool, and we win, I will come to your putrid cubicle and do this dance...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ay-yi-yi, hoo-wah-hoo! I'm filthy rich and you're a loser!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hoo-ah hoo-ah!!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Who won the $100 Dilbert pool?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Whoever picked thirty seconds.

situation: A coworker invites Dilbert to join the lottery pool and Dilbert refuses, calling it irrational. The coworker bets him $100 that he will join, and Dilbert accepts. The coworker then threatens to do an obnoxious victory dance in Dilbert's cubicle if the pool wins, and the final panel reveals the real pool was on how long Dilbert would last before breaking.
punchline: The coworker's elaborate bet was really a setup to start a $100 office pool on how many seconds Dilbert would take to lose his cool, and a winner was picked at thirty seconds.
summary: A man baits a skeptical coworker into a wager that turns out to be fodder for a different office betting pool altogether.

file: 2001/2001-06-26_perfectionist_reasons to hate_rock eroding.gif
title: Perfectionist Seeks More Hating Reasons

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've decided to become a perfectionist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That way I'll have more reasons to hate people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your rock is eroding wrong.

setting: Outdoor hillside path with rocks and mountains
situation: Dilbert walks along a path with Dogbert and announces he has decided to become a perfectionist. He explains that this will give him more reasons to hate people. Later, sitting on a rock next to Dogbert, he criticizes the way the rock is eroding, demonstrating his new perfectionism.
punchline: Dilbert's perfectionism is so extreme and misanthropic that he finds fault even with a rock's natural erosion, as if it were a person failing his standards.
summary: Dilbert adopts perfectionism as a tool to justify disliking everyone and promptly begins nitpicking nature itself.

file: 2001/2001-11-04_cubicle time_isn't productive_set priorities_projects flounder_big raise_either way_cubicle.gif
title: Look Busy Instead of Being Productive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, may I have a word with you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not spending enough time in your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It looks as if our department isn't productive.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But... I can't do my job from my cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to set priorities. Looking productive is very important to this department.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Will I get a big raise for looking busy while my projects flounder?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You won't get a big raise either way.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's a blank piece of paper to carry back to your cubicle.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's department
situation: The Boss pulls Alice aside and scolds her for not spending enough time at her cubicle, saying the department looks unproductive. Alice protests that she can't do her job from her cubicle, but the Boss insists that appearing busy is the priority. When Alice asks if looking busy will earn a raise, he says she won't get one either way, then hands her a blank paper to make her look busy.
punchline: The Boss values the appearance of productivity over real work, and offers no reward for either, ending by giving Alice a blank sheet of paper as a prop to look busy.
summary: A manager tells a frustrated employee to prioritize appearing busy at her desk over doing actual work, with no raise promised either way.

file: 2001/2001-02-14_alice_small alice_kill people_looking at them_smiling_man dies_scary face.gif
title: Alice's Deadly Glare Discovery

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Smile, Alice. It won't hurt.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: GAAAK!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I found out I can kill people by looking at them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wondered why you were smiling.

setting: Office hallway and a conference room
situation: A male coworker tells a stern-faced Alice to smile, and she glares at him so fiercely that he clutches his throat and chokes. In the next scene Alice, seated in a meeting with Dilbert and another colleague, calmly says she has discovered she can kill people just by looking at them.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan remark implies Alice has been smiling because she enjoys her newfound lethal power, which is a dark twist on the 'smile' request that triggered it.
summary: After a coworker pesters her to cheer up, Alice's furious stare seems to strangle him, and she later coolly announces her deadly new talent.

file: 2001/2001-03-22_no opinion_spineless_opinion_unnecessary pain_cry in public.gif
title: Dilbert's Opinions Cost Too Much

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You don't give your opinion on anything. Are you spineless?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you create an environment in which giving an opinion is an invitation to unnecessary pain.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Great! You're making me cry in public!!

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert's date accuses him of being spineless because he never offers an opinion on anything. Dilbert calmly replies that she may have created an environment where sharing opinions invites pain. Offended, she starts crying and angrily accuses him of making her cry in public.
punchline: Dilbert's honest explanation for his silence proves his point, as her reaction to criticism is exactly the kind of painful response that discourages him from voicing opinions.
summary: A date's complaint about Dilbert's lack of opinions backfires when his candid answer reduces her to angry tears.

file: 2001/2001-04-30_next generation_internet project_cute single women_low standard.gif
title: Next Generation Project On Schedule

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: My next generation Internet project is right on schedule.

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: It'll be done sometime in the next generation.

transcript.speaker: Bald Engineer
transcript.text: If you know any cute single women with low standards, it would really help.

setting: Conference room during a project status meeting
situation: At a meeting table, a bald coworker with glasses reports to The Boss that his next generation Internet project is on schedule. He then clarifies that it will be finished only in the next generation, meaning decades away. Dilbert listens as the engineer asks for help finding a date, and The Boss reacts with a scowl.
punchline: The project is 'on schedule' only because the schedule is literally a generation away, and the engineer's sad plea for a date with a woman of low standards implies he needs a descendant to finish it, which says a lot about his love life.
summary: A coworker brags that his project is on time, then admits the deadline is a whole generation away and asks for dating help to make it happen.

file: 2001/2001-08-17_evil hr director_average performance_group to high_lower ratings_actual perfromance_affect erfromance.gif
title: Lowering Ratings or Actual Performance

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The average performance evaluation for your group is too high.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you want me to lower their ratings or their actual performance?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Whatever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is starting to affect my performance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why? I'm not touching you.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss that his group's average performance evaluation is too high. The Boss asks whether he should lower the ratings or the employees' actual performance, and Catbert says either is fine. The Boss then goes to Dilbert's desk and pokes at him, claiming not to touch him while Dilbert complains his performance is suffering.
punchline: The Boss takes the option of lowering actual performance literally and sabotages his employees, while denying any responsibility for the harm he is causing.
summary: An HR chief demands lower group scores, and the Boss responds by actively disrupting his staff's ability to work.

file: 2001/2001-02-26_training facility_training_secret location_blinfolded_drivers.gif
title: Blindfolded Drive to Secret Training

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one knows the secret location of the management training facility.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: If no one knows where it is, how do we get there?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This part can get loud.

situation: The Boss explains that the management training facility is at a secret location and ties a blindfold on Carol, his assistant. When she asks how they will get there if nobody knows where it is, they end up in a car with both of them blindfolded and the Boss at the wheel. He warns her that this part can get loud.
punchline: The Boss's solution to a secret location is to drive there blindfolded himself, so the trip will likely involve crashes, which is what the loud noise implies.
summary: A manager and his assistant wear blindfolds to reach a hidden training site, and the boss cheerfully takes the wheel anyway.

file: 2001/2001-04-20_trust_integrity_teamwork_warm glow_unconditional love_heating vent_under vent.gif
title: Warm Glow of Corporate Values

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company values are trust, integrity and teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: For the first time in my life I feel the warm glow of unconditional love!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're under a heating vent.

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: Oh... well, that's good too.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces the company's values of trust, integrity and teamwork. A bald coworker in glasses claims to feel the warm glow of unconditional love for the first time in his life. Dilbert points out that he is simply sitting under a heating vent, and the coworker shrugs it off.
punchline: The coworker mistakes a heating vent for the emotional warmth of corporate values, and he is just as happy with the vent, which implies the values themselves are empty.
summary: A man swoons over a manager's lofty values speech until a colleague reveals his glow is just warm air from the ceiling.

file: 2001/2001-07-13_rumor of layoffs_nope_friday_monday_day off_boss.gif
title: Boss Denies Layoffs Too Emphatically

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard a rumor that there might be layoffs on Friday. Is it true?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Absolutely not. No way. Nope. Negatory. No, no, no, no, no.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great. Can I take off Friday?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Monday would be better.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether the rumor of Friday layoffs is true. The boss denies it with an over-the-top string of emphatic negatives. Dilbert then asks for Friday off, and the boss lets slip that Monday would be a better day to be absent.
punchline: The boss's reply accidentally confirms the layoffs are real, since he suggests Dilbert take Monday off, implying Dilbert will have no job to go to by then.
summary: A manager's frantic denial of job cuts collapses the moment he steers an employee toward a different day off.

file: 2001/2001-09-07_just working_complaining about work_nightly periods_unconsciousness_sweet death.gif
title: Is There More Than Work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there more to life than just working?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, there's also the complaining about work, the nightly periods of unconsciousness and sweet, sweet death.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should have kids.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: To share the joy?

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit at the breakfast table with coffee and cereal. Dilbert wonders whether life offers anything beyond work, and Dogbert lists complaining, sleep and death as the only extras. Dilbert then considers having kids, and Dogbert sarcastically asks if he wants to share the joy.
punchline: Dogbert's bleak list shows life is just work plus misery, and his sarcastic 'share the joy' suggests that bringing kids into it would only pass the misery along.
summary: Over breakfast, a weary engineer asks whether existence holds anything beyond his job, and his dog bleakly answers that it only gets grimmer.

file: 2001/2001-09-29_cloning th eboss_might hurt_push button_employeees_operating room_doctors offcie_lab.gif
title: Employees Hope Boss Cloning Hurts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Cloning the boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will this hurt?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope so.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We heard it might hurt.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: May I push the button?

setting: A laboratory operating room with a cloning machine
situation: The Boss lies on a table about to be cloned and nervously asks if the procedure will hurt. Dilbert, dressed as a lab technician, answers that he hopes so. Alice, Wally and Asok gather around, eagerly hoping for his pain, and Wally asks to push the button.
punchline: The employees are so resentful of their boss that they are gleefully looking forward to the procedure hurting him.
summary: Staff in lab coats eagerly crowd around their boss's cloning procedure, hoping it causes him pain.

file: 2001/2001-10-26_always a troll_came to accounting_had a look_hair fell out_horns and tail_stopped gym_finance troll_accounting troll.gif
title: Accounting Troll Embraces the Look

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Were you always a troll?

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: No, this happened when I came to accounting.

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: First my hair fell out. Then I stopped going to the gym.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have horns and a tail.

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: When I realized I had a look going I just went for it.

setting: A cramped accounting department office with a computer on a rock-like desk
situation: Dilbert visits the accounting department and asks the hulking troll at the desk whether he was always a troll. The troll explains that his transformation came gradually after he took the accounting job, starting with hair loss and giving up the gym, and ending with horns and a tail that he decided to fully embrace.
punchline: Working in accounting slowly turns people into trolls, and the troll cheerfully leaned into the monstrous look rather than resisting it.
summary: A troll in accounting describes how the job gradually changed his appearance until he simply decided to wear the monster look proudly.

file: 2001/2001-08-03_busy work_cubicle_nice day_took root_man into tree.gif
title: Coworker Takes Root in Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Okay... I think we're done here. Lots of work to do. Busy, busy, busy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll talk to you later. Have a nice day. Bye-bye. Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Looks like someone took root in your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bye-bye.

situation: A coworker standing in Dilbert's cubicle keeps trying to end a conversation, saying goodbye repeatedly but never leaving. In the second panel he is turning into a tree, sprouting branches and leaves. By the third panel he is a full tree stump, and a neighbor peers over the cubicle wall to note that someone has taken root.
punchline: The coworker lingers so long, making small talk and fake goodbyes without leaving, that he literally takes root in the cubicle.
summary: A visitor who can't stop saying goodbye gradually becomes a tree in Dilbert's workspace.

file: 2001/2001-06-15_time to market_benchmark_two hours_stole hours_good mother year.gif
title: Alice Snaps In Boring Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...and incrementally develop a time-to-market benchmark framework...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Spoink

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This meeting stole two hours of my life!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did that help?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm good for another hour.

situation: The Boss drones on about developing a time-to-market benchmark framework while Alice sits beside him. Her hair suddenly pops out wildly and she shouts that the meeting has stolen two hours of her life. The Boss asks if venting helped, and a disheveled Alice calmly says she can now survive another hour.
punchline: Alice treats a furious outburst as a routine pressure-release valve that lets her endure more of the pointless meeting, while the Boss casually checks whether it worked.
summary: After a tirade at a droning meeting, a frazzled coworker admits that shouting has recharged her enough to sit through one more hour.

file: 2001/2001-10-28_human resources_appearence_being evil_catbert_therapy_session_calls therapist hag_debris_jumps on anything_eraser_misspelled psycho_business_psychology.gif
title: Catbert Visits the Therapist

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm a director of human resources.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So naturally I have to keep up the appearance of being evil.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: But you find it difficult to do evil things?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No, I like that part of the job.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Stop jumping ahead, hag.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: My problem is that anytime I see a tiny object fall to the floor, I jump on it and eat it.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I'm not even hungry and I know it's just a piece of debris but I can't stop myself.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Oops... I misspelled psycho.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No! Not eraser debris!

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Who's a hag?

situation: Catbert, the director of human resources, lies on a couch and confesses his problems to a female therapist. After admitting he enjoys being evil, he reveals a compulsion to eat any tiny debris that hits the floor. The therapist quietly writes a note and erases it, and Catbert pounces on the eraser debris.
punchline: The therapist has just written 'psycho' in her notes, and Catbert's compulsion to eat falling debris proves the diagnosis when he lunges at her eraser shavings, while her calm question about the 'hag' insult shows she's unfazed.
summary: A compulsive, evil HR cat reveals his debris-eating habit in therapy and then immediately demonstrates it on his therapist's eraser shavings.

file: 2001/2001-08-13_bob_ex emloyee_died_funeral_barely knew_erfromance review_communication skills_attendance.gif
title: Eulogy From a Performance Review

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Bob was working for you when he died. The family wants you to say something at his funeral.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I barely knew him. Maybe I can read something from his last performance review.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bob needs to work on his communication skills ...and attendance.

setting: Boss's office, then a funeral podium surrounded by flowers
situation: Catbert tells the Boss that a deceased employee's family wants him to speak at the funeral. Since the Boss barely knew Bob, he decides to read from Bob's last performance review. At the funeral he stands at the podium and delivers criticism of Bob's communication skills and attendance.
punchline: The Boss gives a eulogy made of performance-review criticism, complaining about the attendance of a man who is dead and in his coffin.
summary: A manager with no personal memories of his late employee delivers a funeral speech lifted straight from the man's appraisal.

file: 2001/2001-04-19_soul mates_one per person_everyone gets one_monkey_animals.gif
title: One Soul Mate Per Person

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: I believe there is one true soul mate for every person.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He must be very busy.

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: I meant one per person.

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: Your way would be stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can your soul mate be a monkey?

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hillside near a dirt path
situation: Dilbert and a young girl stand outdoors while she states her belief that everyone has one true soul mate. Dilbert misreads her as meaning one soul mate shared by everyone, joking that this person must be very busy. After she corrects him, he asks whether a soul mate could be a monkey.
punchline: Dilbert deadpans a literal misreading of her claim, then pivots to a deliberately absurd question about whether a soul mate can be a monkey.
summary: A girl explains her view of soul mates, and Dilbert responds with a literal-minded joke followed by a question about primates.

file: 2001/2001-07-18_speakerphone_annoy coworkers_sociopth_bit loud_eating lunch_delicious.gif
title: Sociopath Uses Speakerphone, Eats Lunch

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If I use the speakerphone it will annoy my co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Luckily for me, I'm a sociopath.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Two things: You're a bit loud...and you're eating my lunch.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's delicious.

situation: A cubicle worker thinks about how using the speakerphone will annoy his neighbors, then cheerfully reasons that he doesn't care because he is a sociopath. Dilbert walks over to complain that he is too loud and is also eating Dilbert's lunch. The coworker is unapologetic and simply praises the food.
punchline: The coworker's self-diagnosed sociopathy means he feels no shame about being rude or stealing Dilbert's lunch, and he even compliments it.
summary: A thoughtless officemate happily ignores his neighbors' comfort and helps himself to Dilbert's meal without remorse.

file: 2001/2001-01-07_battery technology_question motives_transformation_lying_avoid work_manual labor.gif
title: Dilbert Hypnotizes Skeptical Product Manager

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No known battery technology can handle this load and be this size.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not what you wanted to hear.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So your mind will erase what I said . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: . . . and replace the memory with something totally ridiculous so you can question my motives.

transcript.speaker: Product Manager
transcript.text: Gaah!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The transformation is complete.

transcript.speaker: Product Manager
transcript.text: How can you say there's no such thing as a battery?!

transcript.speaker: Product Manager
transcript.text: You're lying to avoid work! I'm going to talk to your boss!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lately, the only thing keeping me from being a serial killer is my distaste for manual labor.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You're preaching to the choir.

setting: Office meeting table, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert tells a manager that no battery technology can meet the product requirements. He explains in advance that the manager's mind will erase the bad news and replace it with something ridiculous. The manager then misremembers the message, accuses Dilbert of lying to avoid work, and threatens to report him to his boss.
punchline: Dilbert's cynical prediction that the manager will distort bad news comes true, and he ends by admitting that only laziness stops him from becoming a serial killer.
summary: An engineer predicts that a manager will mangle unwelcome news about impossible hardware requirements, and the manager promptly proves him right.

file: 2001/2001-12-24_feel guilty_enhance stockholder value.gif
title: Guilt Over Stockholder Value, Answered by Coffee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I feel guilty that I'm not doing enough to enhance stockholder value.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever feel that way?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Glug glug glug

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take that as a no.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert confides to Wally that he sometimes feels guilty about not doing enough to boost stockholder value. Wally, who is pouring himself coffee, responds by wordlessly gulping down an entire pot of coffee. Dilbert interprets the silence as Wally's answer.
punchline: Wally is so unconcerned about stockholder value that he doesn't bother to answer and just chugs coffee instead, which Dilbert correctly reads as a firm no.
summary: A coworker's pang of corporate conscience is met with nothing but the sound of someone draining a coffee pot.

file: 2001/2001-01-18_ad agency_wise to insult_monirotity groups_commercial_worst thing_spit on flag_difficult client list.gif
title: Insulting Everyone in the Commercial

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Ad Agency

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Is it wise to insult all of these minority groups in our commercial?

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: What's the worst thing that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Does our company have to spit on a flag?

transcript.speaker: Ad Agency Executive
transcript.text: That's it; you're on my "difficult client" list now.

setting: Conference room at an ad agency
situation: A client sits across a table from an ad agency executive and asks whether it is wise to insult many minority groups in the company's commercial. He then asks what the worst outcome could be, and follows up by asking whether the company must also spit on a flag. The executive, tired of the client's hesitation, puts him on the agency's "difficult client" list.
punchline: The agency executive is so intent on shocking, offensive advertising that a client's reasonable concern gets him labeled difficult, as though the agency is the one being burdened.
summary: An advertising executive punishes a client for questioning an offensive commercial by branding him a troublesome customer.

file: 2001/2001-05-25_boyfreind_project_turtlenecks_jeans_fish_training for marathins_cry at movies_the boyfriend project_makeover_clothes_body_animals.gif
title: Remaking a Boyfriend Like a Project

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Boyfriend Project

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm putting you in turtlenecks and jeans.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You don't like to fish anymore. Now you're training for marathons.

transcript.speaker: Boyfriend
transcript.text: Whaa! Whaa!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You can only cry at movies.

setting: A home or apartment, with a pastel teal background
situation: Tina, with her big curly hair, dictates a makeover for her bald boyfriend, choosing his clothes, his hobbies and even his emotional behavior. As she pulls a turtleneck over his head and announces he must give up fishing for marathon training, he begins to wail. She responds by limiting his crying to movies.
punchline: Tina treats her boyfriend as a fixer-upper project, reshaping his wardrobe, hobbies and emotions to her specifications, and even rationing when he's allowed to cry.
summary: A woman reinvents her partner from top to bottom, dressing him differently, changing his pastimes, and finally restricting his tears to appropriate occasions.

file: 2001/2001-11-28_35th of month_earned dogbert miles_live in terminal_permafrost_primitive society_south pole_dogbert airlines.gif
title: Dogbert Airlines Strands Travelers Forever

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Airlines

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Attention travelers! Our hub at the South Pole is experiencing permafrost.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (over loudspeaker)
transcript.text: Please form a primitive society and live in the terminal forever.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The good news is that you'll earn six "Dogbert Miles" that can be used on the 35th of every month.

setting: Airline terminal and airline office under the banner of Dogbert Airlines
situation: Dogbert, running an airline, announces over the phone and loudspeaker that the South Pole hub is frozen over. A crowd of anxious travelers listens as he tells them to form a primitive society in the terminal permanently. He then offers a consolation: frequent flyer miles that are only usable on a date that does not exist.
punchline: Dogbert's airline gives passengers a callous, absurd non-solution to a delay and a worthless loyalty reward that can only be redeemed on the nonexistent 35th of the month.
summary: An airline run by Dogbert abandons its stranded passengers at a frozen hub and compensates them with miles that can never be redeemed.

file: 2001/2001-10-31_evil director_human resources_assistant recovers_cold or flu_should dissolved_winged demon_business.gif
title: Director's Assistant Became Winged Demon

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I want you to work for the Evil Director of Human Resources until his assistant recovers.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: From what is he recovering? Is it a cold or perhaps a flu?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He saw so much evil that his soul dissolved and he became a winged demon.

setting: Office cubicle area and then a stone dungeon-like doorway
situation: The Boss tells Asok he will be temporarily reassigned to assist the Evil Director of Human Resources while the director's regular assistant recovers. Asok innocently asks whether the assistant has a cold or flu. The Boss casually reveals the assistant witnessed so much evil that his soul dissolved and he turned into a winged demon.
punchline: The assistant's 'illness' is a literal transformation into a demon from exposure to HR's evil, a grim warning that Asok is being sent to a terrible fate that the Boss treats as routine.
summary: A junior employee is casually sent to replace a predecessor whose sickness turns out to be a supernatural corruption caused by working for the department of human resources.

file: 2001/2001-01-14_employee personality prefremces_styles of thinking_solve problems_moral and values_randy is idiot_illogical_menacing.gif
title: Personality Types Spark Insult Exchange

transcript.speaker: Human Resources Manager
transcript.text: I have the results of the employee personality type preferences.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remind me again why we're doing this.

transcript.speaker: Human Resources Manager
transcript.text: Your teamwork will be better when you understand that you have different styles of thinking.

transcript.speaker: Human Resources Manager
transcript.text: For example, Dilbert prefers to use logic to solve problems.

transcript.speaker: Human Resources Manager
transcript.text: But Randy relies more heavily on morals and values to solve problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds like a fancy way of saying Randy is an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Randy
transcript.text: Oh, yeah? Well, I might be an idiot but you're illogical.

transcript.speaker: Randy
transcript.text: That didn't sound as menacing as I had hoped.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's okay.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We understand.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: An HR manager presents the results of an employee personality type assessment and tells the team they think differently. When she says Dilbert is logical and Randy relies on morals and values, Dilbert translates this as calling Randy an idiot. Randy retaliates by calling Dilbert illogical, then admits the insult wasn't very menacing, and his coworkers comfort him.
punchline: The only available insult for a logical person is 'illogical', which is so mild that the insulter himself admits it fails as a threat and his coworkers pity him.
summary: A workplace personality assessment turns into a petty argument where one man's attempt at a cutting retort falls embarrassingly flat.

file: 2001/2001-12-08_be a threat_dogbert_recruitment agency_clueless people_bad hair_cadaver program.gif
title: Dogbert's Non-Threatening Recruitment Agency

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need to hire people who won't be a threat to you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Recruitment Agency specializes in the placement of clueless people with bad hair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know... They still look threatening.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Perhaps I can interest you in our cadaver program.

situation: Dogbert advises the Pointy-Haired Boss to hire people who won't threaten him and pitches his recruitment agency, which supplies clueless people with bad hair. The Boss says even those candidates still seem threatening, so Dogbert offers a cadaver program instead.
punchline: The Boss is so insecure that even clueless candidates feel threatening, so the only hires safe enough for him are dead bodies.
summary: A paranoid manager rejects even the most hopeless job candidates, so Dogbert offers him corpses to staff his department.

file: 2001/2001-06-21_loser_no girlfreind_business traveler_call_check her story_order food_waitress_hard time_restaurant.gif
title: Business Traveler Denies Being Loser

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not a loser who can't get a date. I'm a business traveler.

transcript.speaker: Waitress
transcript.text: What's your girlfriend's name? I'll call her and check out your story.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should order.

transcript.speaker: Waitress
transcript.text: Maybe you should.

situation: Dilbert, dining alone and holding a menu, insists to a waitress that he is not a loser who can't get a date but a business traveler. She skeptically offers to phone his girlfriend to verify his story. Dilbert, unable to produce a name, abruptly suggests he should order, and she agrees.
punchline: The waitress calls his bluff by asking for his girlfriend's name, and his retreat to ordering food reveals he has no girlfriend and was just making excuses for dining alone.
summary: A lone diner's defensive excuse about being a traveling businessman collapses when the unimpressed waitress offers to verify it.

file: 2001/2001-07-11_mother could use_moron_mother fed boss_dilbert_desk_computer_together_bug in computer_technology.gif
title: Your Mother Isn't a Moron

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It needs to be so easy that your mother could use it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My mother isn't a moron. Maybe we could use your mother as the test.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What makes you think my mother is a moron?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She fed you.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, at his computer desk
situation: The Boss sits beside Dilbert at his computer and says the software must be so easy that Dilbert's mother could use it. Dilbert takes offence and suggests testing it on the Boss's mother instead. When the Boss asks why that would be a good test, Dilbert replies that she raised the Boss.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss by implying that anyone who nurtured someone as foolish as the Boss must herself be a moron.
summary: A boss's condescending usability standard gets turned back on him when his employee deftly insults the boss's own mother.

file: 2001/2001-08-08_wally_clean desk award_clutter free desk_back to cubicle.gif
title: Wally's Clean Desk Secret

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Clean Desk Award goes to Wally.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe Wally can share some tips on keeping our desks clutter-free.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I usually throw away this sort of thing in the men's room on the way back to my cubicle.

situation: The Boss presents Wally with a Clean Desk Award in front of the staff and asks him to share his tips for keeping a desk clutter-free. Wally, holding the certificate, reveals that he simply throws such papers away in the men's room on his way back to his cubicle.
punchline: Wally's tidy desk is the result of binning everything, including the award itself, so his advice is to treat any paperwork as trash.
summary: A manager praises an employee's spotless workspace, only for the winner to admit he dumps anything cluttering his desk, awards included, in the restroom.

file: 2001/2001-01-01_topper_top you_ruins system_can't go first.gif
title: Topper Can't Go First

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet Topper. He's amazing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No matter what you say about yourself, he'll top it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How are you?

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I can't go first. It ruins my system.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a new employee, Topper, and brags that Topper can outdo anything anyone says about themselves. Dilbert tests this by simply asking how he is. Topper, whose whole act depends on responding to someone else's boast, admits he can't go first.
punchline: Topper's supposedly amazing ability to top anyone is just a one-trick gimmick that collapses the moment he has to speak first, so his 'system' is really just a dependence on others.
summary: A coworker billed as unbeatable at one-upmanship is undone by a simple greeting because his routine only works as a reply.

file: 2001/2001-05-01_day over_cubicle_six o'clock horror_screaming_nightmare_can't leave_more work_over time_stay late_boss_papers.gif
title: Six O'Clock Horror Ambush

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A happy Dilbert prepares to go home after a long day in the cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Too late! The six o'clock horror is upon him!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In your workspace no one can hear you scream.

transcript.speaker: Coworker 1
transcript.text: What was that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker 2
transcript.text: Just keep walking.

setting: Office cubicle area at quitting time
situation: Dilbert cheerfully gets ready to leave the office at the end of the day, humming. The Boss appears holding papers, signaling last-minute work, and Dilbert screams in dismay. Two passing coworkers hear the scream but deliberately ignore it and keep walking.
punchline: Coworkers know that a scream at six o'clock means the boss has dumped late work on someone, and they avoid getting involved so it doesn't happen to them.
summary: Just as Dilbert is about to leave for the evening, his boss arrives with papers, and his scream goes ignored by colleagues who are desperate to escape.

file: 2001/2001-09-04_profits down_profits went up_putting in context_senior mangement_weak economy_meeting_business.gif
title: Management Blames Economy, Credits Itself

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Profits are down. Our senior management blames the weak economy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So they're saying that profits went up because of great management and down because of a weak economy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These meetings will go faster if you stop putting things in context.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry.

situation: The Boss announces to the meeting that profits are down and senior management blames the weak economy. Dilbert points out the double standard that management takes credit when profits rise but blames external factors when they fall. The Boss scolds him for putting things in context, and Dilbert apologizes.
punchline: Management wants to keep its self-serving, inconsistent excuses unchallenged, so applying simple context and logic is treated as an obstacle to efficient meetings.
summary: A sharp observation about executives taking credit for good results while blaming the market for bad ones gets Dilbert reprimanded for being too logical.

file: 2001/2001-04-22_wireless fiber multifage_wrong solution_software bug_budget hardware_business case_get funding_it people approved vendor_better idea.gif
title: Boss Suggests Nonexistent Wireless Fiber Multifage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why don't you try using a wireless fiber multifage?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, first of all, no such thing exists.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it did exist, it would surely be the wrong solution for a software bug.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And there's no extra money in our budget for hardware.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It would take six months to write a business case and get funding.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Yawn

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then our I.T. people would refuse to install it because it's not an approved vendor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a better idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes. I just fixed it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you think you can hold the fort while I go coach someone else?

situation: The Boss suggests that Dilbert fix a software bug with a made-up piece of hardware, a 'wireless fiber multifage'. Dilbert patiently explains why it can't work, including that it doesn't exist, that there is no budget and that IT would reject it. While the Boss yawns and asks for a better idea, Dilbert reveals he has already fixed the problem and the Boss leaves to coach someone else.
punchline: While the Boss was busy giving useless advice and ignoring the lengthy objections, Dilbert quietly fixed the bug himself, and the Boss simply moves on to pester someone else.
summary: An invented gadget proposed by a clueless manager is shot down point by point while the engineer quietly solves the actual problem.

file: 2001/2001-12-02_layoffs_cruel to fire friday_employee appreciation day_employee of the month_evil catbert.gif
title: Cruelest Day for Layoffs Friday

transcript.speaker: Evil HR Director
transcript.text: When should we do the layoffs?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Experts say that Friday is the cruelest day of the week to fire people.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So let's do it Friday.

transcript.speaker: Evil HR Director
transcript.text: Friday is our Employee Appreciation Day.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ah-ah ah-wooo!!!

transcript.speaker: Evil HR Director
transcript.text: What was that?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You don't want to know.

transcript.speaker: Evil HR Director
transcript.text: Congratulations on being named Employee of the Month.

transcript.speaker: Evil HR Director
transcript.text: Now... You know how some months are shorter than others?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ah-ah wooo!!

situation: The horned human resources director asks Catbert when to schedule layoffs. Catbert says Friday is the cruelest day, and when the director notes Friday is Employee Appreciation Day, Catbert howls with delight. The director then congratulates an employee on being Employee of the Month, hinting that the short month will end his employment.
punchline: Naming someone Employee of the Month sets up a cruel twist, since a short month means the honor, and the job, ends quickly.
summary: A malicious HR duo schedules layoffs for the cruelest moment and turns a workplace honor into a prelude to firing.

file: 2001/2001-09-03_down sized_laid off_let go_thrilled to be fired_severance package.gif
title: Employee Celebrates Being Laid Off

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...effective immediately.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ah-ooga! Woo-hoo!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can make the severance packages less generous.

situation: The Boss announces a layoff to an employee, who responds with a wild celebration, cheering and dancing around his cubicle. The Boss then goes to Catbert, the HR director, and suggests cutting severance packages since employees are so happy to be fired.
punchline: Because the laid-off employee was thrilled to lose his job, management concludes it can punish everyone by making the severance packages stingier.
summary: A worker gleefully dances at news of his termination, so management decides to shortchange the payouts for future layoffs.

file: 2001/2001-09-06_broken keyboard_five asterisks_passwords_types asterrisk_tech support.gif
title: Keyboard Only Types Asterisks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My keyboard is broken. It only types asterisks for passwords.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try changing your password to five asterisks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope I can remember it.

setting: The Boss's office and Dogbert's tech support desk
situation: The Boss phones tech support complaining that his keyboard only types asterisks when he enters passwords. Dogbert, working the help desk, tells him to change his password to five asterisks. The Boss accepts the advice and worries only about remembering it.
punchline: The Boss doesn't realize the asterisks are just the password masking, so he happily sets his password to literal asterisks, and Dogbert's tech support exploits his ignorance.
summary: A clueless manager mistakes the hidden-password dots for a keyboard fault and is cheerfully talked into making his password a string of stars.

file: 2001/2001-06-06_new motto_dance hurts_love money_work when people watch_read contract_assign mottos_dilbert_dogbert.gif
title: Dogbert Assigns Cynical Life Motto

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This will be your new motto...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dance like it hurts. Love like you need money. Work when people are watching.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't assign mottos to me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'd better read our contract.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch beside Dilbert, who is holding a soda can, and announces a new motto for him. The motto is a cynical twist on the familiar inspirational 'dance like nobody's watching' saying. When Dilbert objects that mottos can't be assigned to him, Dogbert tells him to read their contract.
punchline: Dogbert's motto cynically inverts a feel-good cliché into advice about pain, money and looking busy, and he enforces it by citing a contract Dilbert apparently signed without reading.
summary: Dogbert hands Dilbert a bleak, inverted version of a self-help slogan and insists a contract lets him do so.

file: 2001/2001-08-07_rave review_buy review_new movie_afford_full price range_new years day_best comedy so far_this year.gif
title: Buying Rave Movie Reviews From Dogbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hello... yes, I'd like to buy a rave review for my new movie.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Can you afford "suspenseful thrill ride" or would you like something more in the "delightful" price range?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm releasing it on New Year's Day; can you give me a price for "best comedy so far this year"?

setting: Office phone call between the Boss's desk and Dogbert's desk
situation: The Boss phones Dogbert, who runs a review-for-hire service, to purchase a glowing review for his new movie. Dogbert quotes prices based on the praise phrases, as if they were menu items. The Boss then cleverly asks about the price of "best comedy so far this year" since his film opens on New Year's Day.
punchline: Movie blurbs are bought and sold like commodities, and the Boss tries to game the system by claiming "best of the year" praise for a film released on the first day of the year.
summary: A man shops for movie-poster praise from a dog who sells quotable superlatives at tiered prices, and tries to snag a bargain award for a January 1st release.
keywords: best comedy so far this year

file: 2001/2001-04-04_can't crush spirit_work in box_cubicle_demoralize_2 jobs_coordinator died_died of boredom_quality assurance guys.gif
title: Dead of Boredom, Extra Work Assigned

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They can make me work in a little box, but they can't crush my spirit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our ISO 9000 coordinator died of boredom. You'll have to do his job plus yours.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And one of the quality assurance guys is looking pale...

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer in his cubicle and thinks defiantly that his spirit cannot be crushed. The Boss then appears and announces that the ISO 9000 coordinator has died of boredom, so Dilbert must take over that job in addition to his own. The Boss adds that a quality assurance employee is also looking pale, implying more work may be coming.
punchline: Dilbert's confidence that his spirit is unbreakable is undercut by the boss piling on a dead colleague's workload and hinting that another coworker is about to succumb to the same boredom.
summary: Just as an office worker boasts that cubicle life cannot break him, his manager dumps a deceased coworker's job on him and hints at another casualty.

file: 2001/2001-03-17_operating system_reboot_mouse pad_monitor_incompatible mouse pad_rebooting system.gif
title: Dogbert's Absurd Tech Support Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your mousepad is incompatible with your operating system.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try rebooting the mousepad. If that doesn't work, I'll call you back.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How will you know?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll watch you through your monitor.

setting: Dogbert's tech support desk and the Boss's office, on the phone
situation: Dogbert works a tech support line wearing a headset and tells the Boss, who has called in, that his mousepad is incompatible with his operating system. He then gives the nonsensical instruction to reboot the mousepad. When the Boss asks how Dogbert will know whether it worked, Dogbert claims he will watch him through his monitor.
punchline: Dogbert's nonsense tech advice is capped by the sinister claim that he can spy on the caller through the monitor, and the Boss is too clueless to question any of it.
summary: A gullible caller gets absurd troubleshooting advice from a canine help desk, which ends with a creepy surveillance promise.

file: 2001/2001-09-21_meeting_across bridge_hard work_intern_carpool lane_business.gif
title: Asok Is Just a Carpool Passenger

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Asok, you're coming with me to an important meeting across the bridge.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Important!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My hard work as an intern is paying off. Already I am invited to an important meeting!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey, we get the carpool lane!

setting: Office, then a car on a congested bridge
situation: Alice tells Asok, the intern, that he is coming with her to an important meeting across the bridge. Asok is thrilled and believes his hard work has earned him recognition. In the final panel, Alice drives happily because having a passenger lets her use the carpool lane.
punchline: Asok was invited not for his merit but because Alice needed a second person in the car to use the carpool lane.
summary: An eager intern thinks he has earned a place in a big meeting, but he was really chosen as a convenient extra body for the fast lane.

file: 2001/2001-05-09_wally in jail_impersonating_dead person_street smarts_survive_temporary tattoos_gift shop.gif
title: Wally's Street Smarts Behind Bars

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally's in jail for impersonating a dead person.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He'll have to use all of his street smarts to survive.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll need some temporary tattoos. Which way is the gift shop?

setting: Office cubicle area, then a prison yard
situation: Alice tells Dilbert that Wally has been jailed for impersonating a dead person and says he will need street smarts to survive. In the final panel Wally, carrying a box and looking small and bespectacled, stands next to a huge muscular inmate lifting weights. He asks where the gift shop is so he can buy temporary tattoos to look tough.
punchline: Wally's idea of surviving prison is buying fake temporary tattoos from a gift shop, which shows he has no real street smarts and is hopelessly out of his depth.
summary: A coworker reports that Wally has landed in prison, where his plan for looking tough is shopping for stick-on body art.

file: 2001/2001-09-12_crossgrain on accounting_system_lose respect_job security_whole job_accounts erceivable_not expense_no complaints.gif
title: Cross-Training Exposes Ed's Incompetence

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ed, I want you to crosstrain Asok on the accounting system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And don't worry that you'll lose respect and job security if Asok learns your whole job in one day.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I don't think "accounts receivable" is an expense.

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: No one has complained yet.

setting: Office and Ed's desk with a computer
situation: The Boss orders Ed, an accountant, to cross-train Asok on the accounting system, reassuring him that teaching his whole job in a day won't threaten his job security. At the computer, Asok points out that Ed has been booking accounts receivable as an expense. Ed's only defense is that nobody has complained.
punchline: The boss's reassurance about Ed's job security is ironic, because Asok instantly discovers that Ed has been doing the job wrong and no one noticed.
summary: A manager has a veteran accountant train the new guy, who immediately spots a basic bookkeeping blunder that went unchallenged for ages.

file: 2001/2001-10-09_become teacher_educate leaders_educate the morons_stop beliveing_eat the sdonut_dreams_crush.gif
title: Dogbert Crushes Dilbert's Teaching Dream

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should become a teacher so I can educate the leaders of tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should educate the morons of tomorrow so they'll stop believing the leaders of tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll just eat this donut and go to work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any more dreams I can crush?

situation: Dilbert muses over coffee and a donut that he could become a teacher to educate future leaders. Dogbert counters that he should instead teach the future morons so they stop trusting those leaders. Deflated, Dilbert gives up on the idea, eats his donut and asks Dogbert if he has any more dreams to crush.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical reframing of Dilbert's idealistic goal shows that tomorrow's leaders can't be trusted, and Dilbert sarcastically notes that Dogbert has crushed his dream.
summary: A hopeful breakfast daydream about shaping young minds gets flattened by his cynical dog's pessimistic twist.

file: 2001/2001-08-18_brain washed_hypnosis_inspire_lowers of communication_must work harder_no good reason_powers of communication_better employees.gif
title: Boss's Communication Powers Brainwash Staff

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My powers of communication will inspire them to be better employees.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Gaaa!! He's using his powers of communication against us!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Must work harder for no good reason.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're too late!

situation: The Boss sits at his computer and thinks that his powers of communication will inspire his employees to be better workers. Wally and Dilbert panic, claiming he is using those powers against them. A coworker, Asok, then robotically announces that he must work harder for no good reason, showing the boss's message has taken hold.
punchline: The boss's attempt at inspirational communication works like mind control, turning employees into zombie-like drones who work harder for no reason.
summary: A manager's motivational messaging is treated as a sinister brainwashing attack that leaves a coworker mindlessly pledging extra effort.

file: 2001/2001-08-06_reviews_movies_havnet seen_night of living squirrel_movie reviews_big pay_studio_dogbert_entertainment.gif
title: Dogbert's Bought Movie Review

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can you write reviews of movies you haven't seen?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Easily.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Throw away your Picasso paintings. 'Night of the Living Squirrel' is the only art you'll ever need."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much is the studio paying you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dang... too obvious.

setting: Dilbert's office or home workspace, with Dogbert typing at a computer
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert how he can write movie reviews for films he hasn't watched. Dogbert types an absurdly over-the-top rave about a movie called 'Night of the Living Squirrel.' Dilbert correctly guesses the studio is paying for the glowing praise.
punchline: Dogbert's review is so ridiculously effusive that it exposes itself as a paid endorsement, and he admits he was too blatant about it.
summary: A dog churning out gushing film praise for a movie he never watched gets caught because the hype is laughably excessive.

file: 2001/2001-03-27_good news_bad news_power utility_company_new vp opeartaions_offcie_wheel attached_generator_business.gif
title: Ratbert's Hamster Wheel Power Company

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, I have good news and bad news.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The good news is I'm starting up a power utility company and you're my new VP of Operations!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The bad news is that your office is inside a wheel attached to a generator.

setting: Outdoors in a grassy field beside a pond
situation: Dogbert tells Ratbert he has good and bad news. The good news is a promotion to VP of Operations at Dogbert's new power utility company. The bad news is that Ratbert's 'office' is a running wheel connected to a generator, meaning he will generate the power by running.
punchline: The impressive executive title disguises the fact that Ratbert is really just a lab rat who will run in a wheel to produce the company's electricity.
summary: Dogbert dangles a lofty job title before Ratbert, then reveals the role involves powering the whole business by running in a hamster wheel.

file: 2001/2001-01-13_hard work_signing praises_then die_reality_inspirational speeches.gif
title: Inspirational Speech Meets Grim Reality

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you work hard, you can achieve great things!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And then you die.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It never pays to mix reality with inspirational speeches.

setting: Office meeting room during a motivational speech
situation: The Boss gives an upbeat speech to his employees with arms spread wide, promising great achievements through hard work. He then adds that you die afterward, and the audience reacts with despair, with some employees apparently brawling or collapsing in the background. He concludes that reality and inspirational speeches shouldn't be mixed.
punchline: The Boss's accidental honesty about mortality destroys the morale he was trying to build, showing that motivational speeches only work when they ignore the bleak truth.
summary: A manager's pep talk turns the staff despondent when he tacks on a morbid truth about where hard work ultimately leads.

file: 2001/2001-07-03_start on monday_service industry_space -time_contiuum_calendar_no mondays.gif
title: Service Industry Has No Mondays

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: Here's my cost estimate. I'll start the job on Monday.

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: When I say "Monday," I am referring to the service industry's space-time continuum.

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: I'm not supposed to show you this, but check out our calendar.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No Mondays.

situation: A contractor with a pencil behind his ear hands Dilbert a cost estimate and promises to start the job on Monday. He then qualifies that Monday means something different in the service industry, and reveals a company calendar that has no Mondays at all.
punchline: Service providers who promise to start on a given day are really using a calendar where that day never arrives, so the job will never begin when promised.
summary: A tradesman's promised start date turns out to refer to a day that his company's calendar conveniently doesn't contain.

file: 2001/2001-01-02_mouse cramp_elbonian prison wall_chained upside down_winning converstaion_topper_annoying_one better.gif
title: Topping a Coworker's Mouse Cramp

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm getting a mouse cramp.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I spent seven years chained upside down to an Elbonian prison wall.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: At the risk of sounding too competitive, I believe I'm winning this conversation.
