situation: Seated around a conference table, Dilbert complains about a mouse cramp in his hand. A coworker immediately tops him by claiming he spent seven years chained upside down in an Elbonian prison. He then smugly declares that he is winning the conversation.
punchline: The coworker turns a trivial complaint into a contest of suffering and openly gloats about winning it, showing how some people can't let anyone else's problem go unmatched.
summary: A minor ache is met with an outlandish tale of hardship from a coworker who treats small talk like a competition.

file: 2001/2001-07-09_understaffed_over worked_stress counselor_another manager_massage_meeting_alice_business.gif
title: Boss Hires Stress Counselor and Glarer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're understaffed and overworked.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I hired a stress counselor and another manager to glare at you.

transcript.speaker: Stress Counselor
transcript.text: Relax... deep breaths... there...

situation: The Boss tells Alice, who is sitting at the meeting table, that she is understaffed and overworked. His solution is to hire a stress counselor and a second manager to glare at her. The counselor then massages her shoulders with soothing words while the new manager stands over her with a scowl.
punchline: Instead of hiring more staff to cut the workload, management adds a counselor to soothe the stress and another manager to glare, which only adds to the pressure.
summary: A manager responds to a burned-out employee by adding a calming counselor and an intimidating overseer rather than any actual help.

file: 2001/2001-11-29_congressional hearings_airline_inhumane service_ratbert.gif
title: Airline Executive Answers With Dog Noises

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Congressional hearings

transcript.speaker: Congressman
transcript.text: Your airline is accused of providing inhumane service. How do you respond?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I wag and sometimes I hold up my paw and say, "Bah!"

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Bah!

transcript.speaker: Congressman
transcript.text: You're not allowed to say bah. Take it back.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hab.

situation: At a congressional hearing, a congressman asks an airline's representatives how they respond to accusations of inhumane service. Dogbert answers by describing his animal behaviors, wagging and saying "Bah!", while Ratbert barks the word. The congressman scolds them and demands they take it back, and Ratbert comically replies "Hab."
punchline: Because the hearing is about inhumane service, the airline's representatives are literally animals, and their nonsensical dog-like replies treat the accusation as a joke while the congressman absurdly polices their word choice.
summary: Questioned by lawmakers about cruel treatment of passengers, two animal witnesses respond with nonsense noises and then fumble an attempt to retract them.

file: 2001/2001-03-16_dot com ceo_no profit_laid off_laid off means_compliment_baby bottle_youngsters_meeting_firing people_business.gif
title: Dot-Com Staff Misunderstand Being Laid Off

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert: Dot-com CEO

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have no profit now and we never will. You're all laid off.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Does anyone know what laid off means?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It must be a compliment.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You're pretty laid off yourself, dude.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Want a hit of this?

setting: Conference room of a dot-com startup
situation: Dilbert, playing a dot-com CEO, tells his staff of very young employees that the company will never make a profit and they are all laid off. The childlike staff don't know what 'laid off' means and decide it must be a compliment, so one tells Dilbert he is pretty laid off himself and offers him a hit of his baby bottle.
punchline: The dot-com staff are so immature that they take being fired as praise and respond by sharing their baby bottle with the CEO, mocking the youthful naivety of the dot-com bubble.
summary: A startup boss announces mass firings to a room of babyish employees who misread the news as flattery and cheerfully return the favor.

file: 2001/2001-12-12_odd shaped foam_design rocess_brainstorm_insightful observations_engineers.gif
title: Engineers Mock Design Facilitator's Brainstorm Notes

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Everyone grab an odd-shaped piece of foam and sit down.

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: We'll continue the design process by pointing to these brainstorm notes and making insightful observations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The notes are all yellow.

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Sweet jeepers!!! You're all engineers!

setting: A design workshop room with brainstorm sticky notes on the walls
situation: A facilitator leads a design brainstorming session, telling the group to sit on odd-shaped foam pieces and make insightful observations about the sticky notes on the wall. Dilbert responds with the most literal, obvious observation possible: the notes are all yellow. The facilitator is horrified to realize he is working with engineers.
punchline: Engineers take the request for 'insightful observations' literally and offer a trivial factual remark, showing they are ill-suited to touchy-feely creative exercises.
summary: A creative workshop leader asks for insights on the wall of sticky notes and gets a flat, literal remark about their colour from an audience of engineers.

file: 2001/2001-11-06_yoga class_harmony and blance_stare at stretchy women.gif
title: Yoga Class Backup Plan

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I signed up for a yoga class.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They say it will help me achieve harmony and balance.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Failing at that, I plan to stare at stretchy women.

situation: Wally stands beside Dilbert's desk holding a coffee mug and announces he has signed up for a yoga class. He explains the supposed benefit of harmony and balance, then reveals his fallback motive. Dilbert sits at his computer and stays silent throughout.
punchline: Wally treats the genuine spiritual benefits of yoga as optional, since his real goal all along is to ogle the women in the class.
summary: A coffee-clutching coworker says he is taking yoga for inner peace but admits he'll settle for watching flexible women if that fails.

file: 2001/2001-04-18_evil robot_annihilates the galaxy_worst means.gif
title: Beta Product Could Destroy Galaxy

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's the worst thing that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our beta product could turn into an evil robot that annihilates the galaxy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently I don't know what "worst" means.

situation: During a meeting about a beta product, a coworker asks what the worst possible outcome could be. Dilbert answers that the product might become an evil robot that annihilates the galaxy. Later, at home with a cup of coffee and Dogbert beside him, Dilbert says he evidently misunderstood the word "worst."
punchline: Dilbert's catastrophic answer was apparently not the worst outcome, implying the real consequences of the product, or of the project's failure, are even worse than galactic annihilation.
summary: A routine risk question in a product meeting draws an apocalyptic answer from Dilbert, followed by his wry realisation that he underestimated the true disaster.

file: 2001/2001-10-06_six sigma consulatant_identify probelms_control fist_give me a belt_second step.gif
title: Six Sigma: We Have No Problems

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Six Sigma consultant

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: The first step is to identify your problems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't have any problems. What's the second step?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... control... fist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope someone gives me a belt.

setting: Conference room during a Six Sigma consulting session
situation: A Six Sigma consultant tells the meeting attendees that the first step is to identify their problems. The Boss claims the company has no problems and asks to skip ahead to the second step. Alice silently struggles to restrain herself from punching him, while the Boss obliviously hopes to earn a Six Sigma belt.
punchline: The Boss is himself the company's biggest problem, and his obliviousness is so extreme that Alice must resist violence, while his hope for a Six Sigma belt unwittingly contrasts with her clenched fist.
summary: A manager who denies his organization has any issues asks a quality consultant to skip to the next step while a coworker fights the urge to hit him.

file: 2001/2001-03-08_afraid to eat sandwhiches_eat sandwhiches_focus group_truth telling_vendor.gif
title: Honest Vendor Scares Focus Groups

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, you have to see this vendor.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think he's telling the truth.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No way!

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: When the focus groups saw this product they were afraid to eat our sandwiches.

setting: Office, then a conference room meeting with a vendor
situation: Dilbert urges Wally to meet a vendor, saying the man seems to be telling the truth, which Wally finds hard to believe. In the meeting, the vendor cheerfully admits that focus groups were so alarmed by his product that they refused to eat the company's sandwiches.
punchline: The vendor's rare honesty reveals that his product is so awful or frightening that it made test subjects distrust even the free food.
summary: A supplier who tells an unusually candid truth about how badly his product went over with test audiences stuns the engineers.

file: 2001/2001-07-28_trapped in offcie_scream_staple remover_claw wall_door is pull not puch.gif
title: Boss Trapped By Pull Door

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been trapped in my office for three days! Didn't you hear me scream?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I used my staple remover to claw through the side wall!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your door is a pull, not a push.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get me a bigger staple remover just to be safe.

situation: The Boss storms up to Alice's cubicle, disheveled, claiming he was trapped in his office for three days and had to claw through the wall with a staple remover. Alice calmly points out that his door simply opens by pulling rather than pushing. Undeterred, he demands a bigger staple remover as his takeaway.
punchline: Instead of recognizing his own mistake in pushing a pull door, the Boss learns nothing and just requests a larger tool for the next time he gets stuck.
summary: A frazzled manager who spent days trapped by a door he misused responds to the simple explanation by asking for better wall-destroying equipment.

file: 2001/2001-11-21_elbonia_mud delivery business_general economic slowdown_dot com meltdown_sell mud_live in mud_call fudge.gif
title: Selling Mud to Mud Dwellers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can anyone tell me why your mud delivery business is failing? Anyone?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it because of the general economic slowdown?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Dot-com meltdown?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And maybe because you sell mud to people who live in mud?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: What if we call it fudge?

setting: A muddy field in Elbonia, with Dilbert sitting in mud among local villagers
situation: Dilbert is consulting with a group of Elbonians about why their mud delivery business is failing. He suggests blaming the economic slowdown or the dot-com meltdown, then points out the real flaw: they sell mud to people who already live in mud. An Elbonian responds by proposing to rebrand the mud as fudge.
punchline: The Elbonians miss the obvious flaw in their business model and think a new name for the product will fix a lack of demand.
summary: A visiting consultant tries to diagnose a failing mud-selling company, only to hear that renaming the product is the villagers' proposed fix.

file: 2001/2001-05-22_bait and switch_first and third wives_invited for drinks_men vs women_pretext_tricked_undertsand.gif
title: Vendor Drinks Invitation Bait-Lube-Switch

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: A vendor invited me for drinks. It's the only time he has to talk about his product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's using the old bait-lube-and-switch trick. That's how I got my first and third wives.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why it works.

situation: Carol tells the Boss that a vendor has invited her out for drinks, which she sees as the only chance he will have to discuss his product. The Boss warns that the vendor is using a 'bait-lube-and-switch' trick and boasts that it is how he landed two of his wives. When Carol says she doesn't understand, he replies that her confusion is exactly why the trick works.
punchline: The Boss implies the vendor's invitation is really a seduction attempt dressed up as business, and that Carol's naivety about it is precisely what makes such tactics succeed.
summary: A manager reveals that a vendor's friendly drink offer is a sleazy seduction ploy, and her bafflement only proves how effective it is.

file: 2001/2001-05-24_dating_unattractive_ugly_woman fixes up_project_combover_stay out of wind_relationships.gif
title: Fixing Up the Boss's Combover

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm dating an unattractive man. What should I do?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Every man is ugly until a woman fixes him up. Think of it as a project.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Next, lose the comb-over, or at least stay out of the wind.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How'd you know about the comb-over?

situation: Carol, standing beside Alice's desk, asks for advice about dating an unattractive man. Alice replies that every man needs a woman to fix him up and should be treated as a project. When Alice continues with tips about the comb-over, it is revealed that Carol is dating the Boss, who is startled that she knows about his hairstyle.
punchline: The unattractive man Carol is dating turns out to be the Boss, and Alice's blunt makeover advice unknowingly exposes his comb-over, which he thought was a secret.
summary: A coworker seeks advice on her unappealing boyfriend, and the blunt makeover tips she receives land squarely on her bald-spot-hiding boss.

file: 2001/2001-03-13_calling in sick_honesty_monday_puked_puked up organs_questioned_suspicious_vomit_glah!_optional guts.gif
title: Alice Vomits Up Optional Guts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm a bit suspicious about you calling in sick yesterday on a Monday, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: GLAH!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Luckily I had lots of optional guts.

situation: The Boss tells Alice he suspects she faked being sick when she called in on Monday. Alice responds by violently vomiting up a pile of internal organs in front of him. Dilbert looks on, and Alice calmly explains she could afford to lose some guts.
punchline: Alice answers the boss's accusation by literally throwing up her organs, then deadpans that she had plenty of spare ones, showing she would go to absurd, gross lengths to shut down his suspicion.
summary: Faced with a manager doubting her sick day, Alice gruesomely expels her innards and shrugs it off as no big loss.

file: 2001/2001-10-23_accounting trolls_explination_budget season_spit on data_95% spit_finance trolls_underground_beneath the earth.gif
title: Accounting Trolls Spit on Data

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Accounting Trolls

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need an explanation for these numbers.

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: This is budget season so I will spit on your data and send you away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't sound too bad.

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: Our bodies are 95% made of spit.

setting: Underground cave lair of the accounting trolls
situation: Dilbert visits the accounting trolls in their cave to ask for an explanation of some budget numbers. A troll announces that because it is budget season, it will spit on his data and send him away. Dilbert shrugs it off as not so bad, until the troll reveals its body is 95% spit, implying the spitting will be enormous.
punchline: Dilbert assumes a little spit is harmless, but the troll's body is almost entirely spit, so the spitting will be massive and disgusting.
summary: A visit to the cave-dwelling accounting department during budget time turns out to be far messier than a simple brush-off.

file: 2001/2001-04-21_company's core values_trust_integrity_team work_borrow a chair_selling on ebay.gif
title: Core Values Versus Borrowed Chair

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I must keep in mind our company's core values of trust, integrity and teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: May I borrow your chair?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you selling on E-Bay?

situation: A coworker sits in his cubicle thinking about the company's core values of trust, integrity and teamwork. Wally, holding a coffee mug, asks to borrow his chair, and the coworker agrees. Dilbert then sees Wally sitting at the coworker's computer and asks what he is selling on eBay, implying the chair was a pretext.
punchline: The coworker's trusting nature is exploited when Wally borrows his chair only to use his computer for personal eBay business, making the company's 'trust, integrity and teamwork' values look naive.
summary: A coworker who earnestly reminds himself of the company's ideals lets a colleague take his seat, only for it to turn into a sly bit of personal moonlighting.

file: 2001/2001-03-05_sould_claim ticket_demoted_non-management_cubicle.gif
title: Reclaiming Soul After Management Demotion

transcript.speaker: Former Manager
transcript.text: I'd like my soul back. Here's my claim ticket.

transcript.speaker: Devil Clerk
transcript.text: You've been demoted back to non-management. Very well.

transcript.speaker: Former Manager
transcript.text: Get back in the cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Soul
transcript.text: No-o-o-o!!

setting: A hellish counter where souls are stored, then an office cubicle area
situation: A woman who has been demoted from management goes to a red-hooded devil clerk at the 'Souls' window and presents her claim ticket to retrieve the soul she surrendered when she became a manager. The devil hands it over, and she orders the small cloud-like soul to return to the cubicle, where it protests in horror.
punchline: Even a soul is horrified at the prospect of going back to cubicle life, implying that management requires selling your soul and that non-management work is a fate worse than hell.
summary: A demoted manager redeems her soul from the devil, only for the soul itself to recoil at being sent back into a cubicle.

file: 2001/2001-01-31_outsourced sales_elbonian company_complex technology_bad string_call back_mud pile.gif
title: Outsourced Sales Via Tin Can Phones

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We outsourced our sales and fulfillment functions to an Elbonian company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Are you sure that's the best way to sell complex technology?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Could you call back? We have a bad string.

setting: Conference room, then a muddy Elbonian village
situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that sales and fulfillment have been outsourced to an Elbonian company. Dilbert questions whether that is wise for selling complex technology. The final panel shows Elbonians standing in mud using tin can telephones, one asking a caller to phone back because of a bad string.
punchline: The outsourced Elbonian sales team has only primitive tin-can-and-string phones, proving it is a terrible choice for selling complex technology.
summary: A manager proudly hands sales to a foreign contractor whose staff turn out to be mud-dwelling villagers talking through cans on strings.

file: 2001/2001-07-17_lives are pathetic_eat_work_sleep_finished lunch_health.gif
title: Eat, Work, Sleep Makes Wally Hungry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our lives are pathetic. We do nothing but eat, work and sleep.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eat, work, sleep... eat, work, sleep... eat, work, sleep.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Great - I just finished lunch and you're making me hungry!

setting: Office break room by the coffee machine
situation: Dilbert stands with a coffee mug and laments to Wally that their lives consist of nothing but eating, working and sleeping. He recites the cycle over and over in a dreary tone. Wally, holding his own mug, ignores the existential point and complains that the word 'eat' is making him hungry right after lunch.
punchline: Dilbert's bleak reflection on a monotonous life is completely missed by Wally, whose only reaction is annoyance that the repeated word 'eat' makes him hungry.
summary: A gloomy complaint about a monotonous routine gets answered with a gripe about appetite instead of any real sympathy.

file: 2001/2001-04-10_animals dna_clone one_dont finish_eating burgers_elbonian unicorn_save unicorn dna.gif
title: Elbonian Unicorn Extinct, Cloning Suggested

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I'm sad to report that our oil drilling has caused the extinction of the Elbonian unicorn.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Save a sample of the animal's DNA so we can clone a new one.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Don't finish that.

setting: An Elbonian oil field in a muddy landscape, and the Boss's office, connected by a tin-can telephone
situation: An Elbonian standing in mud reports over a can-and-string phone that oil drilling has wiped out the local unicorn. The Boss, on the other end in his office, tells him to save some of its DNA so a new one can be cloned. The Elbonian tells a fellow Elbonian not to finish what he is eating, implying the unicorn has just been cooked and eaten at a barbecue.
punchline: The unicorn's DNA is about to be destroyed because the other Elbonian is already eating it, so the Boss's cloning plan is too late.
summary: A simple request to preserve genetic material from a vanished creature collides with the fact that hungry locals are grilling the evidence.

file: 2001/2001-08-29_dunking tank_united charity day_bonk_lines_wait in lines.gif
title: Boss's Dunking Tank Gets Skipped

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've agreed to be in the dunking tank for this year's United Charity Day.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BONK!!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I don't like lines.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces he has volunteered to sit in the dunking tank for the company's United Charity Day. Before he even finishes, Tina hurls a ball at his head, knocking him down with a loud bonk. She then explains that she did it because she dislikes waiting in lines.
punchline: Tina skips the charity event's line entirely by assaulting the Boss on the spot, showing her impatience and open dislike of him.
summary: A coworker spares herself the queue at a charity fundraiser by beating the boss to the punch with a well-aimed ball.

file: 2001/2001-02-28_always right_arrogance_management training_punished_two rules_customer.gif
title: Two Rules of Customer Management

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Management training

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There are two essential rules of management.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One: The customer is always right.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Two: They must be punished for their arrogance!

setting: A management training session in a seminar room
situation: Dogbert, acting as a management trainer, lectures a small audience of attentive trainees. He states the first rule of management is that the customer is always right, then adds a second rule that contradicts it by calling for customers to be punished for their arrogance.
punchline: The second rule undercuts the first by revealing that the supposedly customer-focused rule is only lip service, and managers actually resent and punish the customers they claim to serve.
summary: A dog instructing would-be managers recites a customer-service slogan and then cheerfully reveals the hostile attitude that really lies behind it.

file: 2001/2001-02-12_greedy boss_huge growth earnings_mean boss_miss growth_poised_stock options vest_unrelated move_leave company.gif
title: CEO Leaves Before Options Vest

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO says we are poised for huge growth in earnings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In an unrelated move, he announced that he will leave the company before any of his stock options vest.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The poor guy will miss all of our growth.

situation: The Boss reads from a paper at a conference table, announcing that the CEO predicts huge earnings growth. He then adds that the CEO is leaving before his stock options vest, and calls him a poor guy for missing the growth. Dilbert and a coworker listen, looking increasingly uneasy.
punchline: The CEO's departure before his options vest reveals he doesn't believe his own growth forecast, while the Boss obliviously treats it as unrelated bad luck.
summary: A manager cheerfully relays an optimistic earnings forecast while unwittingly revealing that the executive making it is bailing out before he could profit.

file: 2001/2001-02-17_deadlines_finish on time_forty hours_good news_bad news_boss_dilbert.gif
title: Deadline Extended After Forty-Hour Marathon

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news: The deadline got pushed back a week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good news?! I've been working for forty hours straight to finish on time!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just realized I don't know the difference between good news and bad news.

situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Dilbert, who is typing at his computer, that the project deadline has been postponed by a week. Dilbert angrily points out that he has just worked forty hours straight to meet the original deadline. The Boss, unmoved, privately reflects that he cannot tell good news from bad news.
punchline: The Boss presents news as positive without realizing it makes Dilbert's exhausting effort pointless, revealing he has no grasp of how his announcements affect his employees.
summary: A manager announces a delay as a gift to an employee who has just burned himself out meeting the original date, then muses that he can't distinguish happy tidings from awful ones.

file: 2001/2001-08-01_secretary_carol_order new chair_new chair smell_chair desert roll_not important enough_smelly chair_mean nasty_self centered_delusional boss.gif
title: Boss Refuses Carol His Old Chair

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, order a new chair for me. The old one lost its new chair smell.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Can I have your old chair? My chair doesn't roll anymore.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll try to say this tactfully: You're not important enough to sit in my smelly chair.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to order him a new chair because his current one no longer smells new. Carol asks if she can have his old chair since hers no longer rolls. The Boss refuses, claiming she isn't important enough to sit in it.
punchline: The Boss claims to be tactful while insulting Carol, saying she is unworthy of the very chair he is discarding for being worn out.
summary: A boss discards his chair for lacking that fresh smell, then insists his assistant is too unimportant to inherit it.

file: 2001/2001-11-18_binge eating_both mandatory and prohibited_budget freeze_corporate communications_cubicle_danville font_danville font software_department_negativity_next evaluation_non stop sobbing_approved corporate font_no eating_cubicles.gif
title: Mandatory Font, Frozen Software Budget

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, you didn't use the approved corporate font.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our corporate communications department says we have to use the Danville font.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: No problem. I'll buy the Danville font software today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's a budget freeze on software purchases.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: So... the Danville font is both mandatory and prohibited?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remind me to ding you for negativity on your next evaluation.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I think I'll do some binge eating and non-stop sobbing at my cubicle now.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Unless that's prohibited too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No eating in cubicles.

setting: The Boss's office, with a final panel of the two talking
situation: The Boss scolds Tina for not using the corporate-approved Danville font. When she offers to buy the font software, he reveals a budget freeze on software purchases. She points out the contradiction and is threatened with a negative evaluation, so she announces she will binge eat and sob in her cubicle, which he promptly bans too.
punchline: Management piles contradictory rules on an employee, punishes her for noticing, and even forbids her small act of coping.
summary: A writer is ordered to use a font that she is simultaneously forbidden to acquire, and her boss punishes her for pointing out the absurdity.

file: 2001/2001-09-02_new sales manager_pig boy_makes inappropriate comments_employment screening process_inappropriate comments_swear_date one eyed carpenter.gif
title: Pigboy's Inappropriate Comments Meet Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, meet our new sales manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's a pigboy who makes inappropriate comments every five minutes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Somehow he slipped through our rigorous employment screening process.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa! His five minutes are up.

transcript.speaker: Pigboy
transcript.text: So, Alice...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Inappropriate comment deleted

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That was very clever. Now let me try one.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Inappropriate comment deleted

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did you learn to swear like that?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I used to date a one-eyed carpenter.

situation: The Boss introduces Alice to a new sales manager, a pigboy who makes inappropriate comments every five minutes, and warns her ahead of time. When the pigboy starts to speak, his comment is censored, and Alice responds with an outburst of her own that is also censored. Afterward Dilbert asks how she learned to swear like that.
punchline: Alice's censored swearing is explained by her claim that she used to date a one-eyed carpenter, implying a lifetime of hammer-to-thumb cursing.
summary: A boorish new salesman who can't stop making crude remarks gets out-cursed by Alice, whose colorful vocabulary comes from a very odd former boyfriend.

file: 2001/2001-11-01_evil director_kitty litter_resumes_shredder.gif
title: Resumes Recycled as Kitty Litter

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We're almost out of kitty litter.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Gather all the résumés we got this week and run them through the shredder.

transcript.speaker: HR Employee
transcript.text: Shouldn't we be matching these with our openings?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's what we're doing.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells an HR employee that he's running low on kitty litter. He orders the staff to shred all the week's incoming résumés. When the employee asks whether they should be matching the résumés to job openings, Catbert claims shredding them is exactly what they're doing.
punchline: Catbert's 'matching' of résumés to openings is really just turning job applicants' hopes into cat litter, showing HR's contempt for the people it is supposed to hire.
summary: A feline human resources chief shreds job applications to refill his litter box and calls it the hiring process.

file: 2001/2001-04-24_magazine_key to success_optimistic_fail_point succeeding_feels good.gif
title: Optimism Makes Failure Feel Good

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The key to success is to remain optimistic even when you fail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the point of succeeding if failing feels good too?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll read another page of that magazine article tomorrow and get back to you.

situation: The Boss shares a snippet of advice from a magazine article, saying the key to success is staying optimistic even after failure. Dilbert responds with a logical objection: if failure feels good, success loses its meaning. The Boss, unable to answer, defers the question until he reads more of the article.
punchline: The Boss relies on shallow magazine advice and cannot answer a simple logical question, so he stalls by promising to read further.
summary: Armed with half a magazine article, a manager offers success advice that crumbles under one skeptical question.

file: 2001/2001-06-09_blah blah_escape_gnaw arm_non stop talker_trapped in cucbicle_want to escape_trapped animal_people leave.gif
title: Gnawing Arm to Escape Talker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Blah blah blah blah.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trapped in my own cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I can gnaw off my arm to escape.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And that worked?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People don't stick around when you gnaw on your arm.

situation: A talkative coworker stands at the entrance of Dilbert's cubicle and rambles on, leaving Dilbert feeling trapped. Dilbert thinks about gnawing off his own arm like a trapped animal. Later he tells Dogbert that he actually tried gnawing on his arm, and it got rid of the visitor.
punchline: Dilbert escapes a boring coworker by acting so bizarrely, gnawing on his own arm, that people avoid him.
summary: A cornered cubicle worker borrows a trapped animal's desperate tactic and discovers that looking unhinged is the surest way to be left alone.

file: 2001/2001-10-27_list_on head_pimples_trolls_finance trolls.gif
title: Dilbert Finds the Next Trolls

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, if all trolls were once people, that means some people are already changing and don't know it.

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: This is the list of people we're waiting for.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know something you don't know.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I think I'm getting pimples on my head.

setting: Rocky area where the troll lives, then the office
situation: Dilbert talks with a troll and works out that trolls were once people, so some people must be turning into trolls without knowing it. The troll shows him a list of people they are waiting for. Back at the office, Dilbert sings smugly to a bald coworker, who says he thinks he is getting pimples on his head, hinting that he is on the list.
punchline: The coworker's odd new pimples on his head suggest he is already turning into a troll, and Dilbert gleefully knows his fate before he does.
summary: After learning that people slowly turn into trolls, Dilbert sees a coworker's strange head bumps and gloats about the secret.

file: 2001/2001-09-01_out of engineer_more adminstrative_write reports_gradually shift_writing reports_vegetative.gif
title: Career Shift Toward Vegetative State

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I'd like to make a gradual shift out of engineering and into something more administrative.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: For example, I could write reports that tell other people how to do their jobs better.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Then I could gradually shift out of writing reports and into something more vegetative.

situation: A balding, bespectacled engineer stands before the boss's desk and describes his career plan. He wants to move from engineering into administration by writing reports that tell others how to do their jobs. He then adds that he would next drift out of report writing into something 'vegetative'.
punchline: The engineer's ideal career path ends in doing absolutely nothing, implying that administrative work is just a stepping stone to being a vegetable.
summary: A worker lays out a step-by-step plan to escape real work, finishing with a sly wish to become effectively brain-dead on the job.

file: 2001/2001-10-22_explain charge_budget season_trolls.gif
title: Dilbert Faces the Accounting Trolls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ask the trolls in accounting to explain this charge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaa!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please don't make me talk to the trolls during budget season!

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: Next.

setting: The Boss's office, then outside the accounting department's heavy arched stone door
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a piece of paper and orders him to ask the trolls in accounting to explain a charge. Dilbert begs not to be sent during budget season, but he ends up at the accounting department's stone doorway. A troll in a shirt and tie beckons him in with a curt call of 'Next', while another person leaves the door visibly shaken.
punchline: Accounting staff are literal trolls, so dealing with them during budget season is a terrifying ordeal that leaves people shell-shocked.
summary: Sent to question the monstrous accounting department over a disputed expense, a dreading Dilbert is summoned into their cave-like lair.

file: 2001/2001-07-10_managing by exception_do good job_project important_name.gif
title: Managing by Exception, Silence Means Anything

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on I'll be managing by exception.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I don't talk to you for months, assume you're doing a good job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...or that your project isn't important...or I don't remember your name.

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss stands over a seated, bald, bespectacled employee and announces a new management style of managing by exception. He says that months of silence from him should be read as a sign of good work, then adds that it could equally mean the project is unimportant or that he has forgotten the employee's name.
punchline: The boss's supposedly reassuring policy of silence is meaningless, since it could signal praise, irrelevance or simple forgetfulness, leaving the employee with no real feedback.
summary: A manager promises that no news means good news, then undermines himself by listing less flattering reasons he might stay silent.

file: 2001/2001-01-25_discount brokerage_estate plan_pass away_stay dead_zombie_bad gifts.gif
title: Estate Planning Advice: Stay Dead

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Discount Brokerage

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I need an estate plan for after I pass away.

transcript.speaker: Brokerage Agent
transcript.text: Here's a plan: Stay dead. No one likes a zombie.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What about gifts?

transcript.speaker: Brokerage Agent
transcript.text: Zombies make bad gifts.

setting: Discount brokerage call center, over the phone
situation: A customer phones a discount brokerage asking for an estate plan for after his death. The headset-wearing agent at a computer replies with a flippant 'plan' of simply staying dead because nobody likes a zombie. When the customer asks about gifts, the agent answers that zombies make bad gifts.
punchline: The discount brokerage agent offers absurd, useless zombie jokes instead of real estate planning, showing that cheap service means no actual expertise.
summary: A man seeking serious estate planning from a bargain brokerage gets nonsense about the undead in place of professional guidance.

file: 2001/2001-11-14_pulls knife_pleasure to meet_psycho hillbilly_crazy old coot_network design engineers.gif
title: Network Engineer Dressed as Psycho Hillbilly

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: GAAA!!

transcript.speaker: Network design engineer
transcript.text: Hi. It's a pleasure to meet you.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: You look like a psycho hillbilly.

transcript.speaker: Network design engineer
transcript.text: Thank you very much.

transcript.speaker: Network design engineer
transcript.text: We network design engineers like to dress with a theme.

transcript.speaker: Man in green shirt
transcript.text: May I call you crazy old coot?

setting: Office, with a plain lavender background
situation: A coworker in a green shirt and yellow tie recoils in shock when a shirtless, bearded network design engineer holding a large knife greets him politely. He remarks that the engineer looks like a psycho hillbilly, and the engineer takes it as a compliment, explaining that engineers dress with a theme. The coworker, now calm, asks whether he can call him a crazy old coot.
punchline: The coworker's fear melts into casual banter, treating a knife-wielding lunatic as just another quirky office eccentric whose odd behavior is excused as a dress theme.
summary: A startled employee meets a menacing, knife-brandishing colleague whose costume is dismissed as a quirky engineering tradition, and quickly starts trading insults with him.

file: 2001/2001-02-06_low battery indicator_work day and night_health decline_other peoples problems_creep likes.gif
title: Dilbert Enjoys Others' Feature Request Misery

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Feature Creep

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it too late to give our product a low-battery indicator?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd have to work night and day for a month! My health would decline and I'd miss all my objectives!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just realized that other people's problems make me all warm inside.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether it's too late to add a low-battery indicator to their product. Dilbert anxiously explains that it would mean a month of working day and night, ruining his health and causing him to miss his objectives. The Boss responds with cheerful satisfaction at Dilbert's suffering.
punchline: The Boss is not moved by the hardship his late feature request would cause, and instead admits he takes warm pleasure in other people's problems.
summary: A last-minute feature request from management leads to a bleak list of consequences, and the requester shows he enjoys the misery.

file: 2001/2001-09-28_ethical to clone_boss_borrow cloner_souls abomination_souls irrelevant.gif
title: Cloning The Boss: Soulless Abomination

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss asked me to clone him. Is that ethical?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: You'll either create a soulless abomination or, if the clone is normal, you will have shown that souls are irrelevant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if the original is already a soulless abomination?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: You can borrow my cloner. It's in the truck.

setting: Outdoors by a trash can, where a garbage man is collecting garbage
situation: Dilbert asks a garbage man whether it is ethical to clone his boss, as the boss has requested. The garbage man answers with a philosophical dilemma about souls. Dilbert points out that the boss may already be soulless, and the garbage man cheerfully offers to lend him his cloner from the truck.
punchline: Dilbert implies the boss is already a soulless abomination, and the garbage man not only agrees but happens to keep a cloning device in his garbage truck.
summary: Seeking ethical advice about duplicating his manager, Dilbert gets a philosophy lecture from a sanitation worker who then casually offers him cloning equipment.

file: 2001/2001-12-07_enjoyment_fire you_free country_free speech_outside of work_pastry_criticize government.gif
title: Free Speech, Except Around The Boss

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The great thing about free speech is that I can criticize the government.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd fire you.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I mean outside of work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd fire you for that too.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: May I express enjoyment of my pastry?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure. It's a free country.

setting: Conference room during a meeting with pastries and coffee
situation: At a meeting table, an employee says he loves that free speech lets him criticize the government. The Boss threatens to fire him, even for off-hours criticism. The cowed employee then timidly asks permission to say he enjoys his pastry, and the Boss graciously allows it, calling it a free country.
punchline: The Boss's idea of a free country only allows harmless speech, so the employee must ask permission just to say something positive about a pastry.
summary: A manager threatens to fire a worker for criticizing the government anywhere, then magnanimously permits him to praise his snack.

file: 2001/2001-02-25_achieve goal_analyze incoming email_automate_excellent plan_online tech_software_throw rocks_useful repsonse_wear ski masks_sarcas_supportiveness_engineering.gif
title: Automating Tech Support for Customer Dissatisfaction

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have an idea!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll automate our online tech support.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our software will analyze incoming e-mail and send responses based on key words!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's an excellent plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But what about the one percent of our customers who actually get a useful response?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we could wear ski masks and throw rocks at their houses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we could achieve our goal of 100% customer dissatisfaction!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Woo hoo!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should work someplace where sarcasm and supportiveness are different things.

situation: The Boss proudly announces a plan to automate online tech support with software that auto-replies to emails based on keywords. Dilbert sarcastically praises the plan, then suggests that customers who still get a useful response should be terrorized by masked rock-throwers. The Boss takes the sarcasm as genuine support and cheers the goal of total customer dissatisfaction.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he mistakes Dilbert's biting sarcasm for sincere support, and embraces the absurd goal of 100% customer dissatisfaction.
summary: A manager enthusiastically misreads his employee's mocking suggestions as genuine endorsement of a scheme to make customers miserable.

file: 2001/2001-05-04_software expenses_marketing software expenses_monkeys_wear watches_boss asks_budget_costs_expenses.gif
title: Monkeys Don't Wear Watches Budget Excuse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are our software expenses higher than marketing's software expenses?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: For the same reason that monkeys don't wear watches.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: An hour later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does it involve fur in any way?

situation: The Boss holds a piece of paper and asks Alice why the software expenses in their department are higher than marketing's. Alice answers with a nonsensical analogy about monkeys and watches. An hour later the Boss, still baffled, asks whether the explanation involves fur.
punchline: Alice's absurd non-answer is a sarcastic way of refusing to explain, and the Boss is so clueless that he spends an hour trying to work out the riddle and still can't.
summary: A manager questioning a budget gap gets a cryptic animal riddle from his employee and is still puzzling over it an hour later.

file: 2001/2001-05-21_vendor_drinks_answer questions_works_already wroking_date_private_business_confused_misunderstanding.gif
title: Vendor Drinks Date Misunderstanding

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm meeting a vendor for drinks tonight. He says it's the only time he has to answer my questions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If that works, please let us know.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What do you mean "works"? And who is "us"?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: It's already working!

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Alice tells her coworkers she is meeting a vendor for drinks because it is the only time he will answer her questions. Dilbert asks her to report back if the tactic works, and she bristles at the implication, while a bald coworker says it is already working, implying the vendor is flirting with her or that the meeting is a date.
punchline: The coworkers imply that Alice is being charmed or hit on by the vendor, so her 'business' drinks are a successful flirtation, and she is offended at the insinuation.
summary: A colleague's plan to get answers from a vendor over drinks draws knowing hints that she is being wooed, to her indignation.

file: 2001/2001-11-07_lost two pounds_yoga class_never sick_yoga prodicgy.gif
title: Wally's Yoga Class Without Attending

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've lost two pounds since I signed up for yoga class.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I never get sick anymore.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You haven't had a class yet.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe I'm some sort of yoga prodigy.

setting: Office break area beside the coffee maker
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, brags to Dilbert about the health benefits he has gotten since signing up for a yoga class. Dilbert points out that Wally has not actually attended a single class yet. Wally shrugs it off and concludes that he must be a natural yoga prodigy.
punchline: Wally takes credit for health improvements from a class he hasn't attended, reasoning that merely signing up proves he is gifted rather than admitting it's a coincidence.
summary: A coworker credits a yoga class he has never attended for his weight loss and good health, deciding his talent must be that extraordinary.

file: 2001/2001-02-07_creep_super powers of creep_sexy_oomp_flirt with alice_creep and alice.gif
title: Feature Creep's Sexy Superpower

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Feature Creep

transcript.speaker: Feature Creep
transcript.text: Being a feature creep is like having a super power.

transcript.speaker: Feature Creep
transcript.text: That's what makes me so sexy.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Oomp

transcript.speaker: Feature Creep
transcript.text: That oomp sound just bought you a new feature, Missy.

situation: The Feature Creep, a bald man in a green jacket, brags to Alice that being a feature creep is like having a superpower and that it makes him sexy. Alice reacts with a disgusted 'oomp' sound, and the Feature Creep treats her reaction as a request, announcing it has just earned her a new feature.
punchline: Even Alice's noise of revulsion gets interpreted by the Feature Creep as a requirement, so her disgust only adds to her workload.
summary: A self-admiring feature-adding pest turns a colleague's groan of disgust into one more thing she now has to build.

file: 2001/2001-03-20_phone call_outgoing message_paris_press one_movie_press two_bad feeling.gif
title: Date's Answering Machine Menu Prank

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope she's home.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Beep boop beep

transcript.speaker: Answering Machine
transcript.text: If you'd like to take me to Paris, press one. If you are inviting me to a lousy movie, press two.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got a bad feeling about this.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Beep

setting: Dilbert's home, while making a phone call
situation: Dilbert dials a woman's number, hoping she will be home to take his call. He reaches her automated outgoing message, which offers a menu: press one to take her to Paris, or two to invite her to a lousy movie. Realizing his date idea is probably the lousy movie, he gets a bad feeling and reluctantly presses a button.
punchline: The woman's voicemail menu makes it obvious that only a lavish trip will impress her, so Dilbert's modest movie invitation is doomed to fail.
summary: A hopeful Dilbert phones a woman only to be greeted by a recording that ranks dates by how extravagant they are, leaving him dreading his own plan.

file: 2001/2001-07-25_evolution training_zoltar_graduate_class_new sideburns_speed evolution.gif
title: Speed Evolving Zoltar's Sideburns

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Evolution training

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Zoltar is a graduate of this class. He will demonstrate speed evolving.

transcript.speaker: Zoltar
transcript.text: Unh... errr... hoo... ahh...

transcript.speaker: Zoltar
transcript.text: I hope you're staring at my new sideburns.

setting: A training session where Dogbert stands on a stool next to Zoltar, a bald man in a red sweater
situation: Dogbert, standing on a stool, introduces Zoltar as a graduate of his evolution training class who will demonstrate speed evolving. Zoltar strains and grunts visibly through the second panel. In the last panel he proudly points out that the only visible result is a pair of new sideburns.
punchline: After all the dramatic straining, the supposed speed evolution produces only a trivial change, a bit of sideburn growth, exposing the training as worthless.
summary: A man grunts through a showy demonstration of rapid evolution only to reveal that all he has grown is a little facial hair.

file: 2001/2001-07-14_layoff planning_fire people_creeps_excessive nose haor_called doctor_five minute meeting.gif
title: Layoff Criteria: Nose Hair and Doctors

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Layoff planning

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's fire all the people who give us the creeps...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...all the people with excessive nose hair and anyone who insists on being called "Doctor."

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: You've got a five-minute meeting on Friday, Doctor Wolfington.

setting: Conference room during a layoff planning session, then an office cubicle
situation: The Boss and Catbert sit at a table covered in papers planning layoffs. The Boss proposes firing people who give them the creeps, those with excessive nose hair, and anyone who insists on being called "Doctor." In the last panel a woman tells a balding, bespectacled man with visible nose hair that he has a five-minute meeting on Friday and addresses him as Doctor Wolfington.
punchline: The layoff criteria are petty and arbitrary, and the unlucky Doctor Wolfington matches them perfectly, so his five-minute Friday meeting is almost certainly his firing.
summary: Management drafts absurdly shallow layoff rules, and a nose-haired employee who insists on his title is promptly summoned to a short meeting.

file: 2001/2001-11-17_day off_move my home_one hour_negotiate_can't use vehicle.gif
title: Boss Negotiates Moving Day Down

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I have a day off to move my home?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: One hour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? Why only one hour?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like to negotiate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I can try doing it in one hour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you can't use a vehicle.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a day off so he can move to a new home. The boss offers just one hour, then explains he simply enjoys negotiating. When Dilbert gives in and agrees to attempt it, the boss piles on a further restriction that he can't use a vehicle.
punchline: The boss treats negotiation as a game he can't lose, so Dilbert's concession is rewarded by an even more absurd demand, proving the 'negotiation' was never in good faith.
summary: A worker requesting time off for a house move gets bargained down to a ridiculous limit by a boss who just likes to haggle.

file: 2001/2001-04-02_401k_run that far_10k wheelchair race_whip marks.gif
title: Boss Mistakes 401k for Running Race

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Why aren't you signed up for the 401k?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd never be able to run that far.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I did a 10k wheelchair race once. The guy who pushed me still has whip marks.

situation: Catbert, holding a form, asks the Boss why he hasn't enrolled in the company 401k retirement plan. The Boss misunderstands it as a long-distance race and says he could never run that far. He then boasts about a wheelchair race in which the person pushing him was whipped.
punchline: The Boss confuses a 401k retirement plan with a footrace, then reveals he treated the person pushing his wheelchair like a draft animal.
summary: A manager misreads a retirement savings plan as a marathon and then brags about cruelly driving the person who pushed his wheelchair.

file: 2001/2001-11-08_wally.yoga classes_yoga or yoda_suspicious.gif
title: Wally's Suspicious Yoga Class

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally looks different.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He changed when he started yoga classes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I'm saying is that it might not be a "yoga" class.

transcript.speaker: Yoda
transcript.text: Suspicious you are.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert that Wally has changed since he began taking yoga classes. Dilbert suggests the class might not really be yoga, and a small green Yoda-like figure sitting in a purple chair replies in Yoda's backwards speech.
punchline: Dilbert's doubt about whether it's 'yoga' is turned into a pun on Yoda, who appears and speaks in his inverted syntax, implying Wally may be taking Jedi training instead.
summary: A coworker's odd transformation after yoga lessons prompts a skeptical remark that gets answered by a famous space sage.

file: 2001/2001-06-19_co pilot seat_fly 747_pilot_chiroparcter_people flying plane_commercial airline_over booked_random.gif
title: Dilbert Lies His Way Into Cockpit

transcript.speaker: Gate Agent
transcript.text: We overbooked. But I can give you the co-pilot's seat if you know how to fly a 747.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... yeah, okay. I can fly a 747.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I do something?

transcript.speaker: Pilot
transcript.text: Beats me. I'm a chiropractor.

situation: An airline agent tells Dilbert the flight is overbooked and offers him the co-pilot's seat if he can fly a 747. Dilbert claims he can to avoid being bumped, and ends up in the cockpit. The man in the pilot's seat turns out to be a chiropractor who also lied his way aboard, so nobody is qualified to fly.
punchline: The overbooking workaround rewards lying, so both seats in the cockpit are occupied by unqualified passengers, one of them a chiropractor.
summary: A bumped passenger bluffs his way into a jumbo jet's cockpit only to discover the other seat holder is equally unqualified.

file: 2001/2001-08-05_key employees_catbert_write in_insane_hr department_interoffice envelope_same job as enevelope_funkey_downsize employees.gif
title: Carol Not a Key Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, take this list of key employees to Catbert.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I don't see my name on here. Should I write it in?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... no. You're not a key employee.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What?! Are you insane?!! If I'm not key, who is?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Do you think this list can walk to the H.R. department on its own?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I could put it in an inter-office envelope and mail it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Basically, you have the same job as an envelope.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Why do I need to downsize these employees?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Because they're funkey, just like it says.

setting: Office cubicle area and the H.R. department
situation: The Boss asks his secretary Carol to deliver a list of key employees to Catbert in H.R. Carol notices she isn't on it and is offended, and the Boss compares her job to that of an inter-office envelope. Carol then delivers the list to Catbert and, misreading the list's purpose, tells him that the people on it are 'funkey', so he downsizes them.
punchline: Carol takes revenge by misreading the list of key employees as 'funkey' employees, so the people the Boss wanted protected get downsized instead.
summary: A secretary insulted by her exclusion from a list of important staff gets even by handing the H.R. cat a twisted version of what the list means.

file: 2001/2001-04-27_dilbert_therapy session_everyone is lying_stock market_congress_boss_therapy_scientifically proven_money_psychology_politics.gif
title: Therapist Lies About Therapy Effectiveness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It feels like everyone in the world is lying to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Congress is lying about the budget, stock analysts are lying about their recommendations, my boss is lying...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This therapy stuff is scientifically proven to work, right?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: It's 100% effective.

situation: Dilbert lies on a couch in therapy and complains that everyone around him, from Congress to stock analysts to his boss, is lying to him. At the end of the session he asks his therapist to confirm that therapy is scientifically proven to work. She replies that it is 100% effective.
punchline: The therapist's implausibly perfect claim of 100% effectiveness is exactly the kind of lie Dilbert was complaining about, so she proves his paranoia justified.
summary: A man convinced that everybody lies to him seeks reassurance from his counselor and gets an obviously inflated guarantee in return.

file: 2001/2001-02-21_positive reinforcement_addicted_delivarables_praised.gif
title: Alice Craves Praise, Needs Deliverables

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm addicted to positive reinforcement.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need some deliverables so I can be praised again.

setting: Office cubicle and a conference room with an overhead projector
situation: Alice sits at her desk in thought bubbles, admitting she is addicted to praise and needs more deliverables so she can earn it again. In the last panel, Dilbert presents a 'Results' pie chart showing 10% to an audience, while a hand reaches up from behind an overhead projector in the foreground.
punchline: Alice's thoughts reveal that her drive to complete work is really a craving for praise, like an addict seeking a fix, and her hand reaching up toward the projector gives the final panel a literal 'reaching for a fix' feel.
summary: A employee privately confesses that her work ethic is really a craving for approval, driven by the next round of compliments.

file: 2001/2001-04-17_cubicle_sucking life force_happening faster_life suck 3000_machine_evil catbert.gif
title: Cubicle Life-Sucking Machine Noticed

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My cubicle is sucking the life force out of me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I mean, it always has, but it seems like it's happening faster now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They noticed.

setting: Dilbert's office, then a stone dungeon-like room with a large machine
situation: Dilbert complains to his boss that his cubicle is draining his life force and that it seems to be happening faster lately. In the last panel, the boss stands in a stone chamber beside a huge machine labeled LifeSuck 3000, operated by the red devilish Catbert, and reports that they noticed.
punchline: The cubicle really is draining employees' life force by design, using a machine, and management's only reaction is to acknowledge that Dilbert has noticed it.
summary: A worker's offhand grumble about his soul-crushing workspace turns out to be literally true, as an evil machine is revealed to be draining employees on purpose.

file: 2001/2001-03-10_honest vendor_not nice to meet_weird_spank hamster_business is over reated_repeat business.gif
title: The Honest Vendor Insults Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Honest Vendor

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: It wasn't nice to meet you.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: You didn't buy enough; I'll probably spank my hamster for no reason.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Repeat business is overrated.

situation: A salesman who refuses to be dishonestly polite meets Dilbert and shakes his hand. He tells Dilbert it wasn't nice to meet him, then complains that Dilbert didn't buy enough and says he will take it out on his pet hamster. In the last panel he thinks that repeat business is overrated.
punchline: The vendor says aloud the rude things salespeople normally hide, and his thought that he doesn't need repeat customers explains why he can afford to be this nasty.
summary: A brutally candid salesman drops all pretense of courtesy and grumbles at a customer who spent too little.

file: 2001/2001-12-22_important document_signed petition_nobel peace prize_sip_trade ya.gif
title: Peace Petition Traded for Drink

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob, I hold in my hands the most important document ever created.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a signed petition to end war. I expect to win the Nobel Peace Prize for this.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: May I have a sip of that?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Trade ya.

setting: A table at a cafe or restaurant, with Dogbert and Bob seated across from each other
situation: Dogbert proudly announces that he holds a signed petition to end war and expects to win the Nobel Peace Prize for it. Bob is sitting across from him with a drink. Dogbert then asks for a sip of Bob's drink, and Bob offers to swap it for the petition.
punchline: Bob treats the supposedly world-changing peace petition as just another item to barter for a sip of his drink, deflating Dogbert's grandiose claims.
summary: A self-important dog brags about a document that will end all war, only for his friend to casually propose swapping a beverage for it.

file: 2001/2001-06-10_defective co workers_hall of fame_won't work_components_too close_overheat_explain back_moron_sunflower seed_mimics_bird mimics.gif
title: Parrot Man Repeats Dilbert's Warnings

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Defective Co-Workers Hall of Fame

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Parrot Man

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your idea won't work. The components are too close. They will overheat.

transcript.speaker: Parrot Man
transcript.text: Let me explain something to you, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Parrot Man
transcript.text: These components will overheat. They are much too close.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The reasons involve heat and something I call "proximity."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Parrot Man
transcript.text: I don't have time to explain all the details.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You take everything I say and explain it back to me like I'm a moron!!

transcript.speaker: Parrot Man
transcript.text: Excuse me, but I hear a clicking sound and feel compelled to eat a sunflower seed.

situation: Dilbert tells a green, parrot-like co-worker that his idea will fail because the components are too close and will overheat. The co-worker repeats Dilbert's own words back as if explaining them to him, then repeats Dilbert's follow-up too. Dilbert finally screams in frustration at being condescended to with his own explanation.
punchline: The co-worker literally parrots everything Dilbert says, passing it off as his own explanation, and even ends by acting on a bird instinct to eat a sunflower seed when he hears Dilbert's clicking pen or similar noise.
summary: A co-worker who behaves like a parrot echoes a colleague's technical objections back at him as though lecturing him, driving him to frustration.

file: 2001/2001-10-19_talk about layoffs_hostile questions_reading_newspapaer_reeking slime.gif
title: Boss Prepares for Hostile Layoff Questions

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We need to have an all-company meeting to talk about the layoffs.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You might get some hostile questions owing to the fact that they found out about the layoffs by reading the newspaper.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I've never noticed that I leave a trail of reeking slime wherever I slither.

setting: The Boss's office, then a company meeting podium
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, advises the Boss that an all-company meeting about layoffs is needed and warns that employees may be hostile because they learned of the layoffs from the newspaper. The Boss, now at a podium, answers a question as if someone has accused him of leaving a trail of slime.
punchline: The Boss's reply is a sarcastic rejoinder to a hostile question, with the implication that he is as slimy as employees think and is dismissing their complaints with mock denial.
summary: After the staff learn about downsizing from the press, the HR cat coaches his boss for an angry town hall, where the boss sarcastically brushes off accusations of being slimy.

file: 2001/2001-03-03_manager_alice_big favor_pillow_kidding_struggle.gif
title: Alice Hates Management So Much

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How do you like being a manager, Alice?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do me a big favor; sneak into my house tonight and smother me with a pillow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think she was kidding.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll see if she puts up a struggle.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee mug asks Alice how she likes being a manager. Alice replies with a deadpan request that he sneak into her house and smother her with a pillow. Dilbert says she must be kidding, but the coworker says he will go find out whether she resists.
punchline: Alice's job as a manager is so miserable that she would rather be killed in her sleep, and the oblivious coworker takes her sarcastic request literally as a test of whether she really means it.
summary: A newly promoted manager answers a casual question about her job by begging to be put out of her misery, and a clueless colleague treats the plea as an invitation.

file: 2001/2001-03-14_germs_safe from germs_alice_sneeze_blows up_germ safety device.gif
title: Alice Sneezes Into Hazmat Hood

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm safe from your germs, Alice. You can sneeze all you want.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Aah...

situation: A coworker wearing a yellow protective hood and carrying a filter canister tells Alice she can't infect him anymore and invites her to sneeze. Alice grabs the breathing hose connected to his suit, holds it to her face and sneezes into it. The sneeze inflates his hood like a giant balloon.
punchline: His germ-protection gear has a hose Alice can easily reach, so inviting her to sneeze backfires: her sneeze goes straight into his sealed suit and blows it up.
summary: A smug germophobe in a sealed protective suit dares a coworker to sneeze, and she cleverly redirects the sneeze through his own air hose.

file: 2001/2001-09-18_job market_bad job market_how hard_unemployed_leader.gif
title: Boss Exploits Bad Job Market

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's the ol' job market lately? It's pretty bad, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So no matter how hard I make you work it's still better than being unemployed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who's your leader? Go on, say it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are.

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and gloats about the weak job market. He points out that Dilbert has no better option than to endure any workload, then makes him declare the Boss his leader. Dilbert, slumped with his head in his hands, complies.
punchline: The Boss uses high unemployment as leverage to demand overwork and humiliating deference, and Dilbert has no choice but to submit.
summary: Taking advantage of scarce jobs elsewhere, a manager smugly rubs in his employee's lack of options and forces him to praise his leadership.

file: 2001/2001-11-20_mud delivery business_highly trained engineer_business model_deliver mud_people live in mud.gif
title: Engineer Fixes Absurd Mud Delivery Business

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm supposed to shut down our Elbonian mud delivery business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I'm a highly trained engineer so I will analyze their business model and fix it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They deliver mud to people who live in mud.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have my attention.

setting: Dilbert's home, bedroom while he packs a suitcase
situation: Dilbert is packing a suitcase and tells Dogbert he has been assigned to shut down the company's Elbonian mud delivery business. He then declares that, as a trained engineer, he will instead analyze the business model and fix it. Dogbert points out that the business delivers mud to people who already live in mud, which immediately grabs Dilbert's attention.
punchline: Dilbert's engineering urge to fix things kicks in at the absurdity of the business model, so instead of shutting the operation down he is drawn in by the very flaw that makes it ridiculous.
summary: A man told to terminate a failing foreign venture is instead lured into trying to repair it when his dog reveals how nonsensical its core business is.

file: 2001/2001-04-09_discovered oil_wild life perserve_elbonian_endangered species_no impact_drilled unicorn_dead_animals_drill fields.gif
title: Oil Drilling Impales Endangered Unicorn

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've discovered oil in the Elbonian wildlife preserve.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry about the endangered species. Our drilling will have no impact.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Oops.

setting: Conference room, then an Elbonian oil drilling site
situation: In a meeting, the Boss announces that oil has been found in the Elbonian wildlife preserve and assures everyone the drilling will not affect the endangered species. In the final panel, an Elbonian worker stands at a drilling rig while a unicorn lies impaled on the drill pipe, and he says 'Oops.'
punchline: The Boss's assurance of 'no impact' is immediately contradicted by a unicorn skewered on the drill, showing how companies dismiss environmental harm.
summary: A manager promises that oil drilling in a nature reserve will not harm rare animals, but the drilling site reveals a unicorn impaled on the rig.

file: 2001/2001-11-27_dogcart airplines_flight exits_35 hours_flight delayed_weather_direct sunlight.gif
title: Dogbert Airlines Blames Sunlight

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Airlines

transcript.speaker: Passenger
transcript.text: I've been waiting for 35 hours. Are you sure my flight exists?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to my computer your flight is delayed by weather.

transcript.speaker: Passenger
transcript.text: What kind of weather?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our planes can't handle direct sunlight.

setting: Dogbert Airlines check-in counter at an airport
situation: A passenger who has waited 35 hours asks the Dogbert Airlines agent whether his flight even exists. Dogbert checks his computer and says the flight is delayed by weather. When asked what weather, he says the planes can't handle direct sunlight.
punchline: The airline's excuse of 'weather' is absurdly flimsy, since sunlight is fine weather, which suggests the airline is making up reasons for its incompetence.
summary: An airline agent offers a ridiculous weather excuse to a passenger stranded for a day and a half.

file: 2001/2001-11-11_downsize you_ted_bad job_essentail function_cost reductions_marketing_spent too much_trade show booth_dept phone list._business.gif
title: Layoff List Sent By Accident

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I have to downsize you.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Was I doing a bad job?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, it's more complicated than that.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Is my essential function being eliminated?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, the problem is that someone in marketing spent too much for a trade show booth.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So every manager had to submit a list of potential cost reductions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I might have accidentally sent the department phone list as an e-mail attachment.
