transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There are lots of whiners in "A" through "M."

situation: The Boss tells Ted he has to be downsized, and Ted asks whether it's his performance or his role being eliminated. The Boss explains that a marketing overspend triggered a demand for cost-cutting lists, and that he mistakenly submitted the entire department phone list instead of a list of reductions. Ted's name is on it simply because of the alphabet.
punchline: Ted is being laid off not for performance or necessity but because the boss sent in the phone list by mistake, so people are cut alphabetically, and the boss justifies it by assuming everyone in the cut range is a whiner.
summary: A manager lays off an employee for reasons that turn out to be a chain of unrelated blunders and an alphabetical accident.

file: 2001/2001-09-22_new hircut_gargantuan_mistake_frighten children_froze up_opinion.gif
title: Honest Opinion Of New Haircut

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you guys think about my new haircut?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a gargantuan mistake that will ruin your life, frighten children and bruise fruit.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm all froze up! No one ever asked for my opinion before!

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert asks his pets what they think of his new haircut. Dogbert responds with a long, exaggerated insult about how terrible it is. Ratbert, who has never been asked for his opinion before, freezes up and can't answer.
punchline: Dogbert gives a brutally over-the-top honest assessment, while Ratbert is so unused to being consulted that he panics and can't contribute anything.
summary: Asked to judge a fresh haircut, one pet unleashes a withering critique while the other is paralyzed by the unfamiliar experience of being asked at all.

file: 2001/2001-08-11_cure for carpel tunnel_eat six bananas_hands of teenager_data_medical advice_huge pimple.gif
title: Banana Cure for Carpal Tunnel

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The cure for carpal tunnel is to eat six bananas a day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what I do and I have the hands of a teenager.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Do you have any data to support your medical advice?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does a huge pimple count?

situation: The Boss stands over an employee at his computer and offers unsolicited medical advice, claiming that eating six bananas a day cures carpal tunnel syndrome. When the employee asks for data supporting this claim, the Boss offers a huge pimple as his evidence.
punchline: The Boss's only proof that his banana cure works is the teenager-like pimple he has, which is absurd and not real medical data.
summary: A manager prescribes a banana-heavy diet for wrist pain and, when pressed for evidence, cites his own acne as proof of youthful hands.

file: 2001/2001-12-19_written objectives_hidden objectives_smothered with defectiveness.gif
title: Wally's Hidden Objective: Defective Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, you have failed to achieve any of your written objectives.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But by pure chance you achieved all of my hidden objectives.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's another project I need smothered with defectiveness.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm all over it.

situation: The Boss tells Wally he has failed every one of his formal written objectives. He then reveals that Wally accidentally met all of the Boss's secret objectives, and hands him another project he wants ruined with defects. Wally, holding his coffee mug, cheerfully accepts.
punchline: Wally's chronic incompetence and laziness is exactly what the Boss secretly wants, so his failure counts as success and he is rewarded with more projects to botch.
summary: A manager praises his least productive employee for secretly delivering the sabotage he really wanted and assigns him a fresh project to wreck.

file: 2001/2001-12-04_reserve conference room_everyday_next year_sociopath_beat you to it_slowest sociopath.gif
title: Slowest Sociopath Loses Conference Room

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, reserve the conference room every day for the next year in case I need it.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You're too late. Some other sociopath had the same idea and beat you to it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hate being the slowest sociopath.

situation: The Boss orders his assistant Carol to book the conference room every day for the next year just in case he needs it. Carol flatly informs him that another selfish person already did exactly that. The Boss then grumbles to himself about being outpaced.
punchline: The Boss's only complaint is that he wasn't the first to hoard the conference room, which reveals that he and his colleagues are all equally selfish, scheming sociopaths.
summary: A manager tries to monopolize the meeting space for a year, only to learn a more ruthless colleague got there first.

file: 2001/2001-12-23_use vacation time_finish project_find solution_come to work on vacation_network remotely.gif
title: Vacation Spent Hanging Outside Office Window

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you need to use your vacation time before the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't have time. I need to finish my project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sure that a highly trained engineer like you can find a solution.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well...I could say I'm on vacation and come to work as usual.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. I can't count it as vacation unless you're not in the building.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay...I could take home my computer and work there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No...you're not allowed to access our network remotely.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: *!#%$ Worst vacation ever...

situation: The Boss orders Alice to use up her vacation days before year end, but she says she must finish her project. Each workaround she proposes, working at the office while officially on vacation or working from home, is rejected by the Boss on policy grounds. In the last panel she is dangling from a rope outside the office window, typing on a laptop while technically not in the building.
punchline: Boxed in by rigid rules, Alice finds the only loophole that satisfies them all: working on her laptop hanging outside the building's window, which makes for a miserable vacation.
summary: Cornered by contradictory policies, an overworked engineer ends up dangling from a rope outside her office window to do her job while technically on holiday.

file: 2001/2001-10-01_cloning the boss_problem with clone_dna module_one half horse.gif
title: Boss's Clone Is Half Horse Posterior

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Cloning the boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a problem with your clone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally spilled soda on the DNA module. Your clone is one-half horse posterior.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And one-half that isn't like you.

situation: Dilbert, dressed in surgical scrubs and a mask, tells The Boss, who is lying on a table, that his clone is defective. Wally spilled soda on the DNA module, so the clone came out half horse posterior. Dilbert then adds a second insult about the other half.
punchline: The clone is half horse's rear end, and Dilbert adds that the other half is unlike the Boss, implying the Boss is entirely a horse's rear end.
summary: A lab technician breaks the news that a soda accident left the boss's clone partly a horse's rear, then slips in a dig about the remaining portion.

file: 2001/2001-05-06_new guy_cheese_parmesan cheese_truck loads_offer_world o cheese exhibit_weird obsession_cheese obsession_cheeseboy_wally leather_leather products.gif
title: The Too Helpful Guy's Cheese Obsession

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Too Helpful Guy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet the new guy.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: Do you like cheese, Dilbert?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... yes, I guess so.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: I'll send two truckloads of Parmesan cheese to your house!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks... but I don't need that much cheese.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: Message received!

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: I'll send you some bread and a fondue set too.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: Here are two tickets to the "World-O-Cheese" exhibit in Wisconsin.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: Your new nickname will be "Cheeseboy" to reflect your weird obsession.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hi. I'm Wally.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: Wally, do you like leather products?

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to the new guy, who asks a casual question about whether Dilbert likes cheese. The overeager new guy escalates, offering truckloads of Parmesan, a fondue set, exhibit tickets, and finally a nickname mocking Dilbert's supposed obsession. He then turns to Wally and asks about leather products, about to repeat the pattern.
punchline: One mild admission of liking cheese gets blown into an absurd obsession by an overzealous coworker, and Wally is about to suffer the same fate with leather.
summary: A new coworker takes a polite yes about cheese and spirals into gifts and a mocking nickname before moving on to his next victim.

file: 2001/2001-03-30_agree who's fault_meeting_men_so mature_trip victory lap_won meeting_your fault_delays_business.gif
title: Winning the Meeting, Tripped Up

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: ...And so you agree that the delays are your fault?

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: Yeh.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I won the meeting!!

transcript.speaker: Man with papers
transcript.text: Only a sore loser would trip someone on his victory lap.

transcript.speaker: Man with coffee mug
transcript.text: He is so-o-o immature.

setting: Conference room, then an office hallway
situation: In a meeting, a coworker gets a colleague to admit that the project delays are his fault. He then jumps up and celebrates having won the meeting. Afterward he is seen in the hall, apparently tripped, and the man holding a coffee mug calls the tripper immature.
punchline: The man who won the meeting by pinning blame on a colleague is the one now calling someone else immature, even though his own gloating is just as childish.
summary: A worker celebrates a petty meeting victory over who caused the delays, then complains when a rival trips him as he gloats.

file: 2001/2001-11-03_eliminate vacation days_increase sick days_make themselves sick_evil_hr.gif
title: Evil HR Plan: Replace Vacation With Sick Days

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Asok works in H.R.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If we eliminate vacation days and increase sick days...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Would the employees fall for our trap and make themselves sick to get days off?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What?!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're in H.R. now. It's okay to be evil.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Evil, right.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, floats a policy idea to new HR employee Asok: abolish vacation days and give more sick days instead. He wonders aloud whether employees would deliberately make themselves ill to get time off. When Asok is shocked, Catbert reminds him that being evil is perfectly acceptable in HR.
punchline: Asok's horror at an obviously manipulative policy is dismissed because in the HR department, cruelty toward employees is simply part of the job.
summary: A cat in charge of personnel proposes a devious scheme to push staff into harming their own health, then coaches his shocked new colleague that villainy comes with the department.

file: 2001/2001-08-27_perfromance_exceeds expectations_underachievers_extra money_go get money.gif
title: Alice Hunts Underachievers for Money

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My performance exceeds expectations but my pay is based on market averages.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I figure some underachievers are getting the extra money that I earn.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Give me their names so I can go get my money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's Wally.

situation: Alice stands before the Boss's desk and complains that she outperforms expectations but is paid only a market average. She reasons that underperforming coworkers are collecting the extra money she has earned and demands their names so she can reclaim it. The Boss instantly names Wally.
punchline: The Boss answers without hesitation that Wally is the underachiever, implying everyone knows he is paid for doing nothing and that the Boss knowingly tolerates it.
summary: A high-performing employee demands the names of the slackers she believes are pocketing her rightful pay, and her manager immediately offers up the office's most notorious loafer.

file: 2001/2001-10-14_meeting_vague intrsutcions_morons annonymous_pandemonium_ends_shoe sniffing contest_mom called_arguments_business.gif
title: Carol Mocks Boss's Fake Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, if anyone calls, say I'm in a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What meeting?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It doesn't matter.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Rrring

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: (thought) #@!*# Vague instructions.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He's at his weekly meeting of "Morons Anonymous."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's a long meeting. They usually get into an argument about the definition of "anonymous."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Half of them think it means "angry." Then someone throws a chair and it's pandemonium.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The whole thing usually ends with a shoe-sniffing contest.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your mom called.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to say he is in a meeting if anyone calls, but gives no details. When the phone rings, Carol invents an elaborate story that he is at a weekly 'Morons Anonymous' meeting, complete with arguments and chair-throwing. The Boss, who has been standing nearby, then reveals the caller was her mom.
punchline: Carol's sarcastic cover story insults the Boss to the caller, only for the Boss to reveal the caller was her own mother, leaving her embarrassed.
summary: An assistant given no guidance on her boss's absence invents an insulting fictional support-group meeting, only to learn she was talking to her own mother.

file: 2001/2001-09-20_music in offcie_can't concentrate_turn it down_drive you nuts_complain_cubicles_separation_desks.gif
title: Music Turned Down Just Enough

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could you turn off the music? I can't concentrate.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How about if I turn it down to a level where it still drives you nuts but you're too shy to complain a second time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It might creep up over time.

situation: Dilbert peers over his cubicle wall and asks a neighboring coworker, who is playing music at his computer, to turn it off. The coworker counters with a deal to lower the volume so it remains annoying but not enough to prompt another complaint. Dilbert thanks him, and the coworker adds that the volume may gradually rise again.
punchline: The coworker cynically admits his compromise is designed to exploit Dilbert's shyness, and Dilbert politely thanks him anyway, while the volume is likely to creep back up.
summary: A noisy cubicle neighbor offers a sneaky volume compromise that relies on his colleague's reluctance to speak up again.

file: 2001/2001-03-28_power utility company_director marketing_increase revenue_herbivore.gif
title: Dinosaur Boss Lets Lights Go Out

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Bob, I'm starting a power utility company.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: You'll be my director of marketing. Your job is to increase revenue.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Normally I'm an herbivore, Billy, but when the lights go off...

setting: A pink-walled room with a couch, then a child's bedroom at night
situation: Bob the green dinosaur announces to Billy that he is starting a power utility company and appoints him director of marketing, tasked with increasing revenue. In the last panel, a frightened child in bed, with a stuffed animal and a glowing lamp, hears Bob's ominous warning about what he does when the lights go off.
punchline: Bob's marketing plan for his power company is to terrorize children into keeping their lights on by threatening to turn predatory in the dark, thereby boosting electricity consumption.
summary: A dinosaur launches an electric company and drives up demand by scaring a child into never turning off the light.

file: 2001/2001-02-19_stange_beautiufl_felling_waves_ecstacy_positive reinforcement_tingly_soul_good words from boss.gif
title: Boss Rations Praise, Alice Ecstatic

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What is this strange and beautiful feeling inside of me?!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Waves of ecstasy are pulsing through my soul.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is why I only give positive reinforcement once a year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm all tingly!

situation: Alice, normally hostile and worn down by work, is overwhelmed by a strange euphoria after receiving some positive feedback from the boss. She describes waves of ecstasy in her soul while the boss sits in his chair watching her reaction. He explains that the intensity of her response is why he gives praise only once a year, and he is thrilled by the effect himself.
punchline: The boss rations compliments not to be fair or sensible but because he enjoys the dramatic, intoxicating effect that rare praise has on starved employees, and he gets a thrill from it himself.
summary: After a rare kind word from management, an employee is swept up in rapture, and her boss gleefully admits that scarcity is exactly why he hands out praise so seldom.

file: 2001/2001-10-04_six sigma consulatant_increased profits_industry downturns_flat growth_industries_upturned.gif
title: Six Sigma Consultant's Shrinking Success Claim

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Six Sigma Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Every company that used my Six Sigma program increased profits.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...Except for the ones that were in industry downturns...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...Or flat growth industries...or industries that only upturned a little bit.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a Six Sigma consultant, pitches his program to The Boss and Dilbert by claiming every company that used it increased profits. He then keeps adding exceptions, excluding downturn industries, flat growth industries and those with only slight upturns.
punchline: The consultant's claim of universal success is hollowed out by so many caveats that it only holds true for companies that would have profited anyway.
summary: A consultant touts a flawless track record, then piles on qualifications until the boast means almost nothing.

file: 2001/2001-02-03_sales department_die_deaths_bile_quality control.gif
title: Cursing Sales Department Call Monitored

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Hello, is this the sales department?

transcript.speaker: Hooded Figure
transcript.text: May you die a thousand deaths by choking on your own bile!

transcript.speaker: Hooded Figure
transcript.text: A supervisor may be monitoring this call for quality control.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: It's good.

setting: A modern office desk in panel one; a muddy, swampy landscape with a pig in the other panels
situation: A man at a desk phones what he thinks is a sales department. The call is answered by robed, bearded figures standing in a mud pit with tin-can telephones, who greet him with a vicious curse. A second figure then adds the usual disclaimer that a supervisor may be monitoring the call, and the supervisor approves of the curse.
punchline: The sales department's customer service is a hateful curse delivered with a polite quality-control disclaimer, and the supervisor judges the cruelty to be good service.
summary: A customer who calls for sales gets a malicious curse in place of a greeting, and the monitoring supervisor happily rates it as good quality.

file: 2001/2001-02-24_alice the manager_emptiness_no soul_play air guitar_dance.gif
title: Coping With Soullessness Through Air Guitar

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How do I cope with the emptiness of having no soul?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try doing this with your teeth while you dance.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is there another way?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I can teach you to play air guitar.

setting: Office, under the banner 'Alice the Manager'
situation: Alice, newly a manager, asks the horned human-resources figure how to deal with the emptiness of having no soul. He suggests an odd teeth-and-dancing routine, and when she asks for an alternative, he offers to teach her air guitar.
punchline: Management has hollowed Alice out, and the only remedies on offer are absurd, trivial distractions like air guitar that do nothing to fill the void.
summary: A manager seeking relief from spiritual emptiness is handed silly dance moves and air guitar lessons as her only options.

file: 2001/2001-09-24_email service problem_no email_phone call_playing with tech support_three computers_web function_account information.gif
title: Dilbert Diagnoses Email Outage Himself

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look, I have three computers in the house. All three simultaneously lost e-mail but not web function.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That means the problem is in your e-mail service. Can you grasp that concept?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I'm re-entering my account information... Hey, guess what? That didn't work either.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a computer desk and then on a couch
situation: Dilbert phones his e-mail provider's tech support to report that all three of his home computers lost e-mail while web access still works. He explains that this points to the provider's service, but the support person apparently makes him re-enter his account information. In the last panel he lounges on the couch with a mug, phone to his ear, reporting that it didn't work.
punchline: Despite Dilbert's correct diagnosis that the fault is on the provider's end, tech support still makes him run through its scripted troubleshooting steps, which waste his time and inevitably fail.
summary: A customer who has already pinpointed the cause of his outage is forced to humor scripted support steps that obviously won't help.

file: 2001/2001-04-03_highest priority_totally worthless_empowered_make decison_double edged sword.gif
title: Hope Is a Double-Edged Sword

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which assignment is the highest priority?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it the totally worthless one or the other totally worthless one?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope I'm empowered to make that decision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hope is a double-edged sword.

situation: Dilbert, holding papers, asks his boss which of his assignments should be the top priority, noting that both are worthless. When he says he hopes he is empowered to decide, the boss ominously replies that hope is a double-edged sword, implying he is not actually empowered.
punchline: The boss deflates Dilbert's hope of being empowered with a vague, ominous cliché, signalling that employees have no real decision-making authority despite the empowerment rhetoric.
summary: An employee asks his manager to rank two pointless tasks and hopes he has the authority to choose, only to get a cryptic warning instead of an answer.

file: 2001/2001-01-04_headache_doozy_topper_bangs head_must be more.gif
title: Headache One-Upmanship Gets Painful

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My headache is a doozy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha! That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BAM! BAM! BAM!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Um... you win.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm just getting started!

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Alice complains at a meeting that she has a bad headache. A male coworker brushes it off as nothing and then repeatedly slams his head into the table to prove his headache is worse. Alice concedes, but he insists he is only getting started.
punchline: The coworker's compulsion to top someone else's complaint drives him to inflict real injury on himself, making the headache contest absurdly self-destructive.
summary: A coworker tries to outdo a colleague's headache by pounding his own head on the table until she gives up.

file: 2001/2001-12-25_not answered email_poorly written_didn't undertsnd_dare to start dialogue_talk with boss_email boss.gif
title: Email Too Badly Written to Answer

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Dude, why haven't you answered my e-mail?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your message was so poorly written that I didn't understand it and I didn't dare to start a dialogue.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe I should have a talk with your boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should e-mail him.

situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert for ignoring his e-mail. Dilbert explains the message was so badly written he couldn't understand it and was afraid to ask for clarification. When the coworker threatens to talk to Dilbert's boss, Dilbert suggests he send the boss an e-mail instead.
punchline: Dilbert's suggestion that the coworker e-mail the boss implies the boss will be just as unable to understand his poorly written messages, so the threat is toothless.
summary: A man angry about an unanswered message gets a blunt critique of his writing and a sarcastic suggestion that backfires on his threat.

file: 2001/2001-05-12_call center jobs_angry people_telephone headset_near mouths_operator_faulty mic_ignore problem.gif
title: Angry Call Center Workers, Distant Microphones

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There aren't enough friendly people to fill our call center jobs.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All we can find are angry people who refuse to put their telephone headset microphones near their mouths.

transcript.speaker: Call Center Employee
transcript.text: No, I'm sure the problem is on your end.

setting: Conference room, then a call center workstation
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, explains at a meeting that he can't recruit friendly staff for the call center. He says the only applicants are angry people who won't position their headset microphones near their mouths. In the last panel, an angry call center employee with the headset hanging far from her mouth tells a caller the problem must be on their end.
punchline: The angry employee has the microphone nowhere near her mouth and cheerfully blames the customer for the bad connection, showing the company's hiring compromise produces terrible customer service.
summary: Short on pleasant applicants, the company staffs its help line with irritable people who wear their headsets wrong and then blame callers for the poor audio.

file: 2001/2001-07-04_electrician_fix furnace_invention_plumber_roofer_space time continuum_carpenter_fix furnace 1991.gif
title: Searching Tradesmen in Space-Time Continuum

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My invention will let me search the service industry's space-time continuum.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Plumber, roofer, carpenter, electrician.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Weren't you supposed to fix my furnace in 1991?

transcript.speaker: Repairman
transcript.text: You're my next house.

setting: Dilbert's home lab, then a surreal space-time continuum
situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert his invention for searching the service industry's space-time continuum. Inside a bubble-domed craft, he calls out trades like plumber and electrician while tradesmen float through a strange landscape. He finds a repairman who promised to fix his furnace in 1991, and the repairman says Dilbert is his next house.
punchline: Tradesmen are so notoriously slow to show up that their schedules stretch across time itself, and a repair promised in 1991 is still pending.
summary: A time-travelling gadget tracks down a contractor who never turned up a decade ago, only to learn the wait is still not over.

file: 2001/2001-06-24_email down_ancients do_combustible material_coworker scared_hold me_entire life_hug_bad hug_have coffee_drop off.gif
title: Email Outage Leads to Awkward Hug

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!! E-mail is down!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't panic... think... how would the ancients handle this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got combustible materials... I can start some sort of fire.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: E-mail is down... hold me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll keep my arms straight out so I don't seem too eager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This might be the least satisfying hug of my entire life.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: E-mail is working again.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, do you want to have some coffee?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure! I'll be doing my e-mail. Just drop it off.

situation: Dilbert panics when the email system goes down and considers starting a fire like the ancients would. A female coworker, upset about the outage, asks him to hold her, and he awkwardly hugs her with his arms stiffly out. When email comes back, he immediately loses interest in her and tells her to just drop off the coffee she offers.
punchline: Dilbert's dependence on email is so total that an emotional moment with a coworker is instantly forgotten, and he dismisses her the moment the system works again.
summary: A network outage sends an office into panic and an awkward embrace, which ends the instant the messages start flowing again.

file: 2001/2001-08-19_ratbert_can't sleep_tell story_pointy haired monster_cry_dilbert bedtime story_tells life story_rat crys.gif
title: Dilbert's Bedtime Story Makes Ratbert Cry

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I can't sleep. Would you tell me a story.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Once upon a time there was a pointy-haired monster.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He promised riches to the villagers if they could achieve his random objectives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The villagers worked long hours but they were happy and optimistic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Suddenly the evil monster cut their funding and hired the village idiot to be project manager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that is how the villagers got trapped in meetings for all eternity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The end.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Waaa!! Waaa!! Waaa!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rats cry when they hear about my life.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It never pays to listen.

setting: Dilbert's living room at night, with Dilbert in a robe on the couch and Ratbert in a blanket beside him
situation: Ratbert can't sleep and asks Dilbert for a bedtime story. Dilbert tells a fairy tale that is really a thinly veiled account of his own work life, with a pointy-haired monster, random objectives, funding cuts and an incompetent project manager. Ratbert ends up sobbing, and Dogbert remarks that listening never pays.
punchline: Dilbert's soothing bedtime fairy tale is so accurate and depressing a description of corporate life that it reduces the listener to tears instead of sending him to sleep.
summary: A sleepless rat asks for a lullaby tale and gets a grim fable of office misery that sets him wailing.

file: 2001/2001-02-01_elboninan fullfillment_service_thwart_300 times_string phones_mud pile_pig_laughing_animals.gif
title: Elbonian Service Gets Grunted At

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: This is the Elbonian Fulfillment Service. How may I thwart you?

transcript.speaker: Caller (off-panel)
transcript.text: Grunt grunt grunt grunt grunt

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Okay, it wasn't funny the first 300 times either.

setting: Muddy Elbonian landscape with huts and a dead tree, standing in a mud pit
situation: Two tall-hatted, bearded Elbonians stand in mud holding tin-can string phones. One answers as the Elbonian Fulfillment Service and offers to 'thwart' the caller, who replies only with grunts. The agent then tires of the repeated joke, while a pig in the mud laughs with a tin can of its own.
punchline: The agent is fed up with the caller's endless, unfunny gag of grunting like a pig, and a pig on the line is the only one still laughing.
summary: A weary Elbonian help-desk worker on a tin-can phone refuses to indulge a prankster whose only contribution is animal noises.

file: 2001/2001-01-27_discount brokerage_free investment_money_paid for advice.gif
title: Free Advice Versus Paid Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Discount brokerage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you give me free investment advice?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Give me all of your money now now now!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if I paid for some advice?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's the same except my ears don't flip up in a threatening manner.

situation: The Boss visits Dogbert's discount brokerage and asks for free investment advice. Dogbert agrees, then dramatically demands all of the Boss's money, with his ears flipping up. When the Boss asks about paid advice, Dogbert says it's identical apart from the ear display.
punchline: Free and paid investment advice both amount to handing over all your money to the broker, the only difference being that the free version comes with threatening ear flips.
summary: A man seeking investment tips learns that a broker's advice, paid or not, boils down to surrendering his savings.

file: 2001/2001-04-14_four hundred features_level of complexity_easy to use.gif
title: Four Hundred Features, Add Easy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your user requirements include four hundred features.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you realize that no human would be able to use a product with that level of complexity?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good point. I'd better add "easy to use" to the list.

situation: Dilbert reviews a requirements list containing four hundred features and warns the Boss that no person could operate a product that complex. The Boss responds by simply adding "easy to use" as another item on the list.
punchline: The Boss treats usability as just one more feature to tick off, missing that the sheer number of requirements is what makes the product unusable.
summary: A manager answers a warning about an overloaded product spec by tacking one more bullet point onto it.

file: 2001/2001-06-30_meeting_need bodies_outnumbered_marekting_bucket head_business.gif
title: Recruiting Warm Bodies Against Marketing

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: Hey, come to this meeting. I need some bodies.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: I don't want to be outnumbered by marketing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: He's on our side.

characters: Man with a bucket on his head
situation: The boss stops Dilbert and a coworker in the hallway and orders them to attend a meeting simply to add headcount. In the conference room, Dilbert greets the table, where a marketing rep and a man with a bucket on his head are seated. The boss points to the bucket-headed man and says he's on their side.
punchline: The boss is so desperate for numbers that even a man with a bucket on his head counts as a valid ally, showing meetings are won by headcount rather than substance.
summary: A manager drafts anyone available, even a person with a bucket over his head, to pad his side of a meeting table against the rival department.

file: 2001/2001-12-18_competitive compensation_competitive means not highest.gif
title: Competitive Pay Means Competitive Effort

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to this survey the compensation here is "competitive."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Competitive means not the highest. So we could get paid more if we worked at another company?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should we continue working as hard as we can or should we back off to a more competitive level?

situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that a survey found the company's compensation to be 'competitive.' Dilbert points out that 'competitive' really means not the highest, so employees could earn more elsewhere. He then asks whether employees should keep working at full effort or scale back to a 'competitive' level.
punchline: If pay is only 'competitive' rather than the best, Dilbert turns the logic around and suggests employees should give only 'competitive' effort in return.
summary: A manager spins a salary survey as good news, and an employee cleverly turns the same logic into a threat to slack off.

file: 2001/2001-10-05_selfish_dimwitted_six sigma consulatant_bog down meetings_process_can't hurt anything.gif
title: Six Sigma Bogs Down Meetings

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Six Sigma Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: All of you are selfish and dimwitted but don't worry.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll teach you a process that will bog you down in meetings so you can't hurt anything.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I can't move my arms!

setting: Conference room during a training session
situation: Dogbert, acting as a Six Sigma consultant, insults the assembled employees as selfish and dimwitted. He then explains that his process will tie them up in meetings so they can't cause damage. In the last panel the audience is dozing off, and one employee complains he can't move his arms.
punchline: The Six Sigma process is presented as a deliberate way to keep harmful employees too bogged down in meetings to do any damage, and the audience's paralysis and sleepiness shows it already works.
summary: A dog consultant candidly admits his quality-improvement method is really a way to immobilize unproductive staff with endless meetings, and the drowsy audience is already stuck.

file: 2001/2001-11-16_use my raise_move from home_handicapped stall_storage facility_house warming_gift_flashlight_hesitate_call alice.gif
title: Raise Funds Move From Bathroom Stall

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I plan to use my raise to move from my home in the handicapped stall to a storage facility.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: If you are trying to think of a housewarming gift, I wouldn't say no to a flashlight.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you need help moving, don't hesitate to call Alice.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You are too kind.

setting: Office break room or lunch table
situation: Asok, sitting at a table with Dilbert and Wally, announces he'll use his raise to move out of the handicapped bathroom stall where he has been living and into a storage facility. He hints that a flashlight would make a nice housewarming gift. Wally cheerfully volunteers Alice to help him move, and Asok thanks him.
punchline: Asok's pay is so low that a raise only lets him upgrade from living in a bathroom stall to a dark storage unit, and Wally dodges any effort himself by volunteering Alice to do the moving.
summary: A young employee proudly plans to trade his restroom stall residence for a storage unit, asking for a flashlight as a housewarming present while a lazy coworker offers someone else's labor.

file: 2001/2001-03-24_dental plan_golden handcuffs_prickly panties_retain best employess_bowl of candy.gif
title: Golden Handcuffs and Prickly Panties

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We try to retain our best employees by giving them "golden handcuffs."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The rest of you will experience our other program, the one I call "prickly panties."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then he gave me a huge bowl of candy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, they cut our dental plan again!

setting: Catbert's office and the main office
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, explains that top performers get 'golden handcuffs' while everyone else gets his 'prickly panties' program. The Boss then appears carrying a huge bowl of candy he was given, while Dilbert notices at his computer that the company has cut the dental plan again.
punchline: Employees who aren't prized get punished with cuts to benefits, and the Boss is rewarded with candy that will ruin his teeth just as the dental coverage disappears.
summary: An HR villain splits staff into rewarded stars and everyone else, and the proof arrives as sugary treats for management alongside fresh dental plan cuts.

file: 2001/2001-05-28_incredulous ed_inventing words_what!_answers with questions_annoying_new hire_dumb guy.gif
title: Incredulous Ed Questions Everything

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'd like you to meet Incredulous Ed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No matter what question you ask him, he'll react as if you're inventing words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a family?

transcript.speaker: Incredulous Ed
transcript.text: Do I have a WHAT??

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a coworker named Incredulous Ed and warns that Ed will react to any question as though the words were made up. Dilbert tests this by asking a simple, ordinary question, and Ed responds exactly as predicted.
punchline: Ed feigns disbelief even at the plain, everyday word 'family,' proving the Boss's warning right and making conversation with him impossible.
summary: A manager warns Dilbert about a colleague who treats every question as gibberish, and a basic question about family instantly confirms it.

file: 2001/2001-08-26_process meeting_solve problem_develop process_generating ideas_meeting_cross - discilinary_swat team_offsite meeting_meeting as firewall_business.gif
title: Meetings About Meetings Firewall

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ooh! Ooh! I know how to solve our problem!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not so fast, Asok.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This isn't the solution meeting. This is the process meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our goal is to develop a process for generating ideas to solve the problem.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We don't know how to develop processes. Someone should have a meeting about that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Someone like... a cross-disciplinary SWAT team in an offsite lockup meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm... Good idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I guess this meeting is over.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You see, Asok. You can only thwart a meeting by inventing other meetings to act as a firewall.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I'm putting you on a cross-disciplinary SWAT team.

situation: Asok excitedly offers a solution in a meeting, but the Boss says it is only the process meeting, not the solution meeting. A coworker suggests that someone hold yet another meeting to develop the process, proposing a cross-disciplinary SWAT team in an offsite lockup, which the Boss happily approves to end the meeting. The coworker then explains to Asok that you can only defeat a meeting by creating other meetings as a firewall, and the Boss promptly assigns Asok to the SWAT team.
punchline: Asok learns that the way to escape a meeting is to invent more meetings, and he is immediately punished by being assigned to the very meeting team that was invented.
summary: A worker with a ready answer is stalled by layers of meetings about meetings, and when he learns the trick for dodging them he ends up drafted into the next one.

file: 2001/2001-02-02_83% spat_customer satisfaction survey_the lucky ones_died of dehydration_results of survey.gif
title: Lucky Ones Died of Dehydration

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: The results of our customer satisfaction survey are in.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: 83% spat at their telephones until they died of dehydration.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're calling that group "the lucky ones."

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: Tina, the technical writer, presents the results of a customer satisfaction survey to managers seated around a conference table. She reports that most customers were so enraged they spat at their phones until they died of dehydration. The boss responds by cheerfully giving that group a nickname, implying the other 17% fared even worse.
punchline: If the customers who died of rage-induced dehydration are the 'lucky ones,' the remaining customers must have had an even worse experience, revealing how terrible the company's service is.
summary: A survey report reveals customers so furious they expired spitting at their phones, and management darkly brands them the fortunate minority.

file: 2001/2001-06-22_$35 worth food_15% tip_penne pasta_no log cabin_build log cabin_sitaution_promise.gif
title: Restaurant Order Requires Log Cabin Promise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me $35 worth of food, including your 15% tip.

transcript.speaker: Waitress
transcript.text: If I bring you a penne pasta, will you promise to not build a log cabin on your plate?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't promise that.

transcript.speaker: Waitress
transcript.text: Well then, we have a situation here.

situation: Dilbert sits at a restaurant table and orders exactly $35 of food, tip included, without choosing any particular dish. The waitress, wary of his engineering habits, asks him to promise not to build a log cabin out of penne pasta on his plate. Dilbert refuses to promise, leaving the two at an impasse.
punchline: Dilbert's refusal to promise he won't build a structure out of his food shows he is an engineer who cannot stop tinkering, and the waitress already knows it from experience.
summary: A diner who wants to spend an exact sum on dinner won't guarantee he'll leave his pasta unconstructed, to his waitress's dismay.

file: 2001/2001-03-23_look like losers_give numbers_internal subterfuge_eighty percent_vp.gif
title: Showing the VP Flattering Numbers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can't show these numbers to our VP. They make us look like losers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Find something we're doing well and give him those numbers instead.

transcript.speaker: VP
transcript.text: Wow! Our internal subterfuge is up eighty percent!

setting: Conference room and the VP's office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the real performance numbers make the team look bad and instructs him to substitute figures from something they are doing well. Dilbert hands over the replacement numbers, and the VP reads them happily, discovering that the thing the team excels at is internal subterfuge, up eighty percent.
punchline: The only metric the team could find to look good on is deception itself, which reveals exactly how much of their effort goes into hiding bad results from management.
summary: Desperate to hide bad results, a manager has an employee supply a flattering statistic, and it turns out to measure the very scheming used to cover things up.

file: 2001/2001-05-20_behind the door_busy aisel_counsel_counseling_cubicle_jittery_jumpy_looking over shoulder_most instinct_near doorway_realx_zombie.gif
title: Catbert Counsels Jittery Jeff Into Zombie

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Jittery Jeff. He needs counseling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I put him in a cubicle at the end of a busy aisle near a doorway.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now he's jittery because he thinks people are always looking over his shoulder.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Leave him here. I'll counsel him up.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Relax, Jittery Jeff... it's okay now.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Relax. Relax. Relax. Relax.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: AAAGH!! Someone is behind the door!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Counseling is mostly instinct.

situation: The Boss brings Jittery Jeff, an employee made nervous by people looking over his shoulder, to Catbert for counseling. Catbert soothes him with repeated 'relax' and then suddenly screams that someone is behind the door. Jeff ends up slumped in his chair, tongue hanging out and apparently traumatized.
punchline: Catbert's 'counseling' is actually just his cruel instinct, so he makes the already-paranoid employee far worse by terrifying him.
summary: A nervous employee is sent to the company's feline counselor, who lulls him into calm and then scares him senseless.

file: 2001/2001-02-04_advertise_dogberts_magazine_piece of junk_stand on head_subscribe_ten page ad_totally objective review_technology magazine.gif
title: Objective Review Costs Ten Pages

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm a reporter for "Dogbert's Technology Magazine."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm writing a totally objective review of your newest product.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: First question: Will you advertise in my magazine or is your new product a piece of junk?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... We'll advertise.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Will it be a multi-page ad or is your new product a piece of junk?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It'll be a ten-page ad!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Can you stand on your head for an hour or is your new product a piece of junk?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you like to subscribe to my magazine? It's ten pages of ads.

situation: Dogbert poses as a technology magazine reporter interviewing the Boss about his new product. Every question is framed as a choice between giving Dogbert something or admitting the product is junk, so the Boss agrees to a ten-page ad and ends up standing on his head. Dogbert then tries to sell him a subscription.
punchline: The 'totally objective' review is really extortion: any refusal is treated as an admission that the product is junk, and the magazine itself is nothing but ads.
summary: A dog posing as a journalist shakes down a manager by implying that anything less than total compliance proves his product is bad.

file: 2001/2001-12-15_meeting called_discuss issues_assign tasks_waste of time_meetings_become lifeform_reproducing human josts.gif
title: Meetings Are Self-Reproducing Lifeforms

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who called this meeting?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We thought you did.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I think we should discuss issues and assign tasks so it's not a complete waste of time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe meetings have become a lifeform capable of calling themselves and thus reproducing via human hosts.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good issue.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wow!

situation: Dilbert asks who called the meeting, and the attendees admit they assumed he did. One coworker suggests discussing issues and assigning tasks so the meeting isn't wasted. Dilbert then theorizes that meetings have become a lifeform that calls itself and spreads through human hosts, and his colleagues are impressed.
punchline: Since nobody can say who called the meeting, Dilbert jokes that meetings have evolved into self-propagating organisms, which satirizes how pointless meetings seem to multiply with no one responsible.
summary: Nobody remembers scheduling the gathering, so Dilbert proposes that meetings are parasitic creatures that breed by using employees as hosts.

file: 2001/2001-11-13_psychological profile_start monday_employee handbook_weekend_gentle biker_psycho hillbilly.gif
title: Psycho Hillbilly Passes Personality Test

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your psychological profile test results are excellent. Can you start Monday?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Monday is fine. I'll read the employee handbook over the weekend. Thank you very much.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: The "gentle biker" look is overdone. I'm going for "psycho hillbilly."

setting: Catbert's human resources office, then a conference room
situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells a wild-haired, shirtless, bearded candidate with a knife that his psychological profile test results are excellent and offers him a start date. The candidate politely agrees and promises to read the employee handbook. In the last panel he is sitting at a meeting table with Dilbert and Alice, explaining that his intimidating appearance is a deliberate style choice.
punchline: A man who looks dangerously unstable passes the personality screening with flying colors, and his scary look is just a fashion choice, mocking how meaningless HR psychological tests are.
summary: A menacing, knife-carrying applicant sails through an HR personality screening and cheerfully reveals his frightening look is merely a style statement.

file: 2001/2001-04-28_good job_meeting woman_late_sixty hour week_stock options decline_not impressed.gif
title: Sixty Hours for Worthless Stock Options

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Do you have a good job?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It depends what you mean by good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you consider the decline of my stock options, I work sixty hours a week for nothing.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Hey, look at the time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss thinks I work eighty hours. Hee hee hee!

setting: A social gathering where people hold wine glasses
situation: At a social event, a woman asks Dilbert if he has a good job. He glumly explains that his collapsed stock options mean he is effectively working sixty hours a week for nothing. She suddenly notices the time and tries to leave, while Dilbert gleefully adds that his boss believes he works eighty hours.
punchline: The woman's abrupt exit shows she is bored by his complaining, and Dilbert's giggle about secretly deceiving his boss about his hours shows his sad attempt to cope with a bad deal.
summary: A man's gloomy answer about his job, with worthless stock options and long hours, sends his conversation partner hurrying away.

file: 2001/2001-05-07_threw computer_off roof_killed customer_replace_look a like_worker_clones_coverup.gif
title: Replacing the Dead Customer's Lookalike

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone threw a computer off the roof and killed our biggest customer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We plan to replace him with a look-alike who will continue buying from us.

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: Hey, that's Willy from the club of people who look exactly like me.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that a computer thrown off the roof has killed the company's biggest customer. He explains that management intends to swap in a look-alike to keep the purchases coming. A bald coworker holds up a photo and recognizes the intended stand-in as Willy from his club of people who look just like him.
punchline: The Boss's cover-up plan is absurd, and a coworker casually reveals that he belongs to a club of look-alikes, so the replacement is conveniently someone he knows.
summary: Management plans to hide a customer's death by substituting a double, and a coworker happens to know the perfect candidate.

file: 2001/2001-07-15_save money_each unit_idea_vp_beter ideas_fist of death_something hits me_alice punches.gif
title: Alice's Fist of Death Strikes Boss

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ...and that way we'll save money on each unit we build.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's try that idea with our VP.

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: Wow. Great idea. Who thought of it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I have to admit...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's one of my better ideas.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... control... fist of death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes I'll just be standing there...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And pow! Something hits me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: I tried to control it but I couldn't.

setting: Office and the vice president's office
situation: Alice proposes a cost-saving idea, and the Boss takes it to the VP and claims it as his own. As he brags that it's one of his better ideas, Alice struggles to restrain her 'fist of death' but finally punches him. The boss then blames the punch on some unexplained force, while Alice thanks the VP.
punchline: The boss steals Alice's idea and she punches him for it, and his own earlier claim that he sometimes gets hit by something in the middle of standing there becomes a cover story for the assault.
summary: A boss takes credit for a subordinate's money-saving idea and gets punched by her unstoppable fist.

file: 2001/2001-06-02_set up instructions_read instructions_true engineer_set up_slurping sounds.gif
title: True Engineers Skip the Instructions

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We should read the set-up instructions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice, a true engineer never reads the set-up instructions.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It says to keep it away from any slurping sounds.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Gaaa!!

setting: Office, unpacking a new piece of equipment
situation: Alice, Dilbert and Wally unpack a new device from a box. Alice suggests reading the set-up instructions, but Dilbert declares that a true engineer never reads them. After the device is set up, Alice reads the instructions and finds a warning about slurping sounds, just as Wally slurps his coffee and the device reacts, spewing out paper tape or goo over him.
punchline: Dilbert's pride in ignoring the instructions is punished when the manual turns out to contain an absurdly specific warning that Wally immediately violates by slurping his coffee.
summary: A proud refusal to consult the manual backfires when the new gadget reacts violently to a coworker's noisy drinking.

file: 2001/2001-05-10_wally in jail_try door_guards dont lock_lifers_most embarrassed.gif
title: Wally's Jailbreak Is Just Opening the Door

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally's in jail. Can you help get him out?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tell him to try the door. The guards only pretend to lock them.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: But I'd have to say it was the lifers who were the most embarrassed.

setting: Dilbert's home living room, then a card table with other people
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for help getting Wally out of jail, and Dogbert says the guards only pretend to lock the cell doors, so Wally can just walk out. In the last panel, Dilbert and two others sit at a table playing a board game while a bald man comments on how embarrassed the lifers were.
punchline: The bald man's remark implies that prisoners serving life sentences discovered the cell doors were never locked and could have walked out all along, which left them the most embarrassed.
summary: A cheerfully absurd prison-escape tip reveals that the cell doors were never really locked, to the lasting shame of inmates who stayed put for decades.

file: 2001/2001-10-13_network outages_network room_unplugging server_noisy_server is waitress_lan.gif
title: Noisy Server Room Meeting Culprit

transcript.speaker: Network Technician
transcript.text: I have discovered the cause of our network outages.

transcript.speaker: Whiteboard
transcript.text: LAN

transcript.speaker: Network Technician
transcript.text: Some idiot is using our network room for meetings and unplugging the server because it's too noisy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A server is like a waitress, right?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yeah, a noisy one.

situation: A network technician presents a LAN diagram on a whiteboard and reveals that the network outages are caused by someone holding meetings in the network room and unplugging the server because it is too noisy. The Boss, seated at the conference table, fails to grasp the problem and asks if a server is like a waitress, and Wally sarcastically agrees.
punchline: The Boss, who is likely the culprit, completely misunderstands what a server is, and Wally's deadpan reply confirms the confusion while mocking him.
summary: A tech worker traces recurring network failures to meeting-goers who disconnect a loud machine, while the oblivious boss confuses computer servers with restaurant staff.

file: 2001/2001-03-31_evil hr director_five years expereince_job interview_no profit_dot com president_catbert.gif
title: Dot-Com Experience Wins the Job

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: ...And I have five years experience as a dot-com president.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're in luck. We need someone who can burn through twenty million dollars without making a profit.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: Really? The last nine interviewers said the same thing but they were joking.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office during a job interview
situation: A job applicant tells Catbert, the evil H.R. director, that he has five years of experience as a dot-com president. Catbert says the company needs exactly someone who can burn through twenty million dollars without making a profit. The applicant, surprised, notes that nine earlier interviewers said the same thing but were only joking.
punchline: The applicant's dot-com experience, normally a joke about reckless money-burning, is finally considered a genuine qualification, which Catbert greets with an evil grin.
summary: A former dot-com president finds that his record of squandering money is exactly what an evil HR department wants.

file: 2001/2001-07-21_total sociopath_rifle through purse_call me_ring once_robbed_date_hug_robbery.gif
title: Purse Thief Charms Woman, Steals Wallet

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You're a total sociopath, Ron. I like that in a man.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Oh yes, rifle through my purse! Yes! Yes! Yes!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Call me?

transcript.speaker: Ron
transcript.text: Sure. But you'd better wait by the phone; I only ring once.

setting: A street beside a parked blue car
situation: A woman tells a man named Ron that she likes that he is a total sociopath. He hugs her, and she enthusiastically invites him to rifle through her purse, which he does while embracing her. Afterward she asks him to call her, and he walks away holding her cash, telling her he will only ring once.
punchline: The woman is so thrilled by Ron's sociopathy that she lets him rob her during a hug, and his promise to 'ring once' is really a brush-off, meaning he will never call again.
summary: A woman who is attracted to a predatory man happily lets him pick her pocket and then gets the brush-off she should have expected.

file: 2001/2001-11-19_elbonia_mud delivery business_stockholders_huge profits_illeagal_no law_against optimism.gif
title: No Law Against Optimism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you're going to Elbonia to shut down our Elbonian mud delivery business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meanwhile I'll tell our stockholders that we expect the mud delivery business to make huge profits.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... is this illegal?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no law against optimism! I checked.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to travel to Elbonia and shut down the failing mud delivery business. At the same time he plans to tell stockholders to expect huge profits from that very business. Dilbert asks if this is illegal, and the Boss says he checked and there is no law against optimism.
punchline: The Boss justifies misleading shareholders about a business he is closing by redefining deliberate deception as harmless optimism.
summary: A manager plans to shutter a doomed venture while telling investors it will be wildly profitable, and defends the lie as mere positive thinking.

file: 2001/2001-03-29_dogbert power company_electricity_hard to find_california environmentalists.gif
title: Dogbert Powers Grid With Environmentalists

transcript.speaker: TV Announcer
transcript.text: Buy your electricity from the Dogbert Power Company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We generate all of our power with the help of California environmentalists.

transcript.speaker: Worker
transcript.text: These are getting harder to find lately.

setting: Dilbert's living room, a TV commercial studio, and a power plant furnace room
situation: Dilbert sits in his armchair watching a TV ad for the Dogbert Power Company. In the ad, Dogbert boasts that the company's power comes from California environmentalists. The final panel reveals two plant workers feeding a striped-sweater-clad person into a blazing furnace, complaining that supplies are running short.
punchline: Dogbert's company literally burns environmentalists as fuel, a dark joke implying that the 'help' of environmentalists is their bodies and that the supply is dwindling.
summary: A power company ad reveals its secret fuel source is the very people who campaign against such energy production.

file: 2001/2001-09-26_asked to clone_clone_no soul_pointy hired boss.gif
title: Cloning The Soulless Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our Pointy-Haired Boss asked me to clone him.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What if his clone has no soul?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If?

setting: Office break room or lunch table
situation: Dilbert tells Wally and Alice that The Boss has asked him to clone him. Alice worries that the clone might have no soul. Dilbert and Wally both respond with a skeptical 'If?', implying the Boss has no soul to begin with.
punchline: Dilbert and Wally's 'If?' implies the original Pointy-Haired Boss already has no soul, so a soulless clone is a certainty rather than a risk.
summary: Coworkers at a table joke that cloning their boss would hardly be a problem, since he is already devoid of any soul.

file: 2001/2001-05-27_recommend vendor_internal debvelopers_play out_outside vendor_clueless weasel_begin work_sign contract_internal weasels complain_use_steaming mounds_worthless code_plan too much_practiced yesterday.gif
title: Dilbert Predicts Vendor Plan Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And that's why I recommend using this vendor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why don't we use our internal developers?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me explain how this will play out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Step one: We select an outside vendor because our internal developers are clueless weasels.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Step two: We sign a contract and begin work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Step three: Our internal weasels complain to our VP and she orders us to use them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Step four: The outside vendor sues us while our weasels grunt out steaming mounds of worthless code.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I plan too much?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is this the conversation we practiced yesterday?

setting: Office meeting room with a presentation board, and a final scene with Dilbert talking to Dogbert
situation: Dilbert pitches an outside vendor to the Boss, who asks why internal developers aren't used instead. Dilbert walks through a four-step prediction in which the vendor project ends in a lawsuit and the internal developers produce worthless code anyway. In the last panel it turns out he is rehearsing with Dogbert, who is acting as therapist.
punchline: Dilbert has so thoroughly planned and rehearsed the whole conversation, including the Boss's question, that Dogbert points out they already practiced it yesterday, suggesting Dilbert over-plans.
summary: A cynical engineer maps out exactly how an outsourcing decision will collapse, only for it to emerge that he has been rehearsing the entire scene with his dog.

file: 2001/2001-07-19_dinner_socially defective brain_voicemail_speakerphone.gif
title: Insulted Coworker Accepts Dinner Invitation

transcript.speaker: Speakerphone
transcript.text: Press one to hear...

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Why are you using your speakerphone for voicemail?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I mean, seriously, what is going through that socially defective brain of yours?

transcript.speaker: Man at desk
transcript.text: Would you like to have dinner?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Yeah, why not.

situation: A man at his desk plays his voicemail on speakerphone, and a big-haired female coworker scolds him and insults his social skills. Instead of defending himself, he calmly asks her to dinner, and she casually accepts.
punchline: Despite openly calling him socially defective, she accepts his dinner invitation without hesitation, suggesting she is just as socially dysfunctional as he is.
summary: A coworker's rude lecture about phone etiquette somehow ends with a date that both of them take in stride.

file: 2001/2001-01-21_professional liar_why kind of lie_lousy movie_cover of lousy book_dot commer_filthy_have limits_mena_liar mad.gif
title: Professional Liar Draws the Line

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Professional Liar

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What kind of lie do you need?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's...it's embarrassing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you a producer who needs a good review for a lousy movie?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you an author who needs a slobbering quote for the cover of your lousy book?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's worse than that. Much worse.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Worse? That could only be... Aaack!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Find someone else, you filthy dot-com founder! I have my limits!

transcript.speaker: Dot-com Founder
transcript.text: ...and since your firm underwrote our IPO...

transcript.speaker: Dot-com Founder
transcript.text: Would I get to be on TV?

setting: A storefront office with an awning reading 'Professional Liar', then an interview or meeting room
situation: Dogbert runs a professional lying business and asks a customer what kind of lie he needs. After guessing a shady movie producer or an author seeking a fake blurb, he learns the customer is a dot-com founder and recoils in horror, refusing the job. The final panel shows the founder pitching a banker about being on TV because the banker's firm underwrote his IPO.
punchline: Even a professional liar who will say anything for money finds dot-com founders too repugnant to serve, implying they are worse than the sleaziest film and book hucksters.
summary: A professional liar happily fakes praise for bad movies and books but throws out a customer once he turns out to be a dot-com entrepreneur.

file: 2001/2001-05-14_boss friend_hot in here_huge cutomer_sales people_secretary_childhood friend.gif
title: Salespeople Beat Carol's Call Screening

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, screen my calls and don't let any salespeople through.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson (caller)
transcript.text: Hello, I'm a huge customer or perhaps a childhood friend of your boss.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Give me some flirting and you're in.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson (caller)
transcript.text: Is it hot in here or is it just you?

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to screen his calls and keep salespeople away. A caller then phones in claiming to be a huge customer or a childhood friend of the boss, and Carol says he can get through if he flirts with her. He responds with a cheesy pickup line and she lets him in.
punchline: Carol's call screening has a price, so salespeople get past the boss's gatekeeper simply by flattering her with a cheesy pickup line.
summary: A boss orders his assistant to block salespeople, but she waves a caller through in exchange for some flirtation.

file: 2001/2001-06-03_save money_firings_consultants_flossie_highly technical work_invitation_shake hands_greeting ritual_brain overload_raise rates_over reacts_dumb woman_lost_freak_new hire.gif
title: Consultant Trains Overwhelmed Replacement, Raises Rates

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sorry, Brian. I need to fire all of my consultants to save money.

transcript.speaker: Brian
transcript.text: Who will do your highly technical work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can transfer your knowledge to Flossie.

transcript.speaker: Brian
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Flossie
transcript.text: What's with the hand? Do you want to borrow my pencil?

transcript.speaker: Brian
transcript.text: Um... no. This is an invitation to shake hands. It's a greeting ritual.

transcript.speaker: Flossie
transcript.text: Ouch!! Brain overload!! It's too much information!!

transcript.speaker: Flossie
transcript.text: Purge! Purge! Purge!

transcript.speaker: Flossie
transcript.text: Where am I?

transcript.speaker: Brian
transcript.text: I need to raise my rates.

situation: The Boss tells consultant Brian he is being fired to save money and orders him to transfer his highly technical knowledge to a coworker named Flossie. When Brian offers a handshake, Flossie doesn't understand the gesture, and his explanation overloads her brain so badly that she purges her memory. Brian realizes she is hopeless and thinks he can charge more.
punchline: Flossie is so incapable of absorbing information that she can't even learn a handshake, so the consultant knows the company will never be able to replace him and he can raise his rates.
summary: A manager tries to replace an expensive consultant with an employee who can't even grasp what a handshake is, guaranteeing the consultant a raise.

file: 2001/2001-10-16_stock market expert_microphone_tail off camera_makes me wag_honest work.gif
title: Dogbert's Tail Gives Away Stock Scam

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Stock market expert

transcript.speaker: Camera Operator
transcript.text: Clip this microphone to your fur. We're live in two.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Make sure my tail is off camera. I'll be recommending stocks I own and that sort of thing makes me wag.

transcript.speaker: Camera Operator
transcript.text: Someday I gotta get honest work.

setting: A television studio set with a desk and camera
situation: Dogbert, billed as a stock market expert, is about to go live on air. A camera operator hands him a microphone, and Dogbert asks him to keep his tail out of the shot because he'll be pushing stocks he personally owns, which makes him wag. The disillusioned camera operator thinks to himself that he should find honest work someday.
punchline: Dogbert's tail involuntarily exposes his conflict of interest, and the camera operator is so disgusted by the TV financial-advice racket that he wishes he had an honest job.
summary: A canine market pundit prepares to hype shares he secretly holds, leaving the crew member who helps him wishing for a more ethical line of work.

file: 2001/2001-12-20_another cubicle_office moving budget_transfer to elbonia_relocation budget_budget is shot_mail yourself home.gif
title: Transferred to Elbonia for Cubicle Move

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to move you to another cubicle but my office moving budget is shot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I'm going to transfer you to Elbonia and then back so I can use the relocation budget.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: He says the relocation budget is shot but you can mail yourself home.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, then a muddy village in Elbonia
situation: The Boss wants to move Dilbert to a different cubicle but has no office moving budget. He decides to transfer Dilbert to Elbonia and back so the separate relocation budget can pay for it. In Elbonia, a bearded local speaking through a tin-can telephone tells Dilbert the relocation budget is also spent and he must mail himself home.
punchline: The Boss's budget workaround backfires absurdly, stranding Dilbert in Elbonia with no money to return, since the relocation budget turns out to be exhausted too.
summary: Hunting for a loophole to fund a simple desk change, a manager ships his employee overseas and leaves him stuck there when the other pot of money is empty.

file: 2001/2001-01-28_projects fail_have in common_points to boss_honest_sneezes_figuring the problem.gif
title: Alice's Sneeze Points at Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've got to figure out why all our projects fail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
