transcript.text: What do all our projects have in common?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It might not be obvious.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But if we're honest with ourselves...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We can find the source of the problem.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ah-ah ah-

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Scratch scratch

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ach-itz-you!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gesundheit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, does anyone know what the problem is?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've noticed that Dilbert doesn't work as hard as I think he should.

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: The Boss opens a meeting about why every project fails, and Alice starts to say the cause might not be obvious. As she builds up to naming the problem, she sneezes, and the sound 'Ach-itz-you' comes out sounding like 'Ask Dilbert'. The Boss, who took the sneeze as an answer, asks who knows the problem, and Wally, pointing the way the sneeze did, blames Dilbert for not working hard enough.
punchline: Alice's sneeze sounds like an accusation against Dilbert, and the group is so ready to find a scapegoat that Wally immediately blames him with no evidence at all.
summary: A coworker's sneeze gets mistaken for a clue, and the team seizes on it to pin their failed projects on one absent person.

file: 2001/2001-06-23_temp_sign time sheet_permanent position_dog_has fake owner_dilbert clone_doll_stand in_fake person_animals.gif
title: Dogbert Hires Out Dilbert's Temp

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert! I'm ho-o-ome!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll be right there. I have to sign the temp's time sheet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you're ever interested in a permanent position, give me a call.

setting: Dilbert's home, entryway and living room
situation: Dilbert comes home and calls out to Dogbert, who says he must first sign a temp's time sheet. Dogbert is revealed to have hired a temp worker, who sits on Dilbert's couch dressed like Dilbert, apparently filling in for him at home. Dogbert offers the temp a permanent position while Dilbert stands there, evidently replaced.
punchline: Dogbert has hired a temp to be Dilbert (a stand-in owner), and is now offering the temp a permanent job, implying Dilbert is replaceable even in his own home.
summary: Dilbert returns to find that Dogbert has been using a temporary substitute for him and is now trying to recruit the stand-in full time.

file: 2001/2001-05-29_incredulous ed_budget numbers_request_coworker_budget manager_hard time_over reacts_ed_new hire.gif
title: Incredulous Ed Feigns Budget Ignorance

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Incredulous Ed

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Ed, do you have the latest budget numbers?

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: Budget??? What is a "budget"? And why in the world would I have one?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Because you're the budget manager.

situation: A woman with big curly hair asks coworker Ed for the latest budget numbers. Ed reacts with theatrical shock, pretending not to know what a budget is or why he would have one. When she reminds him he is the budget manager, he calmly hands over the papers.
punchline: Ed's over-the-top incredulity is pure show, since he had the budget numbers all along and just enjoys making a simple request difficult.
summary: A coworker's routine request gets a dramatic, feigned-ignorance response before the requested document is simply handed over.

file: 2001/2001-12-09_teamwork football_carry one day_commitment to teamwork_customers_vacation_used golf ball_football_sports.gif
title: The Teamwork Football Nobody Wants

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I call it the Teamwork Football.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Each of you will carry the ball with you for one day to symbolize your commitment to teamwork.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who wants to be first?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not me. I have a meeting with customers today.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm on vacation. I only came in for coffee.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Not in a trillion years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should have used a golf ball.

setting: Office meeting room and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss unveils a football that each employee must carry for a day to symbolize commitment to teamwork. One by one, everyone dodges the duty with excuses about customer meetings, vacation, or flat refusal. Dilbert sarcastically suggests the Boss keep it in his own desk drawer, and the Boss ends up alone wishing he had chosen a smaller object.
punchline: The Boss's teamwork symbol is so awkward to carry that nobody will take it, and the team's reluctance exposes how little real commitment there is, leaving him wishing he had picked a golf ball.
summary: A manager's bulky motivational prop gets rejected by his whole team, and he realizes too late that a smaller token would have been easier to hand out.

file: 2001/2001-05-11_criminal record_police_fake name_quality of assignments_legal.gif
title: Fake Name Keeps Wally Unimportant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, now that you have a criminal record, I can't let you work on anything important.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't have a criminal record. I gave the police a fake name.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You might notice a change in the quality of your assignments.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and a cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Wally he can no longer be trusted with important work because of his criminal record. Wally replies that he has no record, since he gave the police a fake name. He then walks past a coworker's cubicle holding his coffee mug and warns that the Boss's assignments may start to get worse.
punchline: Wally pretends the Boss's restriction is a threat, implying he will deliberately do poor work, when in fact he already does little and the Boss's mistake only gives him a convenient excuse to slack off.
summary: Wally dodges the consequences of an arrest with a false name, then uses the Boss's misguided punishment as a pretext for even lazier work.

file: 2001/2001-01-26_discount brokerage_free dart board_monkey_drops below_five hundred_order money to kill_strange techniques_animals.gif
title: Brokerage Account Comes With Murderous Monkey

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Discount Brokerage

transcript.speaker: Brokerage Rep
transcript.text: When you open an account, you'll get a free dart board and a monkey.

transcript.speaker: Brokerage Rep
transcript.text: If your balance drops below five hundred dollars, we'll order the monkey to kill you.

transcript.speaker: Brokerage Rep
transcript.text: Well, think about it and get back to me.

setting: A discount brokerage call desk, with the rep wearing a headset at a desk with a phone and computer
situation: A phone representative at a discount brokerage pitches the perks of opening an account, starting with a free dart board and a monkey. He then casually mentions that the monkey will be ordered to kill the customer if the balance falls below five hundred dollars. When the customer hesitates, the rep calmly tells them to think it over and call back.
punchline: The brokerage treats a death threat from a monkey as just another routine account term, mocking financial firms that bury absurd or menacing conditions in the fine print of a sales pitch.
summary: A sales rep happily offers freebies with a new investment account, then drops a lethal catch about minimum balances as if it were standard policy.

file: 2001/2001-03-11_master of delegation_footsteps_third thing_valuable time_vendor_two minute call_funny_conversation.gif
title: Boss Delegates Call, Wastes More Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The master of delegation hears the footsteps of his prey.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hi

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Call this vendor and tell him I want the third thing he told me about.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. That will save two minutes of your valuable time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When the vendor asks me dozens of questions should I just guess at the answers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or would you prefer to spend an hour giving me enough background so you can avoid a two-minute call?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know what's funny? This conversation lasted a minute... and there are two of us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you done?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you wrote down your own phone number.

situation: The Boss ambushes Dilbert in the hall and hands him a note with a vague instruction to call a vendor about 'the third thing' he mentioned. Dilbert points out the vendor will have many questions he can't answer, and the Boss tells him to spend an hour getting background instead. Dilbert notes that the delegation conversation already cost two people a minute, then sees the Boss gave him a note with the Boss's own phone number.
punchline: The Boss's delegation, supposedly meant to save time, is so sloppy that he hands Dilbert his own phone number instead of the vendor's, making the whole exercise pointless.
summary: A manager proud of offloading work hands his employee a useless task with the wrong contact info on it.

file: 2001/2001-07-30_angry dumb guy_opinion_beat it out_self hurting.gif
title: Angry Guy Beats Opinion Out of Himself

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Angry Dumb Guy

transcript.speaker: Angry Dumb Guy
transcript.text: If anyone wants my opinion...

transcript.speaker: Angry Dumb Guy
transcript.text: ...I'll beat it out of me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want your opinion.

transcript.speaker: Angry Dumb Guy
transcript.text: Oh yeah? Let's see if I have one!

situation: At a meeting, the Angry Dumb Guy declares in a bluster that if anyone wants his opinion, he will beat it out of himself. Dilbert calmly says he wants the man's opinion. The Angry Dumb Guy rolls up his tie like a weapon to start hitting himself and checks whether he has an opinion at all.
punchline: The Angry Dumb Guy's macho threat gets called by Dilbert, forcing him to carry out an absurd self-inflicted beating that also hints he may not have any opinion to begin with.
summary: A belligerent coworker's tough-guy boast backfires when a colleague takes him up on it, leaving him to follow through on his own threat.

file: 2001/2001-07-23_growing into job_accelerated evolution_progarm_million years_two day classes_lose fire_opposable thimbs.gif
title: Evolution Crash Course for Underperforming Monkey

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Monty, you're not growing into your job as quickly as I hoped.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I signed you up for an accelerated evolution program. They pack a million years into a two-day class.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hurry up! We've already lost the opposable thumbs module; let's not lose fire too.

setting: Boss's office, then a training classroom
situation: The Boss tells Monty, a monkey-like employee, that he isn't growing into his job fast enough. He enrolls Monty in an accelerated evolution program that compresses a million years into a two-day class. In the classroom, Dogbert, apparently the instructor, rushes the primate students because they have already skipped the opposable thumbs lesson.
punchline: The class is so compressed that entire evolutionary milestones get dropped like skipped training modules, with the instructor hurrying to avoid losing fire as well.
summary: A manager sends a slow-developing primate employee to a cram course that squeezes a million years of evolution into two days, and the teacher is already cutting corners.

file: 2001/2001-09-17_job market_getting worse_employees afraid_power to abuse_grows stronger_evil dance_killing me.gif
title: Bad Job Market Fuels Evil Dance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The job market is getting worse every day!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Excellent!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Employees will be afraid. Our power to abuse them grows stronger by the minute!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha! Stop doing the "evil dance"! You're killing me!

situation: The Boss reads a newspaper and announces the job market is worsening. Catbert, the evil HR director, gleefully explains that frightened employees mean more power for management to abuse them. Catbert then performs an "evil dance" that leaves the Boss laughing helplessly.
punchline: Management and HR openly celebrate a worsening economy because desperate, fearful employees are easier to mistreat.
summary: A gloomy economic headline delights the company's malicious HR chief, who celebrates with a gleeful dance that cracks up his boss.

file: 2001/2001-03-02_class_cloak of invisibility_consultant_invisibility_management cloak_management training_special_students_teacher_education_business.gif
title: Management Cloak of Invisibility Revealed

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Management training

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tim will demonstrate the management cloak of invisibility.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I admit it doesn't seem very special when you know how it's done.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a management trainer, stands on a stool and announces that Tim will demonstrate the 'management cloak of invisibility.' In the middle panel Tim simply slouches down behind his desk so that only the top of his head is visible. Dogbert then admits the trick isn't impressive once you know how it works.
punchline: The 'cloak of invisibility' is just a manager sliding down in his chair to hide behind his desk, a jab at managers who make themselves scarce and avoid their responsibilities.
summary: A trainer unveils a supposedly magical management skill that turns out to be nothing more than ducking out of sight.

file: 2001/2001-01-08_retaining best employees_whittle_confidence_hire.gif
title: Retaining Employees By Destroying Confidence

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do you have a plan for retaining the best employees?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I whittle at their confidence until they believe no one else would ever hire them.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Doesn't that make them sluggish?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, but if they're all sluggish, it looks right.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, asks the Boss how he plans to keep the company's best employees. The Boss admits he erodes their confidence until they think they are unemployable elsewhere. When Catbert points out this makes them sluggish, the Boss says it doesn't matter because everyone being sluggish makes it seem normal.
punchline: The Boss keeps top talent by demoralizing them into staying and then excuses the resulting drop in performance because everyone is equally sluggish, so nobody stands out.
summary: A manager reveals his cynical talent-retention strategy of crushing self-esteem, then shrugs off the lost productivity since uniform mediocrity goes unnoticed.

file: 2001/2001-06-07_contract states_nick names_mottos_political preferences_new contract_fact_skippy_communist now.gif
title: Unread Contract Makes Dilbert Communist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our contract clearly states that I can give you nicknames, mottos and political preferences.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I demand a new contract based on the fact that I didn't read this one before I signed it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Too bad, Skippy. You're a communist now.

setting: A meeting table, likely Dilbert's office or a conference room
situation: Dogbert points out that the contract Dilbert signed lets him assign Dilbert nicknames, mottos and political preferences. Dilbert, arms crossed, demands a new contract because he never read the original before signing. Dogbert refuses, calls him 'Skippy', and declares he is now a communist.
punchline: Dilbert's only defence is that he didn't read the contract, which carries no weight, so Dogbert exercises his contractual right and arbitrarily assigns Dilbert a political affiliation.
summary: A man who signed a contract unread learns, to his cost, that the small print lets his counterpart rename him and dictate his politics.

file: 2001/2001-04-08_punish me_manage annual business plan_beg co workers_information_budget needs_lies_ignore you_underscoring unimportance_combine lies and guesses_ballof data_senior mangement_budget decions_magazine articles.gif
title: Annual Business Plan as Punishment

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Did you call me here to punish me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, no, Asok. I want you to manage our annual business plan process.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How do I do that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: First, you beg your co-workers for information about their budget needs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Half of them will give you lies. The other half will ignore you, thus underscoring your unimportance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then you'll combine the lies and guesses into a worthless ball of data for senior management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then our CEO will make budget decisions based on magazine articles.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How bad was the punishment?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Worse than I expected.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway or break area
situation: Asok is called into the Boss's office and fears he is being punished. The Boss assures him he's only being asked to manage the annual business plan, then cheerfully describes a process of begging for information, getting lies or being ignored, and producing worthless data that the CEO will disregard in favor of magazine articles. Afterward Dogbert asks how bad the punishment was.
punchline: The annual budgeting process is so futile and demoralizing that it turns out to be a worse punishment than Asok feared, even though the Boss insists it isn't one.
summary: A junior employee is handed the yearly planning chore and learns that it is an exercise in futility, making it crueler than any disciplinary action he imagined.

file: 2001/2001-11-26_airline_no planes_sit in crowded room_steal luggage_customers realize_mechanical difficulties.gif
title: Airline With No Planes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to start an airline that has no planes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll take people's money and make them sit in a crowded room while ex-cons steal from their luggage.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happens when your customers realize you have no airplanes?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I call that "mechanical difficulties."

setting: Dilbert's workbench or desk in his home or lab
situation: Dogbert announces a business plan for an airline that owns no planes, in which customers pay, wait in a crowded room, and have their luggage stolen by ex-cons. Dilbert, busy tinkering with electronic parts, asks what happens when customers notice there are no airplanes. Dogbert has a ready excuse.
punchline: Dogbert's scam airline would simply pass off its total lack of planes as 'mechanical difficulties', the same vague excuse real airlines use for delays, implying that airline customers are already treated like this.
summary: Dogbert outlines a scam airline with no aircraft and has a euphemism ready for when passengers catch on.

file: 2001/2001-11-05_more useful_bizarre absolute_feature.gif
title: Bizarre Absolute Feature Argument

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We should add this feature to our product to make it more useful.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Are you telling me that not one person on Earth will use our product without that feature?!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You changed what I said into a bizarre absolute.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, I change everything you say?!

situation: Dilbert suggests adding a feature to make their product more useful. His coworker responds by exaggerating the suggestion into a claim that nobody on Earth could use the product without it. When Dilbert points out the distortion, the coworker feigns offense and says he changes everything Dilbert says, ironically proving the point.
punchline: The coworker's sarcastic reply, 'Oh, I change everything you say?!', accidentally confirms that he habitually distorts Dilbert's words.
summary: A reasonable product suggestion gets blown up into an extreme claim, and the exaggerator's defensive retort proves he does it all the time.

file: 2001/2001-06-05_boost earnings_mass exodus_doorway jam.gif
title: Advertising Cuts Cause Doorway Jam

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're cutting back on advertising to boost earnings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... excuse me. I'll be right back.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Me too.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: We got another mass exodus doorway jam.

setting: Conference room, with a corridor outside
situation: In a meeting, the Boss announces that the company is cutting advertising spending to boost earnings. Dilbert and a colleague immediately excuse themselves, and a pile of employees ends up wedged in the doorway as everyone tries to leave at once. A man on a phone reports it as another mass exodus jam.
punchline: Employees recognize cutting advertising as a sign the company is doomed, so they all rush to quit at the same moment and clog the exit.
summary: Staff stampede for the exit the instant management reveals a desperate cost-saving move that signals the company is failing.

file: 2001/2001-02-08_ceo_goal set_illadvised_impossible goal_life_other people_whats wrong life.gif
title: Dilbert Blames Other People

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have failed to meet a goal set by our CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mean the impossible goal, the ill-advised one, or the one you didn't tell me about?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I figured out what's wrong with life: it's other people.

setting: The boss's office, then Dogbert's home where Dilbert stands by a green couch
situation: The boss, mostly off-panel, accuses Dilbert of failing to meet a goal set by the CEO. Dilbert asks which of the unreasonable goals he means. In the last panel Dilbert stands before Dogbert, who is lying on a green couch, and announces his conclusion about what ruins life.
punchline: After being blamed for impossible, ill-advised and undisclosed goals, Dilbert concludes that the root of all life's problems is other people.
summary: Faced with blame for a CEO objective, a sarcastic engineer decides that human company is the real flaw in existence.

file: 2001/2001-06-29_anyone offers food_dont eat_fill in receptionist_impression visitors_face of company.gif
title: Receptionist Told Not to Eat Food

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I need you to fill in for our receptionist today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, you will be the face of our company, the first impression for visitors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If anyone offers you food, don't eat it.

situation: The Boss asks his assistant Carol to cover for the receptionist for the day. He reminds her that she represents the company's first impression to visitors. In the last panel she sits at the reception desk as a visitor stands in front of her, and the Boss gives her an odd piece of advice about refusing food.
punchline: After stressing the importance of being the company's welcoming face, the Boss's only real instruction is to refuse any food offered, hinting that visitors are not to be trusted, or that the company's hospitality and image are not what he claims.
summary: A manager pressing a colleague into reception duty finishes his pep talk with a suspicious warning about accepting snacks from guests.

file: 2001/2001-08-22_complaints_dating_dog is perfect_improve_list_lose weight_need improvements_new odor_new wardrobe_polish up_new haircut_relationships.gif
title: Girlfriend's Improvement List Favors Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Girlfriend
transcript.text: I made a list of all the ways you need to improve in order to keep dating me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lose forty pounds, new wardrobe, new haircut, new car, new odor...

transcript.speaker: Girlfriend
transcript.text: But your dog is perfect. How'd that happen?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When can you move in?

setting: Living room couch in Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert's girlfriend hands him a list of self-improvements he must make to keep dating her. Dilbert reads the demands, which cover his weight, clothes, hair, car and even his smell. She then remarks that his dog is perfect, and Dogbert seizes the moment to invite her to move in with him.
punchline: Dogbert, who is apparently flawless in her eyes, opportunistically offers to take Dilbert's place as her partner, highlighting how thoroughly Dilbert is being criticized.
summary: A woman hands her boyfriend a long list of personal flaws to fix, then praises his pet as flawless, prompting the pet to make a move on her.

file: 2001/2001-04-13_tight labor market_complicated tasks_harder jobs_dumb employees.gif
title: Logical Limit of Dumber Employees

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Due to a tight labor market and increasingly complicated tasks...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Harder and harder jobs will be staffed with dumber and dumber employees until the logical limit:

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This meeting.

situation: Dilbert gives a presentation with a pointer, using a chart showing a stick figure squeezed between two blocks and yelling. He explains that a tight labor market and complicated tasks will lead to ever-dumber employees being hired for harder jobs. In the last panel, the camera pans to the vacant, goofy-looking attendees at the table, revealing they are the 'logical limit.'
punchline: The people attending the meeting are themselves the extreme example of dumb employees staffing hard jobs, so Dilbert is insulting his audience.
summary: A presenter predicts that hiring shortages will fill demanding roles with ever less capable people, then gestures at the room full of blank-faced colleagues as proof.

file: 2001/2001-05-17_taking bribes_from vendors_feel guilty_getting paid_walk with cup_looks harder.gif
title: Bribes Versus Coffee Cup Walking

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you feel guilty about taking bribes from vendors?

transcript.speaker: Purchasing Manager
transcript.text: No. Do you feel guilty getting paid to walk around with a coffee cup?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I need a bigger cup so this looks harder.

situation: Wally stops by a coworker's cubicle holding his usual coffee mug and asks whether she feels guilty about accepting bribes from vendors. She shoots back by asking whether he feels guilty for being paid to just wander around with a coffee cup. Wally walks away and thinks about getting a bigger cup.
punchline: Wally is not bothered by the accusation of idleness and only wants to make his loafing look like more strenuous work, while the bribe-taker feels no guilt about her own corruption.
summary: A coworker calls out a bribe-taker, who retorts that the accuser's job is carrying a mug around, and he responds by planning a more impressive prop.

file: 2001/2001-09-14_negotiated contract_six weeks_double delivery time_devious weasel_simply incompetent.gif
title: Weasel or Incompetent? Here's a Clue

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've negotiated this contract for six weeks and today you double your delivery time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tell if you're an incredibly devious weasel or simply incompetent.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Here's a clue.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Poink

setting: Conference table in a contract negotiation meeting
situation: Dilbert, holding the contract, complains that after six weeks of negotiation the vendor has suddenly doubled the delivery time. He says he cannot tell whether the man is a devious weasel or just incompetent. The vendor offers a clue by pushing his nose up into a weasel snout.
punchline: The vendor answers Dilbert's either/or question by literally turning his nose into a weasel's snout, confirming he is the devious weasel.
summary: A negotiator caught changing terms at the last minute settles his counterpart's doubt by physically transforming into the animal he was accused of being.

file: 2001/2001-04-26_downsized_job functions_unimportant things_outsourced.gif
title: Dumping Unimportant Work After Downsizing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd downsized Ted and outsourced his important job functions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you to do all of his unimportant job functions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do we do unimportant things?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because we can!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that he has downsized Ted and outsourced Ted's important duties to another company. He then assigns all of Ted's leftover unimportant duties to Dilbert. Dilbert asks why they bother doing unimportant things, and the Boss answers that they do them simply because they can.
punchline: Management keeps pointless tasks alive with no justification other than that it is possible, while the valuable work gets shipped out and the worthless work lands on the remaining employee.
summary: After laying off a coworker and sending his valuable tasks elsewhere, the boss hands the leftover busywork to Dilbert with a shrug of a reason.

file: 2001/2001-09-13_accounting system_dysfunctional_meaningless_payroll exppenses_zero_management genius.gif
title: Broken Accounting Makes Boss Look Brilliant

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Your accounting system is so dysfunctional that the results are meaningless.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: How is it possible that no one has noticed?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've always wondered about that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) My payroll expenses are zero again. I'm a management genius.

setting: Office, at a computer and in the boss's office
situation: Two workers examine the company's accounting system on a computer and conclude that its output is meaningless, wondering why nobody has noticed. The Boss, sitting at his desk, is shown thinking that the system reports his payroll expenses as zero and takes this as proof of his brilliance.
punchline: The boss is oblivious to the fact that the broken accounting system is producing nonsense, and instead credits the impossible zero payroll figure to his own management skill.
summary: A pair of staffers discover the finance software is hopelessly faulty while the boss happily mistakes its bogus numbers for evidence of his genius.

file: 2001/2001-01-10_the motivation fairy_greatest challenge_get paid less_minimum wage_reimburse_travle_career path.gif
title: Motivation Fairy Meets Unmotivatable Employee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Motivation Fairy

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: You will be my greatest challenge.

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: I'll bet you get paid less than minimum wage and they don't reimburse you for travel.

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: Wings... so... heavy...

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: So, what kind of career path you got going?

situation: The Motivation Fairy, a tiny winged figure in a hairnet and pink outfit, visits a bald, bespectacled employee and declares he will be her greatest challenge. Instead of being motivated, he cheerfully points out that she is probably underpaid and not reimbursed for travel. His cynical questions drain her spirit until her wings feel too heavy to carry her.
punchline: The employee's blunt reminders about low pay and a dead-end job demotivate the Motivation Fairy herself, showing how unmotivating the workplace really is.
summary: A fairy sent to inspire a jaded worker is instead flattened by his sarcastic questions about her pay and prospects.

file: 2001/2001-02-16_nature lover_catch and release_torture fish_sounds bad.gif
title: Catch-and-Release Sounds Like Fish Torture

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm a nature lover. When I fish, I only do catch-and-release.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In other words, you torture fish for fun.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder why everything I do sounds bad when it's put in other words.

setting: Office break room with a coffee maker, then the Boss's office
situation: In the break room, the Boss boasts to Alice that he is a nature lover because he only practices catch-and-release fishing. Alice flatly rephrases this as torturing fish for fun. Alone at his desk, the Boss puzzles over why his activities always sound bad when restated.
punchline: The Boss is oblivious that Alice's blunt rewording isn't distorting his behavior but simply describing it accurately, which is why it always sounds bad.
summary: A self-satisfied boss brags about his gentle fishing hobby, gets an honest paraphrase from a coworker, and then wonders why he keeps getting that treatment.

file: 2001/2001-05-08_impersonate dead customer_large purchases_work_acting.gif
title: Impersonating a Dead Customer for Sales

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll impersonate our dead customer and make large purchases from us.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I've never done anything like this before.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called "work."

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Am I doing it right?

situation: The Boss hands a briefcase to a balding employee in glasses and instructs him to impersonate a dead customer and make large purchases from the company. The employee says he has never done anything like this before. The Boss replies that this is simply called work, and the employee anxiously asks whether he is doing it right.
punchline: The Boss treats fraudulent sales inflation as ordinary job duties, and the earnest employee sincerely wants to do the fraud correctly.
summary: A manager casually orders a subordinate to pose as a deceased client to fake big orders, and the compliant worker just hopes he's performing the scam properly.

file: 2001/2001-03-25_documents_emailed documents_end users_now work_poor arting_technical documents_performance rating_seventy hours_open attachments.gif
title: Boss Can't Open Emailed Attachments

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, I have to give you a performance rating of "poor" because you did no work this year.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: No work?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I wrote hundreds of technical documents this year!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I worked seventy hours a week!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I e-mailed every one of the documents to you...

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: ...with instructions to forward them with your approval to the end users.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That reminds me: I don't know how to open attachments.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Why didn't you tell me you never got my documents?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who are you?

setting: The Boss's office, with a final panel in a hallway or cubicle area
situation: The Boss tells Tina she is getting a poor performance rating because she did no work all year. Tina protests that she wrote hundreds of technical documents and e-mailed them all to him for approval, and the Boss admits he doesn't know how to open attachments. Tina then confronts Dilbert by mistake, and he doesn't know who she is.
punchline: The Boss's own technical incompetence, not Tina's work, caused the 'no work' rating, and Tina's frustrated confrontation of a stranger (Dilbert) shows how little anyone knows about her.
summary: A manager penalizes an employee for producing nothing, only to reveal he never read her output because he cannot open email attachments.

file: 2001/2001-01-11_motivation fairy_work hard_gain respect_peers_avoid stress_out live peers_hard work.gif
title: Motivation Fairy Discourages Hard Work

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Motivation Fairy

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: If you work hard, you will gain the respect of your peers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If I avoid the stress of hard work, I will out-live my peers.

transcript.speaker: Motivation Fairy
transcript.text: Hard work can kill me?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If you're lucky.

setting: An office, with a coworker at his desk holding a coffee cup
situation: The Motivation Fairy, a flying fairy in pink pajamas, tries to persuade a bald, bespectacled coworker that working hard will earn him his peers' respect. The coworker counters that avoiding stress would let him outlive them, and the fairy, realizing hard work could be deadly, reacts with alarm. The coworker replies that it would only kill her if she were lucky.
punchline: The coworker flips the motivational pitch by arguing that slacking off is healthier, then implies that dying from hard work would be a lucky escape from the misery of the job.
summary: A fairy's pep talk about earning respect backfires when her listener decides laziness will keep him alive longer than his overworked colleagues.

file: 2001/2001-02-09_flight_three am_slap head_uncross eyes_coffee_crazy_alice crazy_airplane_travel airfare.gif
title: Sleepless Alice Demands Coffee Hostage Exchange

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My flight didn't get in until three this morning.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Would you mind slapping the back of my head until my eyes uncross?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Pour all of your coffee in here and no one gets hurt.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Alice arrives at a meeting with wild, frazzled hair and tells Dilbert her flight got in at three in the morning. She asks him to slap the back of her head until her eyes uncross. When he stands holding up a notepad to do so, she then demands that everyone pour their coffee into her mug, threatening them while a nervous coworker holds his own cup.
punchline: Alice is so sleep-deprived from late-night business travel that she resorts to threatening her coworkers to get their coffee, using her usual aggression as a hostage-style demand.
summary: A badly jet-lagged Alice turns up to a meeting wild-haired and desperate, first begging for a head slap and then essentially holding her colleagues up for their coffee.

file: 2001/2001-12-31_morale boosting_great idea_first meeting.gif
title: Carol Sarcastically Declines Morale Event

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I want you to help me put together a morale boosting event.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Great idea. And after that maybe I can do CPR on a mummy and see if I can save its life.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you hear what I'm saying?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our first meeting will be Tuesday.

situation: The Boss asks his assistant Carol to help organize a morale boosting event. Carol responds with a sarcastic comparison, likening the task to performing CPR on a mummy. The Boss misses the sarcasm entirely and schedules their first planning meeting.
punchline: Carol's sarcasm, implying the task is hopeless and a waste of effort, goes completely over the oblivious Boss's head, and he treats it as agreement.
summary: An assistant mocks her manager's plan to lift morale by comparing it to reviving a corpse, but he hears only enthusiasm and books a meeting.

file: 2001/2001-07-16_life no purpose_scratch back_service to others_feel useful_found something_works.gif
title: Dogbert Finds Purpose Through Back-Scratching

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My life has no purpose.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Scratch my back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying the purpose of life is service to others?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It does make me feel useful.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think we both found something that works.

setting: Grassy bank beside a stream outdoors
situation: Dilbert sits by a stream and laments that his life has no purpose. Dogbert tells him to scratch his back, and Dilbert wonders if service to others is the meaning of life. Dogbert agrees, Dilbert scratches his back, and both declare it a satisfactory arrangement.
punchline: Dogbert cleverly exploits Dilbert's existential crisis to get a free back scratch, reframing his own self-interest as the meaning of life.
summary: A gloomy Dilbert is steered by his dog into believing that scratching the dog's back gives his existence meaning.

file: 2001/2001-02-22_praised alice_lying_stealing.no choice_promote_management.gif
title: Praise Addiction Forces Alice's Promotion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I inadvertently gave Alice verbal praise.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Is she addicted?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She's been lying and stealing to get more.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She leaves us no choice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to promote you to management.

situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the evil HR director, that he accidentally gave Alice some verbal praise. Catbert asks if she is addicted, and the Boss says she has been lying and stealing to get more. He then tells Alice he has no choice but to promote her to management.
punchline: Management treats the desire for recognition as a drug addiction and responds by promoting Alice, as if promotion were a punishment or a way to dispose of a problem employee, implying that managers are people who lie and steal for approval.
summary: A boss treats an employee's hunger for a little praise as a dangerous addiction and decides the only remedy is to make her a manager.

file: 2001/2001-07-24_evolution training_make it  thourgh_banana_peel_gorillas_neanderthal_monkeys_jungle naimals.gif
title: Evolution Training Banana Peel Slip

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Evolution Training

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Some of you will not make it through the class.

transcript.speaker: Animal student
transcript.text: May I move to a different seat?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure... Oops. Problem solved.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Carl, don't leave that where someone will slip on it.

characters: Man in white shirt and tie
setting: A classroom for animals at an evolution training session
situation: Dogbert teaches an evolution training class to an audience of apes, a giraffe and other creatures, and warns that some will not make it through. A student asks to move to a different seat and Dogbert agrees, but the student is now missing, apparently having been removed. Dogbert then scolds Carl, a banana peel dressed as a student, for leaving a peel where someone could slip on it.
punchline: Dogbert is literally enforcing survival of the fittest, eliminating a student with a banana peel, then feigns concern about safety while blaming Carl for the mess.
summary: An instructor at a class on natural selection quietly disposes of a complaining student and then calmly reprimands a colleague about the banana peel left lying around.

file: 2001/2001-12-13_creative design_design_build mock up_common materials_worst team memeber_ignore suggestions.gif
title: Ignoring Alice's Suggestions in Teambuilding

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Creative design

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Each team has one hour to design and build a mock-up using these common materials.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Doesn't this sort of exercise usually get dominated by the worst team member?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't worry. We can just ignore Alice's suggestions.

situation: A facilitator explains a creative design exercise where teams must build a mock-up in an hour using common materials. Dilbert asks whether the worst team member usually dominates such exercises. Wally reassures him that the team can simply ignore Alice's suggestions, while Alice stands right beside them.
punchline: Wally assumes Alice must be the worst team member and cheerfully says they'll ignore her, oblivious that she's standing right there and furious.
summary: A team-building exercise turns awkward when a worry about domineering teammates leads a coworker to casually dismiss the person standing next to him.

file: 2001/2001-12-17_serve food_homeless on christmas_extra hungry_one day_news crews arrive.gif
title: Starving the Homeless for Publicity

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm signing up volunteers to serve food to the homeless on Christmas Day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you know in advance that they'll be extra hungry on that one day?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Our P.R. firm makes sure they don't get fed for two days before the news crews arrive.

situation: Carol, holding a clipboard, tells Dilbert she is signing up volunteers to serve food to the homeless on Christmas Day. Dilbert wonders how the company can be sure the homeless will be especially hungry that day. Carol matter-of-factly reveals that the company's PR firm deliberately withholds food from them for two days before the news crews show up.
punchline: The company's charity photo-op is staged so cynically that its PR firm starves the homeless beforehand to make the volunteers' generosity look more dramatic on camera.
summary: A corporate holiday charity drive turns out to rely on a public relations firm deliberately keeping the needy hungry so the cameras get a better show.

file: 2001/2001-09-19_dogcart consults_create a strategy_increase market share_change_valuable advice.gif
title: Dogbert's Cheap Strategy Formula

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's easy to create a strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Write down everything you do, preceded by the phrase, "Increase our market share by..."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if we change what we do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Call me and I'll sell you some more valuable advice.

setting: The Boss's office, across his desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that creating a strategy is easy: just list everything the company already does and prefix each item with 'Increase our market share by...'. When the Boss asks what to do if the company wants to change what it does, Dogbert invites him to call back and buy further advice.
punchline: Dogbert's 'strategy' is a trivial relabeling of existing activities, and he exploits the Boss's obvious follow-up question as a chance to upsell more consulting.
summary: A consultant dog reduces corporate strategy to a fill-in-the-blank exercise and then monetizes the client's inevitable next question.

file: 2001/2001-02-10_all night flight_came to work_usual_jeopardize_missing work_park in lobby_out of it_disheveled.gif
title: Disheveled Employee Parks in Lobby

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My flight took all night but I still came to work on time as usual.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I didn't want to jeopardize the company by missing work.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: You're not allowed to park in the lobby.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Since when?!

situation: A wildly disheveled Carol, wearing a pink outfit and sporting enormous messy hair, tells the Boss that she came straight to work after an all-night flight so she wouldn't jeopardize the company. In the final panel a security guard tells her she isn't allowed to park in the lobby, which suggests she drove her car into the building, and she indignantly asks since when.
punchline: Carol is so sleep-deprived and dedicated to showing up that she drove her car right into the lobby, and she is indignant when told that's against the rules.
summary: A frazzled, jet-lagged worker boasts about her dedication to attendance, only for a guard to reveal she has parked her vehicle inside the building's entrance.

file: 2001/2001-08-31_parts department_give parts away_vicious cycle_reordering_brief customer survey_fill out.gif
title: Parts Counter Ends Reordering Cycle

transcript.speaker: Parts Clerk
transcript.text: We don't give out parts anymore.

transcript.speaker: Parts Clerk
transcript.text: We're trying to end the vicious cycle of reordering.

transcript.speaker: Parts Clerk
transcript.text: Would you mind filling out a brief survey of customer satisfaction?

situation: Dilbert goes to the parts counter to get a part, and the clerk announces that the department no longer hands out parts. He explains this is to stop the cycle of having to reorder stock. He then cheerfully asks Dilbert to fill out a customer satisfaction survey.
punchline: The parts department has defined its job as never giving out parts, then absurdly asks the frustrated customer to rate his satisfaction.
summary: A parts clerk refuses to hand over any parts to avoid restocking, then politely requests feedback on the service.
themes: missing the point of the job

file: 2001/2001-06-18_meeting_monday morning_travel all day_stealing life_reschedule_social plans_business.gif
title: Rescheduling Only for Social Plans

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told them you would be at the meeting on Monday morning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?? That means I have to travel all day Sunday. You're stealing my life!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then he said he'd reschedule if I had social plans.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ouch.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's home living room
situation: The Boss commits Dilbert to a Monday morning meeting, forcing him to spend all of Sunday traveling. Dilbert protests that his life is being stolen. At home on the couch with snacks and Dogbert, he recounts that the Boss offered to reschedule only if Dilbert had social plans.
punchline: The Boss's offer assumes Dilbert has no social life, which is painfully true as he sits alone at home eating snacks, and Dogbert's 'Ouch' confirms the insult.
summary: A boss's condescending offer to move a meeting only if his employee has a social life lands as a sting because the employee clearly has none.

file: 2001/2001-01-06_give away prodcut_for free_deinstall it_bill customers_consumer despaitations.gif
title: Free Product, Billed for Removal

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My plan is to give away our product for free.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll only bill customers who ask us to deinstall it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For once, those reports of consumer decapitations will work in our favor.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss announces a business plan of giving the product away for free. He then explains that customers will only be billed if they ask to have it uninstalled. He concludes that rumors of customers being decapitated by the product will finally help the company, since dead customers cannot request removal.
punchline: The Boss's plan only generates revenue from customers who survive to uninstall the product, so reports that the product kills its users are cheerfully treated as a business advantage.
summary: A manager pitches a free-product scheme with a fee for removal and gleefully notes that rumors of lethal side effects will keep the costs down.

file: 2001/2001-04-29_slump_make changes_management style_paternal_new management style_we hate employees_volunteer_nineties_kick off_kick intern_bent over.gif
title: New Management Style: Kicking Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our industry is in a slump. We need to make changes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our current management style could be described as paternal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new management style doesn't have a name yet.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ooh ooh! I have a suggestion.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: The new management style could be called "We hate our employees."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a volunteer to help with our "Back to the Nineties" kick-off.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How is this like the nineties?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop wiggling!

situation: The Boss tells a meeting that the industry is slumping and shows that the old management style was paternal, with a picture of a father giving a child ice cream. The new style shows a man being thrown through the air. Asok eagerly suggests naming it "We hate our employees," the Boss approves, then asks for a volunteer for a "Back to the Nineties" kick-off and ends up literally kicking Asok.
punchline: The Boss takes the honest label "We hate our employees" as a good idea and then literally kicks the volunteering intern as a "kick-off," showing that management really does mistreat its staff.
summary: A boss unveiling a harsher management philosophy gets an honest name suggestion from an eager intern, then rewards his volunteering with a literal boot to the backside.

file: 2001/2001-09-08_learn take risks_quitting company_someplace better_understand.gif
title: Boss Urges Risk, Alice Suggests Quitting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you have to learn how to take risks.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You mean like quitting this putrid company and going to work someplace better?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why doesn't anyone understand anything I say?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Three o'clock.

setting: The Boss's office, at a desk during a one-on-one conversation
situation: The Boss lectures Alice in his office, telling her she needs to learn to take risks. Alice responds that the riskiest thing she could do is quit the company and work somewhere better. The Boss then complains to Catbert that no one understands him, and Catbert answers with a non-sequitur about the time.
punchline: Alice understood the Boss perfectly and turned his advice against the company, while Catbert's irrelevant answer 'Three o'clock' mocks the Boss's complaint by showing he isn't actually listened to or answered meaningfully.
summary: A manager's pep talk about risk-taking backfires when his employee points out the obvious risk of leaving, leaving him baffled and answered only by a cat's random reply.

file: 2001/2001-08-14_customer service_serial number_pulverizing case_hammer_void warranty.gif
title: Smash Device for Serial Number

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Find the serial number by pulverizing the case with a hammer.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Are you sure this won't void my warranty?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's not always about you.

situation: Dogbert, working as a customer service rep wearing a headset, tells a caller to find the serial number by smashing the product's case with a hammer. The customer, hammer in hand, worries about voiding the warranty. Dogbert dismisses the concern as irrelevant to him.
punchline: The customer service rep gives absurdly destructive advice and shows no concern for the customer's welfare, dismissing the warranty worry with a deadpan brush-off.
summary: A support agent advises a caller to destroy his own device with a hammer, then waves off his worry about the consequences.

file: 2001/2001-12-29_hard work_nights_weekends_demand 10 percent.gif
title: Ten Percent Change to Guesswork

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, all of your hard work — the nights and the weekends — are finally paying off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We increased our five-year forecast of demand by ten percent!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You changed a wild guess by ten percent?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks to you!

situation: The Boss tells Alice that her nights and weekends of hard work have finally paid off. He explains that the result is a ten percent increase in the company's five-year demand forecast. Alice, her hair bristling, points out that this is just a wild guess that got tweaked, and the Boss cheerfully credits her anyway.
punchline: Alice's long hours produced nothing of substance, since the forecast was a wild guess to begin with and the Boss is celebrating an arbitrary ten percent bump as an achievement.
summary: A manager praises an exhausted employee for her overtime, only for it to emerge that her effort merely nudged an invented projection up a notch.

file: 2001/2001-08-23_mismatch_improve yourself_my level_gaining weight_terrible haircut_few teeth_wear stained clothes_tobacco.gif
title: Meeting Dilbert Halfway By Getting Worse

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: We're such a mismatch that I doubt you'll ever improve yourself all the way to my level.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Maybe I could meet you in the middle by gaining thirty pounds and getting a terrible haircut.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: ...Knock out a few teeth, wear stained clothes, chew tobacco...

setting: Outdoor grassy hillside with mountains in the background
situation: Dilbert is out with a woman who tells him they are such a mismatch that he could never rise to her level. She then suggests she could meet him halfway by making herself less attractive, and she sits with him on a hillside listing ever more unappealing changes she could make.
punchline: She insults Dilbert by implying she would have to become physically repulsive, with bad hair, missing teeth, stained clothes and tobacco chewing, just to be on his level.
summary: A date tells Dilbert she is far out of his league and offers to close the gap by deliberately making herself unattractive.

file: 2001/2001-12-16_work from home_know working_wearing uncomfortable hat_extremely uncomfortable.gif
title: Uncomfortable Hat Proves Home Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it okay if I work from home one day a week?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How would I know you were working?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How do you know I'm working when I'm here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you're here I know you're unhappy and that's the same thing as work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What if I invent a hideously uncomfortable hat to wear when I'm working at home?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well... that might be okay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But it has to be extremely uncomfortable or else it isn't work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hee hee! The joke's on him - it isn't that uncomfortable.

setting: The Boss's office, then Wally's home living room
situation: Wally asks his boss for permission to work from home one day a week. The boss says he can only judge work by how unhappy someone looks, so Wally proposes wearing a hideously uncomfortable hat at home as proof of suffering. The boss agrees, and in the last panel Wally relaxes in an armchair at home wearing a hat that isn't really uncomfortable.
punchline: Wally fools his boss, who equates misery with productivity, by wearing a hat that only appears uncomfortable while he lounges at home.
summary: A slacker talks his misery-measuring manager into letting him stay home by promising to wear a painful hat, then secretly enjoys a cushy day off.

file: 2001/2001-05-18_terrific conversationalit_write code_while you complain_embraced_date_end of date_kiss good night_hug_mean things_said.gif
title: Coding While He Complains Over Dinner

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thanks for taking me to dinner. You're a terrific conversationalist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With you it's easy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I discovered that I can write code in my head while you complain about your job all night.

setting: Outside a doorway at the end of a dinner date
situation: Dilbert and Alice stand at a door after a dinner date. Alice sincerely thanks Dilbert and calls him a terrific conversationalist, and he happily replies that talking to her is easy. As he moves in for a hug or kiss goodnight, she reveals she only tuned him out by writing code in her head while he complained about his job.
punchline: The compliment was really an insult: Dilbert's constant job complaining was so boring and one-sided that Alice treated it as background noise for doing her own programming work.
summary: A date ends with a warm thank-you that turns out to be a cutting reveal about how little attention was paid to the dinner talk.

file: 2001/2001-12-27_dogbert_eat for a day_fish_ugly hat_you're consultant_animals.gif
title: Dogbert's Twisted Fishing Proverb

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you give a man a fish he will eat for a day.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But if you teach a man to fish he will buy an ugly hat.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And if you talk about fish to a starving man then you're a consultant.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, sits across a table from The Boss and recites a variation of the 'give a man a fish' proverb. He first gives the standard line, then a silly twist about an ugly hat, and finally defines a consultant as someone who merely talks about fish to a starving man. The Boss listens impassively, holding a coffee mug.
punchline: Consultants offer only talk and no real help, yet get paid for it while the starving man gets nothing.
summary: Dogbert mangles a famous proverb to reveal that a consultant's contribution is conversation rather than food.

file: 2001/2001-03-01_unlock skull_management training_twist ears_moral compass_deactivate_leadership_working weekends_adjustng_dogbert.gif
title: Dogbert Deactivates Boss's Moral Compass

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Management training

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You twist the ears to unlock the skull.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Find the moral compass and deactivate it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The result is something called leadership.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're working weekends!

setting: Management training session, with Dogbert standing on a stool beside the Boss
situation: Dogbert, acting as a management trainer, demonstrates on the Boss by twisting his ears to unlock his skull and opening it up. He then switches off the Boss's moral compass inside. The Boss immediately becomes a ruthless 'leader' and orders his staff to work weekends.
punchline: Management training works by removing conscience, so becoming a 'leader' means gaining the ability to demand unreasonable overtime without guilt.
summary: A canine trainer opens up a manager's head and switches off his ethics, instantly producing a boss who casually demands weekend work.

file: 2001/2001-09-15_english_imcomprehensible_weseleze_sign something_lawyer_miss deadline_frat brother_legal.gif
title: Incomprehensible Contract Meets Devil Frat Brother

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, we negotiated this deal in English but your contract is incomprehensible weaseleze!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My only choices are to sign something I don't understand or get my lawyer involved and miss my deadline!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha! Now you're going to heck!

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: Are you hassling my frat brother?

situation: Dilbert complains to a man across the table that the contract he's been given is written in confusing legalese, even though the deal was negotiated in plain English. He explains he is stuck choosing between signing blindly or involving his lawyer and missing his deadline. He then gleefully tells the man he's going to hell, only for a devil in a red costume holding a giant spoon to appear and say the man is his frat brother.
punchline: Dilbert's gloating threat that the contract-writing weasel is going to hell backfires when the devil himself shows up and defends the man as a fellow fraternity member.
summary: After griping about a deliberately baffling contract, Dilbert wishes damnation on its author, only to have Satan appear and stand up for his fraternity buddy.
